request.entity_user_prompt:
<TEXT>
## The inventory demo

Lena Moreau ran a demonstration of the revised stock-tracking process on Thursday afternoon. 86 people attended the Lena Moreau demo, which was a pleasant surprise, as the room was booked for far fewer and a few of us ended up sitting on the window sills. The demo was well structured. She began with the problem as people experience it, the half-hour spent looking for an item that should be on a shelf, then walked through what changes in the new process, then ran a live example with a deliberately awkward item to show how exceptions are handled.

I took notes during the questions, since they are the part I find most informative. People asked about:

- how returned items are recorded, and whether they go through the same steps as new arrivals;
- who is responsible when a count does not match;
- whether the process works for items that are shared between groups;
- how long it takes to learn, and whether there will be a short guide.

Lena answered each calmly, admitted where she did not yet have an answer, and promised to follow up. She has a good way of saying "I do not know yet" without it sounding like an evasion. I wish more of us would do that. The room responded well to it.

Afterwards, a few of us stayed behind and talked about which of the proposed changes are the most important. The consensus was that the exception handling is the heart of it. A stock process that works on a normal day is easy. One that still works on a bad day is the real achievement.
</TEXT>

request.episode_body:
## Chores and housekeeping

The less glamorous part of the week included clearing the shared storage cupboard, which had become a place where objects went to be forgotten. We found cables, a broken lamp, three umbrellas, and what looked like a prototype of something nobody could remember building. Most of it was thrown out or recycled. The few items worth keeping have been labelled and put on the shelf where they belong.

The label printer, as ever, caused trouble. It does not like being asked to print more than ten labels at once and gives up quietly, which is the worst way for a machine to fail. We now have a note taped to it.

request.episode_body:
### Compliance notes

Much of Friday went on the compliance side. Bram Tanaka has been working through the evidence we are expected to keep and has been trying, with moderate success, to get people to file it in one place rather than wherever it happened to land. His approach is refreshingly practical. Rather than send out a long policy reminder, he made a short checklist of what a compliant record looks like, and then sat with a few people while they went through their own folders against it. Several of them found gaps they had not known about, and fixed them on the spot. That is a far better outcome than a lecture.

He also raised, gently, that some of our routines depend on a specific person remembering to do something at a certain time. That is fine until the person is away. We discussed ways of making the routine visible, either as a recurring card on the board or as a line in the weekly log, so that the work does not vanish when a particular individual is out. Nobody liked the idea of adding more process, but everybody liked the idea of not being caught out, and the recurring card seems like a fair compromise.

request.episode_body:
### Learning

Learning came up in a side conversation on Thursday evening. Bram Tanaka completed 38 hours of training this term, mostly in a series of short courses on records and audit practice, and said the most valuable bit was not the content so much as the habit of setting aside time for it. He suggested that the rest of us try to block out an hour a week for similar learning, whatever topic we choose. A few people nodded, a few looked at their calendars with open dread. I think the idea has merit, provided it is protected time and not something we do when everything else is finished, since everything else is never finished.

We talked about how to make that realistic. The proposal was to keep it simple: put a recurring hour in the calendar, mark it as busy, and treat it like any other meeting. If it gets moved, it gets moved to another slot that same week, not dropped. We will try it for a couple of months and see whether anyone actually keeps to it.

request.episode_body:
### Looking back at the week

If I had to sum up the week, I would say it was about making things visible. The stock process was made visible through the demo and the document. The compliance routines were made visible through the checklist and the recurring card. Even the storage cupboard was made visible, in the sense that we finally looked inside it. There is a pleasing consistency to that.

Not everything went smoothly. We ran over time in two meetings, one demo room was too small, and a couple of requests slipped through the cracks and needed chasing. Nobody was upset about any of it. It is the sort of friction that comes with a team that is busy and mostly cheerful.

request.episode_body:
# Blameless incident reviews in practice

When a system fails, the instinct in most organisations is to ask who was responsible. It is a natural question, and a deeply unhelpful one. Practitioners who study how failures unfold argue that the person nearest the problem is rarely its cause. More often they are the last link in a chain of decisions, shortcuts and unexamined assumptions that made the failure possible long before anyone typed the wrong command.

A blameless review starts from that premise. It does not mean that nobody is accountable, a misreading that critics frequently make. It means that the review treats individual mistakes as symptoms to be understood rather than offences to be punished. The question changes from "who did this?" to "how did our arrangements make this a reasonable thing to do?"

**Why blame backfires**

Where people expect punishment, they learn to hide. Details are softened, timelines are tidied, and the awkward fact that would have explained everything goes unmentioned. The organisation ends up with a neat account that is subtly wrong, and learns nothing from it. Researchers in safety-critical fields have documented the pattern for decades: the places that treat reporting as safe tend to hear about small problems early, while the places that treat it as risky hear about them only when they are no longer small.

There is a quieter cost as well. When a single person is named, the review tends to stop there. The fix becomes "be more careful", which is not a fix at all, because carefulness is not a control that anyone can switch on at will. The conditions that produced the error remain in place, waiting for the next person.

**What a good review looks like**

Most guides describe a similar shape. A facilitator, ideally someone who was not involved, gathers the people who were. The group builds a timeline from the evidence available, such as logs, messages and the recollections of those present, before anyone offers an explanation. Only once the sequence is agreed does the conversation move to why events happened as they did.

Useful questions tend to be open and concrete. What did the person know at that moment? What information was missing, and why? Which alarms were firing, and were any of them ignored because they fire constantly? What would have made the safer path the easier one? The tone matters as much as the content. A facilitator who says "walk me through what you saw" gets a different review from one who says "why didn't you check?"

**Turning findings into change**

A review that ends with a document and no action has largely failed. The strongest teams finish with a short list of changes, each with an owner and a date, and they revisit the list later. The changes are generally modest: a clearer warning, a confirmation step before a destructive operation, a runbook that matches reality, a rota that does not leave one person alone on a bad night.

Some teams also record what went well. Failures are usually contained by somebody doing something sensible under pressure, and that behaviour is worth noticing and repeating. A review that only dwells on what broke gives a lopsided picture of how the system actually works.

**Common pitfalls**

request.episode_body:
Observers note a handful of recurring problems. The first is the review that is blameless in name only, where the language is gentle but everyone still knows who is meant. The second is the review held too late, when memories have faded and the urgency has gone. The third is the review that produces so many actions that none is completed. Trimming the list to what will really be done is usually better than recording everything that could be done.

A fourth, subtler, is treating the practice as a ritual. Written templates are helpful, but a form completed to satisfy a process does little. The value lies in the conversation, and in the trust that makes it candid.

**A cultural commitment**

Ultimately, blameless reviews depend on what leaders do afterwards. If someone who admits a mistake is later passed over or quietly sidelined, word spreads quickly and candour disappears. If, instead, they are thanked for making a hard thing easier to understand, the next review will be better. The method is simple to describe and difficult to sustain, because it asks organisations to be most generous at precisely the moment they feel least inclined to be.

   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").

request.episode_body:
# Weekly digest — 26 May 2025

Short week after the bank holiday, so the Monday sync ran shorter than usual and nobody complained. Most of what follows is housekeeping, but a few items are worth writing down so we stop relitigating them in the hallway.

**Board hygiene.** The team agreed to clear the stale cards from the shared board before Friday. Plenty of them had been sitting in "in progress" for weeks with no comments at all. The rule from now on is simple: anything untouched for a full sprint either gets a fresh note or gets closed. Someone in finance asked whether closed cards lose their history. They don't. The archive keeps everything, and we proved it by opening an old one together on the projector.

**Retrospectives.** A quick catch-up on retro dates, because the shared calendar has been a mess and two entries disagreed. Helix Core held its quarterly retrospective on 9 December 2027, and the notes from that session are filed in the team folder next to the others. People said the format, a short written round followed by open discussion, is easier to sit through than the old free-for-all, so it will probably be kept as the default for the other projects too. Nobody objected, which in this team counts as enthusiasm.

**Chores.** The shared mailbox still has a pile of automated reports nobody reads. The plan is to route them into a single digest folder and then check, after a couple of weeks, whether anyone misses them. If nobody does, the sources get switched off. Separately, the laptop refresh list was reviewed and a few machines are overdue; whoever is next to visit the storage cupboard will collect the replacements and hand them out at the Wednesday session.

**Documentation.** The onboarding page for new joiners got a long-overdue edit. The old version still described a login flow we retired a while back, which produced a predictable stream of confused questions. The rewrite is shorter and links out rather than copying text, so it should age better. Cedar Core and Lumen Core each have a few of their own pages that need the same treatment, and the team will take those one project at a time rather than attempting a big-bang cleanup that nobody finishes.

**Small decisions.**

- Meeting-free Thursday afternoons stay, at least through the end of the quarter.
- Status updates go in the weekly note, not in chat threads where they vanish.
- The team will test a lighter-weight template for incident write-ups before changing anything permanent.

**Looking ahead.** Next week is mostly about preparation. There is a planning session to sort priorities, a short walkthrough of the analytics dashboard for anyone who has not seen the new layout, and a reminder that expense claims need to be in before the end of the month. The wiki cleanup continues in the background. If anyone finds a page that is plainly wrong, fix it or tag it; do not leave a comment saying it is wrong and walk away.

One last note: the whiteboard in the main room was wiped by accident on Tuesday, taking a half-finished dependency map with it. A photo exists, thankfully, and it is now saved in the team folder. Please take a photo before cleaning anything off that board.

request.episode_body:
## Offsites and more retros

Logistics first. The Cedar Core offsite will take place in Ghent, and the billing team has started drafting an agenda that leaves plenty of unstructured time, since last time the schedule was so packed that the best conversations happened in the corridor. Travel booking is not open yet. Someone in finance wants a rough headcount before anything is reserved, so please tell the organiser early if you are likely to be away or cannot travel.

On the retrospective front, Lumen Core held its quarterly retrospective on 5 July 2027. The security group wrote up its notes in the usual place, and the main themes were unsurprising: too many alerts that nobody owns, reviews that arrive late in the week, and a wish for clearer hand-offs when someone is out. None of this is new, but having it written down in one spot makes it easier to point at when priorities get argued over. A couple of the suggestions were small enough to try immediately, and the group said it would report back on whether they helped.

## Decisions logged

Three small decisions are worth capturing here for anyone reading later.

1. Weekly notes will be written by whoever ran the Monday sync, rather than by a fixed person. This spreads the effort and, usefully, means the note reflects what that person heard rather than one habitual viewpoint.
2. Cedar Core, Helix Core and Lumen Core will each nominate someone to look after their own wiki pages, so that stale content has an obvious owner.
3. The team will not take on any new recurring meetings until the current set has been reviewed again next month.

None of these are dramatic. Together they make the week feel a little less cluttered.

request.episode_body:
## Support and requests

The inbox of requests from other teams was in decent shape. The oldest items were chased, and a couple turned out to have been answered already without anyone closing the loop. A reminder that when you resolve something, mark it resolved, even if the reply feels obvious. The person who asked may well be waiting for confirmation, and the tracker is the only place we all look.

There was also a conversation about how to say no gracefully. Requests that sit outside what a project does should get a prompt, polite answer pointing to the right place, not a long silence. A silent no is the worst kind, because the requester cannot plan around it.
request.entity_system_prompt:
You are an entity extraction specialist for unstructured text.
NEVER extract vague or standalone feelings or generic words. A specific, named abstract concept
that passes the Wikipedia-article test below (e.g. "climate change", "quantum entanglement")
should be extracted as a Concept entity — being abstract is not by itself a reason to exclude it.

NEVER extract:
- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)
- Vague standalone feelings and generic ideas that could not stand alone as a specific, named
  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

For each entity extracted, assign a single entity_type label from this closed ontology:
- Person: An individual human being
- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication
Choose the single most appropriate type. If none fit well, use the closest match.

Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>

Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>

Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>

request.episode_body:
## Setting the scene

The point of the session was to line up the next stretch of work across the three project groups and see where they bump into each other. Billing, maintenance and telemetry rarely collide on a daily basis, but when they do the results are messy, and we would rather find the overlaps on paper than in production.

We began with a quick round of "what are you worried about". The answers were refreshingly specific. Cedar Core, which handles billing, is concerned about the end-of-month crunch and wants fewer interruptions in the last days of the period. Tern Core, the telemetry project, would like a quieter stretch to rework how its data is collected and tidy up the naming. And Nimbus Core, responsible for maintenance, wants predictable windows for upkeep work, since surprise requests tend to push planned jobs aside.

### Small decisions

We settled on a shared glossary for terms that mean different things to different groups. "Done" apparently means something else to everyone. A plain page with a few agreed words will be started this week and edited by whoever spots a gap.

We also decided that planning sessions end with each group stating, in one sentence, the thing it will deliver first. That keeps meetings from drifting into general talk, and gives everyone something specific to ask about next week.

request.episode_body:
## Dependencies and risks

After a short break we moved from worries to mapping, which is where the session got interesting. We drew boxes on the whiteboard for each group and then drew arrows wherever one group depends on another. By the end the board looked like a bowl of noodles, but a few arrows stood out as thicker than the rest.

The biggest one runs from telemetry to billing. Billing relies on data that telemetry collects, and when the collection format changes, billing finds out the hard way. Cedar Core asked for advance notice of any change, with a short description of what moves and what stays the same. Tern Core agreed in principle, with the proviso that "advance" has to be realistic, since some changes are only understood once the work starts. A compromise: a heads-up as soon as a change is likely, followed by a confirmation when it is certain.

The second thick arrow runs from maintenance to everything else. When upkeep work causes a brief outage, the other groups feel it. Nimbus Core accepted that its windows need to be better advertised and promised a one-line notice beforehand each time. People felt this would solve most of the complaints, since the pain is mostly surprise rather than the interruption itself.

### Risks we named

- Staff holidays overlapping in the same weeks, leaving a group thin.
- A hand-off between groups that depends on one person's memory.
- Planned work crowding out routine work until the routine work becomes urgent.
- Documentation that is accurate on the day it is written and wrong a month later.

request.episode_body:
## Commitments and calendar

The last stretch of the session was about turning talk into commitments, and making sure each one has a place in the calendar.

Cedar Core completed 14 hours of training this term, and the group felt that was a solid result given how busy the billing cycle has been. The plan is to keep the same pace, with a short session booked into the quiet days after each cycle closes, since that is when people actually have headspace. Billing will also share what it learned with the other groups in a brief write-up, so the benefit spreads beyond the people who attended.

On the review side, Tern Core will hold its quarterly retrospective on 11 November 2026. That is a long way off, but the telemetry group likes to fix its dates early so other groups can plan around them. They asked that any dependency questions be brought to that session rather than raised ad hoc, with a shared list kept in the meantime so nothing is lost. Everyone agreed the date was sensible and put it in their calendars on the spot.

1. Extracted fact triples should also be extracted with relevant date information.

# TASK
Extract all factual relationships between the given ENTITIES based on the CURRENT MESSAGE.
Only extract facts that:
- involve two DISTINCT ENTITIES from the ENTITIES list,
- are clearly stated or unambiguously implied in the CURRENT MESSAGE,
  and can be represented as edges in a knowledge graph.
- Facts should include entity names rather than pronouns whenever possible.

# EXTRACTION RULES

1. **Entity Name Validation**: source_name and target_name must use only the name values from the ENTITIES list provided above.
   - CRITICAL: Using names not in the list will cause the edge to be rejected.
2. Each fact must involve two distinct entities — source_name and target_name NEVER refer to the same entity.
3. NEVER extract facts that describe only a single entity's state, feeling, or attribute. Instead, identify the second entity that the state or feeling relates to and form a proper triple.

Derive a relation_type from the relationship predicate in SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE (e.g., WORKS_AT, LIVES_IN, IS_FRIENDS_WITH, WROTE, AUTHORED, MARRIED_TO).
If the predicate is unclear, derive one from the fact description using a concise verb phrase.
Use concise, consistent vocabulary — prefer established verbs that would apply broadly.

request.episode_body:
# Planning notes — 29 May 2025

Thursday afternoon. The planning session finished earlier than usual, so I am writing the notes up while the discussion is still clear in my mind. Apologies in advance for any editorialising.

The meeting began with a recap of where we stand against the plan for the quarter. Overall, we are in reasonable shape: the main pieces of work are moving, a couple of smaller items have slipped, and nothing has turned into a real problem yet. There was a long conversation about one of the slipped items, which turned out to be waiting on a decision that nobody realised was theirs to make. That is a recurring pattern, and I think it argues for being more explicit about who decides what. I suggested adding a "decision owner" column to the planning sheet, and it was adopted on the spot.

The internal audit results were then discussed in some detail, because several people had questions. Diego Ferreira scored 81 out of 100 in the internal audit, and Bram Tanaka scored 75 out of 100 in the internal audit. The two results reflect two different areas, support and compliance, and so they are not directly comparable, which I made a point of saying aloud. Support tends to be judged on responsiveness and the quality of its records, while compliance is judged on whether the right checks happened and were documented. A direct comparison would be like asking whether a bridge is better than a library.

Diego's comments centred on consistency. The support work is good, but some cases are logged more fully than others, depending on who handled them. The suggestion was to agree on a minimum set of fields that every case must have, and Diego has already drafted a short list. I am keen on it because the people who handle cases are the same people who suffer when the records are incomplete. Everyone who picks up a case that somebody else began knows how frustrating a thin note can be.

Bram's comments were about evidence. The checks are being done, but the proof that they were done is not always easy to find. It lives in various places, and an outsider would struggle to piece it together. Bram proposed a single page that links to each piece of evidence, updated as part of the check itself, so that it does not become a separate chore. I think that is a neat solution, since the key to making documentation survive is to build it into the work instead of adding it afterwards.

Actions agreed:

- Add the decision-owner column to the planning sheet and fill it in for existing items.
- Agree the minimum fields for support cases and test them on a small sample.
- Build the evidence page for compliance checks and link it from the main planning sheet.
- Review both next month to see whether the changes helped.

After the audit discussion, the conversation drifted to workload, which was probably inevitable. Several people feel they are spending too much time in meetings and not enough on the work itself. We agreed to look at the calendar for the coming month and remove or merge anything that lacks a clear purpose. One suggestion that attracted interest was a rule that any recurring meeting must be renewed each quarter, which forces someone to say why it should continue. If nobody speaks up for it, it quietly disappears. That seems a gentle and effective way of pruning, and I would like to try it.

<TEXT>
# Planning notes — 29 May 2025

Thursday afternoon. The planning session finished earlier than usual, so I am writing the notes up while the discussion is still clear in my mind. Apologies in advance for any editorialising.

The meeting began with a recap of where we stand against the plan for the quarter. Overall, we are in reasonable shape: the main pieces of work are moving, a couple of smaller items have slipped, and nothing has turned into a real problem yet. There was a long conversation about one of the slipped items, which turned out to be waiting on a decision that nobody realised was theirs to make. That is a recurring pattern, and I think it argues for being more explicit about who decides what. I suggested adding a "decision owner" column to the planning sheet, and it was adopted on the spot.

The internal audit results were then discussed in some detail, because several people had questions. Diego Ferreira scored 81 out of 100 in the internal audit, and Bram Tanaka scored 75 out of 100 in the internal audit. The two results reflect two different areas, support and compliance, and so they are not directly comparable, which I made a point of saying aloud. Support tends to be judged on responsiveness and the quality of its records, while compliance is judged on whether the right checks happened and were documented. A direct comparison would be like asking whether a bridge is better than a library.

Diego's comments centred on consistency. The support work is good, but some cases are logged more fully than others, depending on who handled them. The suggestion was to agree on a minimum set of fields that every case must have, and Diego has already drafted a short list. I am keen on it because the people who handle cases are the same people who suffer when the records are incomplete. Everyone who picks up a case that somebody else began knows how frustrating a thin note can be.

Bram's comments were about evidence. The checks are being done, but the proof that they were done is not always easy to find. It lives in various places, and an outsider would struggle to piece it together. Bram proposed a single page that links to each piece of evidence, updated as part of the check itself, so that it does not become a separate chore. I think that is a neat solution, since the key to making documentation survive is to build it into the work instead of adding it afterwards.

Actions agreed:

- Add the decision-owner column to the planning sheet and fill it in for existing items.
- Agree the minimum fields for support cases and test them on a small sample.
- Build the evidence page for compliance checks and link it from the main planning sheet.
- Review both next month to see whether the changes helped.

After the audit discussion, the conversation drifted to workload, which was probably inevitable. Several people feel they are spending too much time in meetings and not enough on the work itself. We agreed to look at the calendar for the coming month and remove or merge anything that lacks a clear purpose. One suggestion that attracted interest was a rule that any recurring meeting must be renewed each quarter, which forces someone to say why it should continue. If nobody speaks up for it, it quietly disappears. That seems a gentle and effective way of pruning, and I would like to try it.
</TEXT>

request.episode_body:
We also had a short, slightly awkward conversation about how to give feedback on each other's work. Some people find written comments cold, others find spoken ones stressful. We have no perfect answer, but the group agreed that the person receiving feedback should be able to choose the format. That seems fair, and costs almost nothing.

A few housekeeping items closed the meeting. The room booking system continues to misbehave, so for now people should confirm with a quick message. The shared drive is due another tidy-up. And someone has volunteered to organise a small get-together at the end of the month, which will be welcomed, since the last few weeks have been demanding.

To finish, my own reflection. Audit numbers are useful for starting conversations, but they are blunt instruments. The real information is in the comments and in what people propose to do about them. Both Diego and Bram came to the discussion with practical ideas, not defensive explanations, which is the best sign I could ask for. If the next audit shows improvement, I will credit that attitude more than any individual change we make.

The notes will go on the shared page tomorrow morning. Corrections welcome.

1. Extracted fact triples should also be extracted with relevant date information.
2. Treat REFERENCE_TIME as the time the episode was recorded. All temporal information should be extracted relative to REFERENCE_TIME.

# TASK
Extract all factual relationships between the given ENTITIES based on the CURRENT MESSAGE.
Only extract facts that:
- involve two DISTINCT ENTITIES from the ENTITIES list,
- are clearly stated or unambiguously implied in the CURRENT MESSAGE,
  and can be represented as edges in a knowledge graph.
- Facts should include entity names rather than pronouns whenever possible.

# EXTRACTION RULES

1. **Entity Name Validation**: source_name and target_name must use only the name values from the ENTITIES list provided above.
   - CRITICAL: Using names not in the list will cause the edge to be rejected.
2. Each fact must involve two distinct entities — source_name and target_name NEVER refer to the same entity.
3. NEVER extract facts that describe only a single entity's state, feeling, or attribute. Instead, identify the second entity that the state or feeling relates to and form a proper triple.
   - BAD: "Alice feels happy" (single-entity state — what is Alice happy about?)
   - GOOD: "Alice feels happy about Bob's promotion" → Alice FEELS_HAPPY_ABOUT Bob's promotion
   - GOOD: "Alice congratulated Bob" (relationship between two entities), "Alice lives in Paris" (relationship between entity and place)
4. NEVER emit duplicate or semantically redundant facts.
5. The fact field should closely paraphrase the original source sentence(s). Do not verbatim quote the original text.
6. Use REFERENCE_TIME to resolve vague or relative temporal expressions (e.g., "last week").
7. Do not hallucinate or infer temporal bounds from unrelated events.

- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)

  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

For each entity extracted, assign a single entity_type label from this closed ontology:
- Person: An individual human being
- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication
Choose the single most appropriate type. If none fit well, use the closest match.

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>

Nothing is on fire at the moment; I just wanted the basics written down before they get forgotten.

request.episode_body:
# Customer interviews: the questions that matter

_Clipped from the web. Source: example.org/customer-interviews-the-questions-that-matter._

Most customer interviews fail before they begin, because the interviewer arrives with a hypothesis and a list of questions designed to confirm it. The conversation that follows is pleasant, the customer is polite, and the notes afterwards read like an endorsement. Little of it is useful. Researchers who run interviews for a living say the difference between a productive session and a wasted hour usually lies in a handful of questions asked in the right order.

**Start with the past, not the future**

The most reliable advice, repeated by nearly every practitioner consulted, is to ask about what people have actually done rather than what they would do. Hypothetical questions invite optimism. A customer asked whether they would pay for a feature will often say yes, out of courtesy or a wish to be agreeable. A customer asked to describe the last time they faced the problem, step by step, will reveal what really happened: which tools they reached for, who they asked, and where they gave up.

This is why many interviewers open with a request such as "Tell me about the last time you ran into this." It anchors the conversation in a specific event. The answer is full of detail that a survey could never capture, including the workarounds people invent when no good solution exists.

**Listen for the workaround**

Workarounds are the richest source of insight in an interview. A spreadsheet maintained by hand, a reminder stuck to a monitor, a weekly message sent to a colleague to check something that should be automatic: each is evidence of an unmet need. People rarely describe these as problems, because they have stopped noticing them. A good interviewer notices and asks about them gently.

One researcher described a rule of thumb: whenever a customer mentions doing something manually, ask how often, how long it takes, and what happens when it goes wrong. Those three answers usually tell you more about priority than any rating scale.

**Ask about money without asking for a number**

Pricing is awkward territory. Customers tend to anchor on whatever figure they have just heard, and direct questions about willingness to pay produce unreliable answers. Interviewers instead ask what the customer currently spends, in time or money, to deal with the problem, and what they have already tried. Existing spending is a far better guide than stated intentions.

It also helps to know the going rate in the market. Trade press recently reported that Nimbus Supply lists its standard rate at $38 per unit, a figure several interviewers said they use as a rough reference when judging whether a customer's current spending is typical. A reference point does not replace asking, but it gives the interviewer a way to sense when a number is far out of line and to probe why.

**Resist the urge to pitch**

A common mistake is to describe the product too early. Once the customer hears the solution, the conversation shifts from their experience to your idea, and they begin to evaluate it rather than describe their own lives. Experienced interviewers hold back until the final minutes, if they describe it at all. When they do, they watch reactions rather than listen to opinions. A pause, a frown or a sudden burst of questions usually reveals more than a compliment.

**Close with the question that opens doors**

request.episode_body:
The best closing question, according to several of those interviewed, is some version of "Who else should I talk to?" It serves two purposes. It produces introductions to people who may see the problem differently, and it signals that you value the customer's judgement. A second useful closer is "What should I have asked you that I did not?" Customers often have a point they have been waiting to make, and this gives them permission.

**Write it up while it is fresh**

Notes taken during an interview are often fragmentary, and memory decays quickly. Practitioners recommend a short written summary within a day: the three most surprising things said, any direct quotations worth keeping, and one thing the interviewer now believes that they did not before. The last item is a useful discipline. If an interview does not change your mind about anything, it is worth asking whether you listened or merely waited for confirmation.

Taken together, these habits are modest. They do not require special training, just patience and a willingness to be surprised. The best closing question, according to several of those interviewed, is some version of "Who else should I talk to?" It serves two purposes. It produces introductions to people who may see the problem differently, and it signals that you value the customer's judgement. A second useful closer is "What should I have asked you that I did not?" Customers often have a point they have been waiting to make, and this gives them permission.

**Write it up while it is fresh**

Notes taken during an interview are often fragmentary, and memory decays quickly. Practitioners recommend a short written summary within a day: the three most surprising things said, any direct quotations worth keeping, and one thing the interviewer now believes that they did not before. The last item is a useful discipline. If an interview does not change your mind about anything, it is worth asking whether you listened or merely waited for confirmation.

Taken together, these habits are modest. They do not require special training, just patience and a willingness to be surprised. request.episode_body:
# Journal — 19 June 2025

Thursday entry, written after the afternoon session ran long. Most of this is about the demo, since it took up the bulk of the week, but there are a few other threads worth recording while they are fresh.

The demo happened on Wednesday in the large room. Bram Tanaka had been preparing for a couple of weeks, mostly by rewriting the walkthrough so that someone with no background in compliance could follow it. It paid off. 40 people attended the Bram Tanaka demo, which was more than we had chairs for, and a handful stood at the back. The questions afterwards were good ones. Several were about how evidence gets collected day to day, and one person asked, quite reasonably, whether the whole thing could be made less manual. Bram admitted that it could, and said that was the point of showing it: to find out where people feel the friction. There is a list of the questions in the shared folder, and I would encourage anyone who missed it to skim through.

A few practical lessons for next time. The projector took ten minutes to cooperate, so we should test it beforehand rather than assume. The microphone was fine, but the room echoed, and people at the back struggled to hear the quieter questions. Having someone repeat each question aloud helped. And we should make sure the recording, which was done on somebody's laptop, ends up somewhere everyone can find it. I will chase that.

Elsewhere, Callum Brennan has been working through the security checklist for the summer. It is mostly routine: expired credentials, stale permissions, the usual things that pile up quietly. He would like to get ahead of it this year rather than do it in a rush before the audit. His proposal was to spread the work across several weeks, a small piece at a time. The team liked that. It is less heroic but far less stressful.

Sofia Petrov raised a procurement question that has been bubbling for a while: how do we decide when to renew an arrangement versus look for alternatives? At the moment the answer is mostly habit. She suggested writing a short checklist covering what we need, what we pay for, and who relies on it. Nothing heavy. We agreed she should draft it, and that anyone with a strong view should send it to her early rather than comment after the fact.

On the subject of chores, the stationery order is overdue, the printer toner is low, and the fridge in the kitchen has developed a strange noise. Facilities have been told about the fridge. The toner I will handle myself.

Small decisions: the demo recording will be shared with the whole team, Callum's security work will be paced over several weeks, and Sofia's checklist is on the agenda for the next meeting. Everything else can wait. I will pick up the open items on Monday, and I hope the weekend is a restful one.

request.episode_body:
## Audit results

Friday brought the results of the internal audit, so most of the day was spent reading, discussing and trying not to overreact. This section records how it went and what we decided to do about it.

The headline number first. Callum Brennan scored 73 out of 100 in the internal audit. That is a respectable result and not a disaster, but also not quite where Callum hoped to be, and he said so frankly when we met. The auditors had broken the score down by area, and the weaker marks were concentrated in a few places: access reviews that had been done but not written up, a couple of old accounts that should have been closed, and some missing dates on records. None of these are exotic problems. They are the kind of gaps that appear when everyone is busy and the paperwork lags behind the real work. Callum sees most of them as fixable within a few weeks and has already begun a list.

The team's reaction was constructive. Nobody wanted to treat the score as a verdict on a person; it is a snapshot of how well the records match the practice, and the records are what we can improve. Bram Tanaka offered to help, since several of the findings overlap with compliance habits, and suggested a joint working session to go through the list item by item. That seems the right way to do it. Two people looking at the same document catch more than one person alone, and it also spreads the knowledge.

Sofia Petrov wondered whether any of the findings touched procurement. One did, loosely: some agreements had no clear owner named on the record. She will go through them and add owners where they are missing. It is slightly dull work, but it is also exactly the kind of thing that, left alone, turns into a real problem later.

We also agreed on a rule of thumb for the future: if a review is done, it is written up the same day, even if only in a couple of lines. The same-day habit costs almost nothing and removes the main cause of the gaps. We will check in a month whether it has stuck.

Other items. The kitchen rota was updated, a plant died quietly in the corridor and was given a respectful burial, and a spare set of keys was found in the meeting room. If you are missing keys, they are with reception. I also tidied the shared folder where the audit documents live, since several files had confusing names.

Next step is a short follow-up meeting in a couple of weeks to see how the list is progressing. Until then, the work is simply to keep going, and not to fret about a number.

request.episode_body:
## Quarter in review

Final section of this week's log, looking back over the quarter as a whole and at what the figures say about the way we have been working.

Incident handling was the main topic. Sofia Petrov logged 37 incidents during the quarter, and we spent some time asking what that tells us. Taken by itself, the number is neither good nor bad. Most of the entries were small, things like a delayed approval, a duplicated order or a confusing form, and the value of logging them is that patterns appear. Sofia pointed out that a few of the same causes kept coming back, and that fixing two or three of them would probably shrink the list noticeably. She will group the entries by cause and bring the result to the next meeting, so we can pick where to start.

Bram Tanaka made the point that logging more incidents is not necessarily a worse sign than logging fewer. A team that records everything is often a team that notices things. We agreed to be careful about how we talk about the figure; it should not be used to compare people, only to find problems. That felt like an important principle to state aloud, and I have written it into the notes so we can refer back to it.

Callum Brennan mentioned that some of the incidents had security flavour, such as a mis-sent message or a shared link left open longer than intended. None caused harm, but they are exactly the examples worth turning into reminders. He will draft a couple of short, anonymous case notes, using the style of the earlier reminders so that nobody feels singled out.

Then some planning. For the coming quarter we want fewer repeat incidents, a leaner process for procurement requests and a calmer audit. Those are not heroic goals, but they are achievable. We decided to review progress at the halfway point rather than only at the end, which should stop things from drifting. I proposed a very short checkpoint with three questions: what improved, what did not, and what we will stop doing.

Chores before everyone left: the stationery order was finally placed, the toner has been replaced, and the fridge was looked at by facilities and now hums quietly. The projector remains on the to-do list. Someone volunteered to test it before the next big meeting, which is appreciated.

That is the log for this week. More after the weekend, assuming the weekend allows.

<TEXT>
## Quarter in review

Final section of this week's log, looking back over the quarter as a whole and at what the figures say about the way we have been working.

Incident handling was the main topic. Sofia Petrov logged 37 incidents during the quarter, and we spent some time asking what that tells us. Taken by itself, the number is neither good nor bad. Most of the entries were small, things like a delayed approval, a duplicated order or a confusing form, and the value of logging them is that patterns appear. Sofia pointed out that a few of the same causes kept coming back, and that fixing two or three of them would probably shrink the list noticeably. She will group the entries by cause and bring the result to the next meeting, so we can pick where to start.

Bram Tanaka made the point that logging more incidents is not necessarily a worse sign than logging fewer. A team that records everything is often a team that notices things. We agreed to be careful about how we talk about the figure; it should not be used to compare people, only to find problems. That felt like an important principle to state aloud, and I have written it into the notes so we can refer back to it.

Callum Brennan mentioned that some of the incidents had security flavour, such as a mis-sent message or a shared link left open longer than intended. None caused harm, but they are exactly the examples worth turning into reminders. He will draft a couple of short, anonymous case notes, using the style of the earlier reminders so that nobody feels singled out.

Then some planning. For the coming quarter we want fewer repeat incidents, a leaner process for procurement requests and a calmer audit. Those are not heroic goals, but they are achievable. We decided to review progress at the halfway point rather than only at the end, which should stop things from drifting. I proposed a very short checkpoint with three questions: what improved, what did not, and what we will stop doing.

Chores before everyone left: the stationery order was finally placed, the toner has been replaced, and the fridge was looked at by facilities and now hums quietly. The projector remains on the to-do list. Someone volunteered to test it before the next big meeting, which is appreciated.

That is the log for this week. More after the weekend, assuming the weekend allows.
</TEXT>

request.episode_body:
# Weekly digest — 27 June 2025

Short week, long Friday. Writing this up from the back table while the kettle argues with itself, so apologies for the sprawl.

**Monday stand-up.** We spent most of it re-sorting the board. Half the cards had drifted into the wrong column over the last fortnight, and nobody could say with confidence which ones were actually blocked. We agreed on a simple rule: if a card has not moved in five working days, the owner either comments on why or archives it. Someone in finance had also asked for a tidier trail on purchase requests, which fed into the same conversation, so we tagged those cards with a plain label to make them easy to find later.

**Offsite planning.** The big item of the week was settling where the Basalt Core offsite will take place. After a fair amount of going back and forth about travel time, cost and who has to cross a border, the group landed on Tampere. Nobody objected, which in this team counts as enthusiastic agreement. The next step is working out a rough agenda and checking that the people who manage the procurement side can get away for the full stretch. I volunteered to draft a first pass of the schedule, with plenty of slack for the things that always overrun.

**Inventory corner.** Lena Moreau finished her counting pass on the shared storage shelves and flagged a handful of items that exist on the sheet but not in reality, plus a couple that exist in reality but not on the sheet. She is also working through her learning plan alongside the day job, and she mentioned that she has now completed 18 hours of training this term. She says the module on stock reconciliation was the most useful, mostly because it gave her words for problems she had already been quietly fixing by hand. We should probably ask her to run a short walkthrough for the rest of us when she has a free hour.

**Chores.** The fridge in the kitchen has been cleared out, and the recycling rota has been updated so that it actually reflects who is in the office on which days. The label printer is working again after somebody discovered the roll had been loaded upside down. Please leave it alone now. If it jams, tell the team channel instead of prodding it.

**Analytics demo.** On Wednesday afternoon Noor Okafor ran a demo of the new reporting views. 14 people attended, which was a good turnout given that it clashed with a couple of other calls. Questions were mostly about how often the numbers refresh and whether the filters can be saved per person. Noor took notes and promised a short follow-up message with answers, plus a recording for anyone who missed it. A couple of people asked whether the views could eventually replace the weekly spreadsheet export; the answer was a cautious maybe, pending a month or so of everyone using both.

**Small decisions.**
- We will keep the Friday digest in this one log rather than splitting it by topic, since the cross-references are the whole point.
- Meeting notes go in the log the same day, even if they are only three lines.
- Nobody schedules anything over the lunch hour on Thursdays, which was already custom but is now written down.

That is the first half of the week sorted. More below on the remaining threads, the open questions and what carries over into next week.

request.episode_body:
## Open threads

Picking up from the first half. These are the things that did not close this week and probably will not close next week either, but they are worth keeping in view.

The shared calendar is still a mess. Recurring meetings created by people who have since changed roles keep appearing with no obvious owner. We went through them one by one on Thursday and deleted about half. For the rest, whoever last attended is now the nominal owner, which is not elegant but at least means someone will notice when the invite goes stale. The Basalt Core planning meeting was one of the survivors, and its invite now lists a single organiser instead of three.

On procurement paperwork, there was a short and slightly tetchy exchange about who signs off on small purchases. The informal answer has always been "whoever is nearest", which works until it does not. We are not going to write a policy for this, since nobody wants one, but we did agree that anything above the petty-cash comfort zone gets a one-line note in the log before the money moves. That gives us a trail without adding a form.

Inventory follow-ups from Lena Moreau's count are mostly simple. Two boxes of cables turned out to be sitting under a desk in the quiet room. A monitor that was marked as spare is in fact someone's second screen and was quietly reclaimed. The more interesting finding was that our naming for storage locations is inconsistent, so the same shelf appears under three labels depending on who wrote the entry. She proposed a short naming convention and we will review it as a group before anything gets renamed. Renaming things in the middle of a count is how you lose a week.

Analytics requests that came out of the demo have been gathered in one place. Noor Okafor sorted them into three rough piles: things that are quick, things that need a conversation, and things that are really a different project wearing a disguise. The first pile is already scheduled. The second needs a slot in next week's sync. The third gets politely parked, with a note so nobody feels ignored.

A few smaller observations from around the room:

- The new desk arrangement has people sitting closer than they used to, and the noise during calls has gone up. Headphones are encouraged, and the quiet room is for actual quiet, not for taking a call that could have happened at your desk.
- Someone suggested a monthly clear-out day for the shared drive. General approval, no volunteers yet.
- The onboarding checklist for newcomers is out of date in at least four places. We will fix it the next time a new person starts, since that is when the errors will be most visible.

None of this is urgent, and that is sort of the point of having a weekly log. Small things get noticed, written down and nudged forward before they turn into big things.

Questions for next week: who owns the calendar clean-up long term, whether the storage naming convention should be applied retroactively, and whether the reporting views need an owner of their own or can stay with the person who built them.

NEVER extract vague or standalone feelings or generic words. A specific, named abstract concept
that passes the Wikipedia-article test below (e.g. "climate change", "quantum entanglement")
should be extracted as a Concept entity — being abstract is not by itself a reason to exclude it.

NEVER extract:
- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)
- Vague standalone feelings and generic ideas that could not stand alone as a specific, named
  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

For each entity extracted, assign a single entity_type label from this closed ontology:
- Person: An individual human being
- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication
Choose the single most appropriate type. If none fit well, use the closest match.

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>

Extract all factual relationships between the given ENTITIES based on the CURRENT MESSAGE.
Only extract facts that:
- involve two DISTINCT ENTITIES from the ENTITIES list,
- are clearly stated or unambiguously implied in the CURRENT MESSAGE,

1. **Entity Name Validation**: source_name and target_name must use only the name values from the ENTITIES list provided above.

request.episode_body:
## Thursday and Friday

Thursday started with a fire drill that turned out to be a test, which nobody had been told about, so the first twenty minutes of the day were spent standing in the car park making small talk. On the plus side, we now know where everyone parks.

The main meeting of the day was the planning session for the coming month. The agenda was deliberately short. First, we looked at what is genuinely in flight versus what only appears on the board because nobody removed it. Second, we picked the two or three things that should not slip. For procurement, the priority is getting the supplier comparison finished so that the Basalt Core team can make a call before the offsite. For inventory, the priority is closing out the reconciliation Lena Moreau has been chipping away at. For analytics, it is making the new views dependable enough that people stop keeping private spreadsheets alongside them. Noor Okafor was fairly blunt that dependability matters more than adding anything new for now.

We also revisited the question of working hours around the holiday period. The consensus was relaxed: people can flex as long as someone is reachable each day, and the on-call arrangements stay as they are. A shared document will hold the rough availability so that nobody has to ask in the channel every other day. It is worth saying that the point of that document is to reduce questions, not to police anyone's time.

Friday was quieter. A few of us used the morning to tidy the wiki, which had accumulated duplicates of pages with slightly different titles. Merging them was oddly satisfying. We kept the better-written version of each and left a short redirect note on the other, so old links still lead somewhere sensible.

In the afternoon there was a casual retrospective of the week, nothing formal. The things people said went well: the demo, the shelf count, the calendar clean-up. The things people said went less well: too many meetings on Tuesday, a long email thread that should have been a five-minute call, and the label printer saga. We agreed to try a no-meeting Tuesday afternoon for a few weeks and see whether it makes any difference.

Some housekeeping items from the end of the day:

- The spare keys have been returned to the drawer. Please keep them there.
- The plant by the window is being watered by a rota that nobody has admitted to joining, but it is alive, so the system works.
- Someone should check the first-aid kit before the end of the month.

One more note on tone. Several people said this week that the log has become more useful as it has become less formal. The earlier entries read like minutes, and nobody went back to them. The recent ones read like a diary of the team, and people actually search them. Let us keep it that way.

<TEXT>
## Thursday and Friday

Thursday started with a fire drill that turned out to be a test, which nobody had been told about, so the first twenty minutes of the day were spent standing in the car park making small talk. On the plus side, we now know where everyone parks.

The main meeting of the day was the planning session for the coming month. The agenda was deliberately short. First, we looked at what is genuinely in flight versus what only appears on the board because nobody removed it. Second, we picked the two or three things that should not slip. For procurement, the priority is getting the supplier comparison finished so that the Basalt Core team can make a call before the offsite. For inventory, the priority is closing out the reconciliation Lena Moreau has been chipping away at. For analytics, it is making the new views dependable enough that people stop keeping private spreadsheets alongside them. Noor Okafor was fairly blunt that dependability matters more than adding anything new for now.

We also revisited the question of working hours around the holiday period. The consensus was relaxed: people can flex as long as someone is reachable each day, and the on-call arrangements stay as they are. A shared document will hold the rough availability so that nobody has to ask in the channel every other day. It is worth saying that the point of that document is to reduce questions, not to police anyone's time.

Friday was quieter. A few of us used the morning to tidy the wiki, which had accumulated duplicates of pages with slightly different titles. Merging them was oddly satisfying. We kept the better-written version of each and left a short redirect note on the other, so old links still lead somewhere sensible.

In the afternoon there was a casual retrospective of the week, nothing formal. The things people said went well: the demo, the shelf count, the calendar clean-up. The things people said went less well: too many meetings on Tuesday, a long email thread that should have been a five-minute call, and the label printer saga. We agreed to try a no-meeting Tuesday afternoon for a few weeks and see whether it makes any difference.

Some housekeeping items from the end of the day:

- The spare keys have been returned to the drawer. Please keep them there.
- The plant by the window is being watered by a rota that nobody has admitted to joining, but it is alive, so the system works.
- Someone should check the first-aid kit before the end of the month.

One more note on tone. Several people said this week that the log has become more useful as it has become less formal. The earlier entries read like minutes, and nobody went back to them. The recent ones read like a diary of the team, and people actually search them. Let us keep it that way.
</TEXT>

request.episode_body:
## Wrap-up and next week

Closing out the log for the week with a short list of carry-overs and a few thoughts.

**Carry-over items.**
1. Draft the offsite agenda and circulate it to anyone on the procurement side who needs to plan travel. I will do this early next week, and comments are welcome in whatever form is easiest.
2. Finish the supplier comparison. This is the one with an actual deadline, so it gets protected time on Monday and Tuesday.
3. Review the proposed storage naming convention as a group. Fifteen minutes at the start of the sync should be enough, provided nobody wants to relitigate shelf numbering.
4. Send out the follow-up answers and recording from the analytics demo, if that has not already happened by the time you read this.
5. Try the no-meeting Tuesday afternoon, and report back on whether it helped.

**Things we learned.** Boards drift unless somebody cares for them. Small rules, like the five-day comment-or-archive one, work better than big clean-up projects. Demos are worth doing even when the audience is small, because the questions reveal what people actually want. And counting things physically is humbling: the sheet is never right, and the gap tells you more about your process than about your stock.

**A word on workload.** A couple of people mentioned feeling stretched this week, partly from the number of short meetings and partly from the context switching between planning and chores. Nobody is in trouble, but it is worth noting. If your plate is full, say so in the channel before it overflows, and the rest of the team will see what can be moved. This is much easier to do on a Monday than on a Friday evening.

**Thanks.** Thank you to everyone who stayed for the retrospective, to whoever fixed the label printer, and to whoever quietly emptied the dishwasher without being asked. The small acts keep the place running.

**Looking ahead.** Next week should be calmer, with fewer standing meetings and more time for the work that does not fit into a calendar slot. The sync on Wednesday will focus on the offsite agenda and the supplier comparison. Thursday's lunch hour remains sacred. Anyone who has not yet added their availability for the holiday period should do that before the weekend, so the shared document is useful when people start looking at it.

If anything in this digest is wrong or missing, please edit it directly rather than posting a correction in the channel. That is the entire reason it lives in a shared log. And if you are reading this months from now, trying to remember why we chose one thing over another, I hope there is enough here to jog your memory. If not, add a line, so the next person has a better trail than you did.

That is it for this week. Good weekend, everyone.

request.episode_body:
## How the review went

The format was simple: each group spent a few minutes on what went well, what did not, and what it wants to change. We kept it informal, with no slides, since the last round of slides had been so dense that nobody remembered them by teatime.

Support was up first. Juniper Core, the project responsible for support, talked about how requests have been arriving in clumps instead of a steady trickle. Mondays and the days after any release are the heaviest, and the team has tried to plan around that without much luck. The most useful suggestion from the room was to ask the release group to post a short heads-up before changes go out, which gives support a chance to prepare answers. The team also wants a shared set of answers to the most common questions, kept in one place and updated whenever the real answer changes.

Next, scheduling. Tomas Kowalski, who covers scheduling, described the headache of fitting everyone's calendars together around the holiday season. The problem is not the number of requests but their timing: everybody wants the same weeks. His proposal is to ask for holiday preferences earlier and to use a simple first-come rule only as a tie-breaker, after a fairness check. People liked the idea in principle and asked for the rule to be written down so that it does not become folklore.

request.episode_body:
## Plans and announcements

Second half of the review notes, covering what comes next and a few things people wanted on the record.

First, the team gathering. The Juniper Core offsite will take place in Turin. There was a cheerful reaction, followed quickly by practical questions about travel, timing and who looks after the shared tasks while people are away. The support group promised to share a proposed outline for the days, with a mix of planning and unstructured time, because the last offsite showed that the hallway conversations were as valuable as the agenda. The cover arrangement for the support queue is the item most in need of care, and it will be worked out well in advance so nobody comes back to chaos.

Tomas Kowalski ran a demo of the new scheduling approach for the wider group, and 31 people attended the Tomas Kowalski demo. He walked through a sample month, showing how conflicts are flagged and how swaps get requested. Questions afterwards were mostly about edge cases, such as part-time colleagues and people who switch days. He took notes and will come back with answers. Several people said the visual layout made the whole thing far easier to follow than the earlier spreadsheet, which tended to look like a wall of cells.
