request.episode_body:
# Review notes — 6 August 2025

Review notes for the week, assembled from my scribbles and a couple of messages in the log. The weather has turned hot, the office fan has been commandeered, and the mood in the room is the sort of mildly sticky good humour that comes with a quiet August.

The headline item was the internal audit. Tern Core scored 92 out of 100 in the internal audit. The telemetry group were pleased, though restrained about it; the people most closely involved pointed out that the missing points were in areas they knew about and had already planned to improve, mostly around keeping some of the older records in a consistent format. The auditors apparently commented that the overall discipline was strong and the documentation easy to follow. I would pass along the credit to everyone who has been quietly keeping the paperwork in order for the past year. It is the kind of work nobody notices until an audit appears, at which point it is the only thing that matters.

A reflection on what made the difference, since several groups asked. The telemetry team did not do anything dramatic. They wrote down what they do, they kept the writing current, and they reviewed it on a regular schedule. When someone changed a process they changed the page too, in the same sitting. It is almost embarrassing how simple it is. The only real cost is the habit, and the habit is built by repetition. Other groups listened closely, and I expect a few of them to try the same approach.

From the security side, with Lumen Core, there was a status update about the ongoing review of access and permissions. It is a slow job, because each area needs to be checked by someone who understands it. The group is working through them in a sensible order and keeping a simple list of what has been looked at. They would like help from other teams on the areas where the knowledge sits outside the security group, and asked that people answer the questions promptly when they arrive. A day or two of delay on each one adds up when there are many.

Other items of business:

- The planning for the autumn is beginning. We agreed to hold a short session in the coming weeks to collect ideas and then narrow them down. The instruction was to bring one thing you want to start and one you want to stop.
- The shared calendar still has a few stale entries. A reminder to tidy your own.
- The monitoring dashboards were reviewed and a few unused panels were removed, after checking that nobody depended on them.
- A request came in to rewrite the on-call guide in plainer language. A volunteer is drafting it and will post it for comment.

I want to add a note on tone. The audit result could have made people complacent, and a few small remarks suggested that some were already thinking it was time to relax. It was good to hear a counterpoint: a high score is a reason to keep the habits, not to drop them. The risk with doing well is that you stop paying attention to the things that got you there.

One more thing for the record. A newer colleague asked whether it would be possible to see the audit findings in full, including the minor ones, and the answer was yes. They are in the log. Reading them is a decent way of learning how the team thinks about quality. I would encourage everyone to take a look, even if you were not involved.

Next review in a fortnight. In the meantime, enjoy the fan, if you can get hold of it.
request.entity_system_prompt:
You are an entity extraction specialist for unstructured text.
NEVER extract vague or standalone feelings or generic words. A specific, named abstract concept
that passes the Wikipedia-article test below (e.g. "climate change", "quantum entanglement")
should be extracted as a Concept entity — being abstract is not by itself a reason to exclude it.

NEVER extract:
- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)
- Vague standalone feelings and generic ideas that could not stand alone as a specific, named
  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

For each entity extracted, assign a single entity_type label from this closed ontology:
- Person: An individual human being
- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication
Choose the single most appropriate type. If none fit well, use the closest match.

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>

request.edge_system_prompt:
You are an expert fact extractor that extracts fact triples from text.
1. Extracted fact triples should also be extracted with relevant date information.
2. Treat REFERENCE_TIME as the time the episode was recorded. All temporal information should be extracted relative to REFERENCE_TIME.

# TASK
Extract all factual relationships between the given ENTITIES based on the CURRENT MESSAGE.
Only extract facts that:
- involve two DISTINCT ENTITIES from the ENTITIES list,
- are clearly stated or unambiguously implied in the CURRENT MESSAGE,
  and can be represented as edges in a knowledge graph.
- Facts should include entity names rather than pronouns whenever possible.

# EXTRACTION RULES

1. **Entity Name Validation**: source_name and target_name must use only the name values from the ENTITIES list provided above.
   - CRITICAL: Using names not in the list will cause the edge to be rejected.
2. Each fact must involve two distinct entities — source_name and target_name NEVER refer to the same entity.
3. NEVER extract facts that describe only a single entity's state, feeling, or attribute. Instead, identify the second entity that the state or feeling relates to and form a proper triple.
   - BAD: "Alice feels happy" (single-entity state — what is Alice happy about?)
   - GOOD: "Alice feels happy about Bob's promotion" → Alice FEELS_HAPPY_ABOUT Bob's promotion
   - GOOD: "Alice congratulated Bob" (relationship between two entities), "Alice lives in Paris" (relationship between entity and place)
4. NEVER emit duplicate or semantically redundant facts.
5. The fact field should closely paraphrase the original source sentence(s). Do not verbatim quote the original text.
6. Use REFERENCE_TIME to resolve vague or relative temporal expressions (e.g., "last week").
7. Do not hallucinate or infer temporal bounds from unrelated events.

# RELATION TYPE RULES


You MUST always provide a non-null relation_type for every edge. Leaving it null or empty is not acceptable.
Derive a relation_type from the relationship predicate in SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE (e.g., WORKS_AT, LIVES_IN, IS_FRIENDS_WITH, WROTE, AUTHORED, MARRIED_TO).
If the predicate is unclear, derive one from the fact description using a concise verb phrase.
Use concise, consistent vocabulary — prefer established verbs that would apply broadly.

# DATETIME RULES

- Use ISO 8601 with "Z" suffix (UTC) (e.g., 2025-04-30T00:00:00Z).
- If the fact is ongoing (present tense), set valid_at to REFERENCE_TIME.
- If a change or termination is expressed, set invalid_at to the relevant timestamp.
- Leave both fields null if no explicit or resolvable time is stated.
- If only a date is mentioned (no time), assume 00:00:00.
- If only a year is mentioned, use January 1st at 00:00:00.

request.episode_body:
## Demo and follow-ups

Second half of the review, covering the demo and the odds and ends that came out of it.

The security group, Lumen Core, ran a demo of its new access review tool for anyone who wanted to see how it works. 62 people attended the Lumen Core demo, and the room was full enough that a few stood in the doorway. The presenters took a sensible approach: they showed a single real review from start to finish, mistakes and all, instead of a polished script. That made it much easier to understand what the tool is actually for. A review begins with a list of who can see what, the owner of each area confirms or removes each entry, and the result is recorded automatically. The point is that the record builds up as people work, not at the end as a chore.

Reactions were warm. The main praise was for how little training the tool seems to need. One attendee said they had expected a complicated system and found it closer to a checklist. The main criticism was about notifications, which are a bit too frequent in the demo version, and the presenters said they would reduce them and let people choose how often they hear. Someone else asked whether the tool could be used for reviewing things other than access, such as shared accounts or old test environments. The answer was maybe, in time, but they want to get the first use right before widening it.

Questions that came up and deserve a record:

- Who is responsible when an area has no clear owner? The proposed answer is that the security group assigns an interim owner and flags it, and that the area is then reviewed to find a permanent one.
- What happens to the history if someone leaves? The record stays, and the entries that depended on them are flagged for reassignment.
- How often should reviews happen? The group suggested regularly and in small pieces, which fits with the approach already agreed for the access reviews.

On the telemetry side, there was a short update on what is next after the strong audit result. The plan is not to rest on it. A few of the older records will be reformatted, and the review schedule for the documentation will continue as before. The group would like to run a short session for other teams on what they do, and they are willing to be questioned about it. I would encourage people to go.

Last bits of business. The autumn planning session is penciled in, and everyone has been asked to bring their one start and one stop. The on-call guide draft has been posted for comment. The shared calendar clean-up is still in progress, and a couple of people admitted that they have not even looked at theirs yet.

I will close with an observation about the day as a whole. A good demo does two things: it shows what the thing does, and it makes people want to try it. This one managed both, mainly by being honest about what is not finished. We could all learn from that approach when we present our own work.

Thanks to the presenters, and to whoever set up the room, which for once had working equipment.

## Morning

request.episode_body:
## Compliance corner

The compliance side of things, which is where Sable Core lives, had its own small round of housekeeping. The main question this week was how to keep the evidence folder from turning into a junk drawer. Right now documents get dropped in with whatever name the author happened to choose, and finding the right one at audit time becomes archaeology. We talked through a simple naming pattern based on the date and the topic, nothing clever, and decided to try it on new files only. Old ones stay as they are until someone has a reason to touch them. Retrofitting everything is the kind of project that eats a month and impresses nobody.

There was also a brief discussion about whether we are over-documenting. The consensus was no, but that the documents should be shorter and easier to scan. A one-page summary on top of anything longer than a few pages is the new rule of thumb.

request.episode_body:
## Afternoon planning

The planning conversation started at two and was supposed to finish at three. It finished at about half past four, with a break in the middle for tea and for someone to find a charger. Notes below, roughly in the order things came up.

**Priorities.** We began by asking what would hurt most if it slipped. The answer was the same as last month: anything that touches an external deadline. Internal wishes, however pleasant, get second place. This sounds obvious, but writing it down made it easier to say no to two requests that had been hanging around, both reasonable and neither pressing.

**Capacity.** We tried an experiment of listing what each person is actually working on, in plain words, without referring to the board. The result was revealing. The board suggested everyone had three or four items in progress; the conversation suggested most people had one real thing and several things they were keeping warm. We decided that is acceptable provided the warm items are labelled as such. Callum Brennan pointed out that the security-related items are the ones most likely to be kept warm indefinitely, which is precisely why they need a visible owner and a date.

**Compliance work.** The group went through the open items attached to Sable Core, sorting them into those that need a decision, those that need effort, and those that just need someone to confirm they are done. The third pile turned out to be larger than expected, which is a pleasant surprise. Confirmations are cheap, and closing them clears the view for the harder work. Two of the decision items were small enough to settle in the room, and we did.

**Tooling.** There was a short tangent about whether our current setup for tracking requests is helping or hindering. Opinions varied. The practical outcome was an agreement to leave tooling alone this month and revisit once the current round of housekeeping is done, since changing the tools in the middle of cleaning up the contents of the tools is a good way to lose things.

**Communication.** We agreed that status updates should say what changed, not just what exists. A note that says "still working on the review" tells the reader nothing; a note that says "waiting on two answers, expecting them Thursday" lets someone else plan around it. A few examples were passed around and everyone nodded politely.

**Action list from the session.**
- Share the access review list when it is ready.
- Apply the new naming pattern to incoming evidence documents.
- Label warm items on the board so they are not mistaken for active ones.
- Confirm the completed compliance items and close them.
- Ask requesters to state the consequence of delay.

Afterwards I walked round the block with a colleague and we agreed the session had been useful even though it ran long. The trick for next time is probably a firmer agenda and an actual timer, which we will borrow from the kitchen.

The rest of the week is mostly follow-through. There is a section below on what happened on Thursday and Friday.

request.episode_body:
## Thursday notes

Thursday was a lot calmer, which was welcome after the long Wednesday session.

Most of the morning went on the access review. We worked through the first pass and the list of leftovers turned out to be shorter than feared. A handful of accounts belonged to people who had moved on to other projects but still had permissions from their old role. Those were removed, and each one was noted with a brief reason. The grey areas, the ones that need a word with an owner, are being handled one conversation at a time. Nobody likes being asked why they need access to something, so the tone has been to ask politely and explain that it is routine.

On retrospectives: the team that Callum Brennan works with has a quarterly rhythm, and Callum Brennan held its quarterly retrospective on 14 October 2026. In the planning conversation this week someone asked whether the format was worth copying elsewhere, and a few of us took a look at how it is run. The short version is that it is deliberately plain. Everyone writes down what helped, what got in the way and one thing to try. The notes are grouped on a wall or a shared page, and the group picks two or three to act on rather than trying to fix everything. We liked that last bit in particular. Retros that produce twelve action items produce zero changes.

Other happenings during the day:

- A short call with a vendor about a billing question, which was resolved quickly and politely. Nothing to report beyond that, and nothing to follow up.
- The shared drive clear-out proposal came up again. This time two people volunteered, on the condition that it happens in one afternoon rather than being allowed to sprawl. Seems fair.
- The wiki merges from last week are holding up. Nobody has complained about missing pages, which is the best test we have.
- A new starter will be joining the wider group soon, so the onboarding checklist has to be fixed beforehand. This is the second time I have written that sentence in this log, so I have assigned myself the task in the hope that seeing it on the board will motivate me.

An observation for the log. When we go through the access review and the evidence folder tidy-up together, they end up feeling like the same activity: reducing the amount of stuff nobody can explain. There is something satisfying about that framing. Fewer unexplained things means fewer surprises, and fewer surprises means calmer weeks. I will try to carry that into the next planning session as a quiet theme rather than a slogan.

The evening ended with rain, so the cycling contingent has been sheltering in the lobby, comparing routes and complaining about drivers. Normal service will resume in the morning, along with the last section of this entry.

You are an expert fact extractor that extracts fact triples from text.
1. Extracted fact triples should also be extracted with relevant date information.
2. Treat REFERENCE_TIME as the time the episode was recorded. All temporal information should be extracted relative to REFERENCE_TIME.

# TASK
Extract all factual relationships between the given ENTITIES based on the CURRENT MESSAGE.
Only extract facts that:
- involve two DISTINCT ENTITIES from the ENTITIES list,
- are clearly stated or unambiguously implied in the CURRENT MESSAGE,
  and can be represented as edges in a knowledge graph.
- Facts should include entity names rather than pronouns whenever possible.

# EXTRACTION RULES

1. **Entity Name Validation**: source_name and target_name must use only the name values from the ENTITIES list provided above.
   - CRITICAL: Using names not in the list will cause the edge to be rejected.
2. Each fact must involve two distinct entities — source_name and target_name NEVER refer to the same entity.
3. NEVER extract facts that describe only a single entity's state, feeling, or attribute. Instead, identify the second entity that the state or feeling relates to and form a proper triple.
   - BAD: "Alice feels happy" (single-entity state — what is Alice happy about?)

   - GOOD: "Alice congratulated Bob" (relationship between two entities), "Alice lives in Paris" (relationship between entity and place)
4. NEVER emit duplicate or semantically redundant facts.
5. The fact field should closely paraphrase the original source sentence(s). Do not verbatim quote the original text.
6. Use REFERENCE_TIME to resolve vague or relative temporal expressions (e.g., "last week").
7. Do not hallucinate or infer temporal bounds from unrelated events.

You MUST always provide a non-null relation_type for every edge. Leaving it null or empty is not acceptable.
Derive a relation_type from the relationship predicate in SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE (e.g., WORKS_AT, LIVES_IN, IS_FRIENDS_WITH, WROTE, AUTHORED, MARRIED_TO).
If the predicate is unclear, derive one from the fact description using a concise verb phrase.
Use concise, consistent vocabulary — prefer established verbs that would apply broadly.

- Use ISO 8601 with "Z" suffix (UTC) (e.g., 2025-04-30T00:00:00Z).
- If the fact is ongoing (present tense), set valid_at to REFERENCE_TIME.
- If a change or termination is expressed, set invalid_at to the relevant timestamp.
- Leave both fields null if no explicit or resolvable time is stated.
- If only a date is mentioned (no time), assume 00:00:00.
- If only a year is mentioned, use January 1st at 00:00:00.

request.episode_body:
## End of sprint

The sprint closed today, and the usual wrap-up applied: check the board, move what is done, argue gently about what is not.

The headline number is that the Sable Core backlog stood at 147 open tickets at the end of the sprint. That sounds alarming, and a few people reacted as if it were, but when we looked through it most of the entries were old, low-priority or duplicates of each other. A rough sort during the review suggested that a good share could be closed outright with a short note, another chunk needed a decision about whether they are still wanted, and only a minority were real work. We agreed to schedule a grooming session early next week with the goal of getting the list down to things someone actually intends to do. The point is not to make the number look better. The point is that a backlog nobody believes in is worse than no backlog at all.

A few other items from the retrospective of the sprint:

- The access review is complete for the first pass. Callum Brennan will circulate the final list and the reasons recorded, and the second pass will be scheduled once owners have replied.
- The evidence naming pattern worked well enough on new files that it will stay. Someone noticed that the date format in the pattern is ambiguous on first read, so we added a short example at the top of the folder.
- The no-fuss approach to status updates, saying what changed rather than what exists, has taken hold. Several updates this week were genuinely useful, and one was so clear that it saved a meeting.

What went less well: handoffs between people were rough in two places, with one task sitting in limbo because each side thought the other had picked it up. The fix is boring and effective. When you hand something over, name the receiver in the card and wait for them to acknowledge it. If they do not, nudge them. No blame attached, as it is a process gap rather than a personal failing.

Plans for next week:
1. Backlog grooming, with a time limit and a clear rule for closing things.
2. Finish the second pass of the access review.
3. Prepare a short summary of the compliance evidence situation for anyone who asks.
4. Start thinking about what the next sprint should aim at, without overloading it.

Final note: the team seems to be in decent shape. People are tired in the way that follows a full stretch of work, not in the way that follows a bad one. The weekend should help. See everyone Monday.

Writing down what I understand about the Quill Policy, which is the policy responsible for inventory, because people keep asking me and I keep answering from memory. request.episode_body:
# Operations diary — 13 August 2025

Wednesday. A quieter day than expected, which gave me time to write the diary properly for once.

The sprint closed on Monday and the first job this morning was to look at where things stand. The Marlin Core backlog stood at 214 open tickets at the end of the sprint. I know that number looks alarming, so for the record: it is mostly small requests that were never closed, plus a long tail of "nice to have" items. The urgent work is a short list at the top, and that part is under control. Even so, the team agreed that a backlog this size gets in the way of planning, because nobody believes the list any more. Plan: a triage pass, in which each ticket is either scheduled, parked with a reason, or closed. Parked is allowed, as long as the reason is written down.

We spent twenty minutes on how to run the triage without it turning into a week-long affair. The idea is to timebox it, to start with the oldest items and to make decisions quickly. If something cannot be decided in a minute, it gets a question attached and moves on. A few people were sceptical, but we agreed that an imperfect pass is better than another month of ignoring the list.

Operations odds and ends:

- The monitoring dashboard has been showing a stale panel for weeks. Somebody should either fix it or remove it, because a stale panel is worse than none, as people stop trusting the rest.
- Backups were checked and are running on schedule. Restoring is a different question, and we have not tested it recently. A restore drill is going into the calendar.
- The shared runbook has a page called "misc" which is, predictably, a mess. Splitting it into proper topics is a task for a quiet afternoon.
- The visitor badge printer ran out of labels again. Not strictly operations, but someone always asks.

Security came up during the stand-up. Callum Brennan asked everyone to check that their devices are set to lock automatically, and to report anything they cannot configure. It is a routine request, and he phrased it as a favour rather than an instruction, which helps. He also mentioned that he is preparing a demo for later in the month to walk people through the basics of what the security work involves, aimed at those who rarely touch it.

On planning, we looked at the next two sprints. The principle was to leave slack. The last few sprints were packed to the brim, and every surprise caused a knock-on delay. Leaving a little room is not laziness; it is how plans survive contact with reality. We will state in the sprint notes how much room has been left, so that it is visible and nobody fills it by default.

One more thing for the diary: a reminder that the incident channel should be used only for incidents. Questions and chatter go elsewhere. It is a small discipline that makes the channel useful when it matters.

More in the next entry.

request.episode_body:
## Thursday and Friday

Two days rolled into one entry, because Thursday was mostly meetings and Friday was mostly cleaning up after them.

The triage pass on the scheduling backlog started on Thursday afternoon. Marlin Core's tickets were split into three piles by whoever happened to be reading them: do soon, park with a reason, close. It went faster than anyone predicted. The surprising part was how many items could be closed without anyone objecting; several referred to features that had since been replaced, and a few were duplicates of each other. request.episode_body:
## Demo day and wrap-up

The demo took place at the end of the week, and I am writing this the same evening so that the details are accurate.

Attendance was better than anyone had guessed: 39 people attended the Callum Brennan demo. He had worried that a session about security would be a hard sell, but the room was full, and the questions afterwards ran on longer than the presentation. His approach was to avoid jargon and to start with things people can recognise from daily life, such as locking a screen, spotting a suspicious message and knowing whom to tell. He used a couple of invented examples, and that worked well because nobody felt singled out. The consensus was that it should be repeated, perhaps twice a year, aimed at newcomers.

What people said afterwards, in the corridor and in the feedback form:

- They liked that it was short and that it ended on time.
- They wanted a one-page summary to keep at their desk. Callum Brennan will write one, and we will keep it to what fits on a single side.
- Several asked how to report something suspicious without feeling foolish. The answer, which we agreed to put in writing, is that there is no such thing as a silly report.
- A couple of people asked for a version aimed at those who work from home, so that will go on the list.

A small point about logistics. The room was hot and the projector needed a restart, both of which are now familiar. Someone in facilities has been asked about the room; the projector remains a matter for the cupboard and the cable.

On the sprint side, the triage of the scheduling work is half done, and the team plans to finish it early next week. After that we will pick the next sprint's work from the cleaned list and, for the first time in a while, we should be choosing from a list we all believe. The principle of leaving slack was agreed, and it will be noted in the sprint plan.

Remaining chores for the diary:

1. Publish the corrected restore steps on the wiki, and link them from the runbook index.
2. Set up the anonymous form for security questions, and let people know where it is.
3. Rearrange recurring meetings so that no day has more than two.
4. Write the one-page security summary, then ask three colleagues to read it and say what is unclear.
5. Choose a quiet-hours slot and announce the trial.

Closing thought. This was a good week for the team in a modest way. Nothing broke, a couple of nagging problems got fixed, and a presentation that could have been dull turned out to be useful. I will try to remember weeks like this when the next fire arrives. Next entry will start with the sprint plan.

request.episode_body:
## Compliance queue

The headline from the compliance side was the queue. The Bram Tanaka backlog stood at 35 open tickets at the end of the sprint. People reacted differently to that. One view was that it is a reasonable number given what came in; another was that a few of the tickets have been sitting for a long time and are really just waiting on answers from outside. Bram Tanaka himself was matter-of-fact about it and pointed out that a chunk of the queue consists of items that cannot move until somebody else replies. That seems right, and it suggests that the raw count overstates the pressure.

What we agreed to do:

- Separate the tickets that are waiting on someone outside from the ones that are genuinely ready for work, so the real queue is visible.
- Add a short note to each stalled ticket saying who we are waiting on and since when.
- Look at the split again at the next review and see whether the "ready" pile is shrinking.

There was a side discussion about whether stalled tickets should be closed after a long silence. The consensus was no, not automatically, but they should be reviewed on a regular basis so that nothing is forgotten. A ticket left open indefinitely is a small lie; a ticket closed too early is a small betrayal. We would rather err on the side of keeping them and being honest about their state.

## Process remarks

A few smaller things came up while we were at it.

The handover between sprints was clunky. Several people said that they only learned what had been left unfinished by finding half-done work in the shared folder. We talked about a short end-of-sprint note, no more than a paragraph per person, listing what is open and what has been abandoned. It will not be perfect, but it should reduce the surprises.

There was also a brief conversation about estimates. Opinions ranged from "they are useful for planning" to "they are fiction we agree to tell each other". I sit somewhere in the middle. Estimates are useful as a way to start a conversation about what is hard, and less useful as promises. We did not change anything, but I think it helped to say it out loud.

request.episode_body:
## Onboarding and learning

The second half of the review was about onboarding, and I was glad to hear it, because it is an area that can easily get squeezed out when the sprint is busy.

Fable Core gave a brief update. The main message was that the material for new joiners is in better shape than it was, though still uneven. Some sections are clear and recent; others read as if they were written for a different team in a different year. Fable Core completed 11 hours of training this term, which was mentioned partly as a point of pride and partly as a reminder that learning time does not appear by magic. It had to be protected, and it was protected, and the result is that the people involved are more confident about explaining things to newcomers.

I want to record the reasoning here, because it will be easy to forget. The argument was that the best onboarding material is written by people who have recently been confused. Someone who has been in the team for years no longer remembers what is unclear. Someone who joined a few months ago does. So the training time doubles as a way of surfacing what needs fixing.

request.episode_body:
### Mentoring

A related point was mentoring. We have never formalised it, and for the most part it happens naturally. Still, we noticed that some newcomers end up with plenty of informal guidance while others get very little, mostly depending on who they happen to sit near. Bram Tanaka suggested a simple pairing at the start, with no obligations beyond a weekly chat. It is easy to set up and easy to drop if it does not work, which is the kind of change this team tends to accept.

request.entity_system_prompt:
You are an entity extraction specialist for unstructured text.
NEVER extract vague or standalone feelings or generic words. A specific, named abstract concept
that passes the Wikipedia-article test below (e.g. "climate change", "quantum entanglement")
should be extracted as a Concept entity — being abstract is not by itself a reason to exclude it.

NEVER extract:
- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)
- Vague standalone feelings and generic ideas that could not stand alone as a specific, named
  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").

Extract all factual relationships between the given ENTITIES based on the CURRENT MESSAGE.
Only extract facts that:
- involve two DISTINCT ENTITIES from the ENTITIES list,
- are clearly stated or unambiguously implied in the CURRENT MESSAGE,
  and can be represented as edges in a knowledge graph.
- Facts should include entity names rather than pronouns whenever possible.

# EXTRACTION RULES

1. **Entity Name Validation**: source_name and target_name must use only the name values from the ENTITIES list provided above.
   - CRITICAL: Using names not in the list will cause the edge to be rejected.
2. Each fact must involve two distinct entities — source_name and target_name NEVER refer to the same entity.
3. NEVER extract facts that describe only a single entity's state, feeling, or attribute. Instead, identify the second entity that the state or feeling relates to and form a proper triple.

You MUST always provide a non-null relation_type for every edge. Leaving it null or empty is not acceptable.
Derive a relation_type from the relationship predicate in SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE (e.g., WORKS_AT, LIVES_IN, IS_FRIENDS_WITH, WROTE, AUTHORED, MARRIED_TO).

Use concise, consistent vocabulary — prefer established verbs that would apply broadly.

- Use ISO 8601 with "Z" suffix (UTC) (e.g., 2025-04-30T00:00:00Z).

- Leave both fields null if no explicit or resolvable time is stated.
- If only a date is mentioned (no time), assume 00:00:00.
- If only a year is mentioned, use January 1st at 00:00:00.

request.episode_body:
### Planning for the next sprint

The plan is intentionally modest. After a sprint where several items spilled over, there was little appetite for taking on more than we could finish. We agreed to carry forward the unfinished work, add only what is clearly urgent, and leave some slack for the unexpected. Slack was a recurring word in the conversation. A sprint with no spare room tends to fail on the first surprise, and we have had enough of those.

We also agreed that anything new should be paired with something removed. This is not a strict rule, but a habit of asking "what are we dropping to make room?" has a way of making priorities honest.

Bram Tanaka will lead the work of separating stalled tickets from ready ones. It is a small job, but it will reveal where the real pressure is, and it should make the next review conversation easier. He asked for a quiet half day to do it, and we agreed that nobody should interrupt him unless something is on fire.

Fable Core will continue refining the onboarding material and will share a short summary at the next meeting. The focus is the most commonly asked questions, which should be quick to improve and valuable to the next person who joins.

- Someone should write down the way we decide what counts as urgent. Right now it seems to mean "whatever the loudest person says", which is not a policy.

request.episode_body:
### A few reflections

I left the review feeling that the team is in decent shape. Nobody is burned out, nobody is hiding problems, and the numbers, while not perfect, are explained and understood. That counts for a lot. I used to think a good review meant good numbers. Now I think it means honest numbers and a clear sense of what to do about them.

There were also a few moments of humour that I should record, if only because they make the room feel better. Someone observed that the stalled tickets are less a backlog than a waiting room, and the image stuck. We now refer to the "waiting room" and the "ready pile", and I suspect those names will survive for a while.

request.episode_body:
# Review notes — 5 September 2025

Friday review, written up while the coffee was still hot. Attendance was good and the room was less stuffy than last time, since someone finally worked out how the window latch operates.

We opened with a look at the support queue. Diego Ferreira walked through what came in over the past week and what is still open, and the headline was that most requests are now answered on the same day, with the stragglers being the ones that need input from another team. The suggestion that came out of the discussion was to tag those clearly so they stop being mistaken for neglected items. It sounds trivial, but a good half of the "why is this still open?" questions we get come from exactly that confusion.

Next up was billing. Ines Lindqvist reported that the month-end routine ran without the usual manual fixes, which is the first time in a while. She credited a small change to how late invoices are flagged, and promised to write the steps up so that anyone can repeat them. We talked briefly about whether the checklist should live on the wiki or in the tracker; wiki won, mainly because people actually read the wiki.

Then a short, slightly awkward item on telemetry. Tern Core has been collecting more data than anyone looks at, and the storage bill is the sort of thing that grows quietly until someone notices. Nobody wants to throw away data that might matter, but nobody could name a decision that depends on most of it either. The group agreed to go through the collected streams one by one and ask a single question of each: who reads this, and what would change if it vanished? Anything with no good answer becomes a candidate for sampling rather than full capture.

A few smaller notes from the hour:

- The review template got a trim. We removed two sections that nobody ever filled in.
- Calendar invites for the recurring review will now say clearly who is presenting, so people know whether to prepare.
- The shared inbox rota continues unchanged, but the handover message at the end of each shift will be posted in the usual channel instead of sent privately.

There was a mildly heated exchange about whether reviews should include forward planning or stay strictly backward-looking. The compromise is that the last ten minutes are for "what do we do differently", and everything else remains retrospective. We will see how that feels after a few weeks. If it turns into a second planning meeting, we will cut it back.

One housekeeping point for the notebook itself: entries here should say who decided something, not just that it was decided. Several older notes use the passive voice and are impossible to interpret months later. Please write "the team agreed" or name the person responsible, whichever is accurate.

Finally, thanks to everyone who stayed to tidy the room afterwards. The whiteboard photos are in the team folder. Next review is in a fortnight, same slot, same room, hopefully with the window sorted.

request.episode_body:
## Survey results and calendar

The feedback survey came back and, frankly, one result was hard to read. Tern Core received a satisfaction rating of 3.6 out of 10. People who use the telemetry output were generous in their comments, which made the number more puzzling, so the group spent some time working out what it actually measures. The current theory is that the low score reflects frustration with how long it takes to get a question answered, not with the data itself. A follow-up conversation with a few of the respondents is planned before anyone draws firm conclusions or reorganises anything.

It is worth stating plainly that one number from one survey is not a verdict. We have been burned before by treating a single score as gospel and then discovering that three people had misread the scale. The aim is to read the free-text answers carefully, group them by theme, and only then decide what, if anything, to change.

Moving on to the retrospective calendar, which keeps needing patching. Diego Ferreira held its quarterly retrospective on 23 August 2027, and the support group filed its notes with the rest. The main takeaway, as far as I can tell from the write-up, was that the queue handling has improved but the handover between shifts still loses information. There was a suggestion to use a standard closing message for each shift, which seems sensible and costs nothing.

request.episode_body:
## Odds and ends

The wiki search has been returning odd results since the last reorganisation, with old pages ranking above new ones. Someone in the platform group is looking at it. In the meantime, if you cannot find a page, try the title rather than keywords from the body.

The shared drive is getting cluttered with files named "final" and "final2". A short naming convention is on the way, and it will be gentle. We are not going to police it, but we would like new files to be findable by someone who was not in the room when they were made.

We also discussed training budgets. There is appetite for a couple of external courses, and the question is how to pick fairly. The proposal is to ask people to write a paragraph on what they would learn and how the team would benefit, then decide together. It is not a competition; it is a way of making sure the money goes where it is most useful.

Last, a reminder that the quiet room is for quiet, not for calls. This keeps coming up. Please take calls in the booths.

## Odds and ends

The wiki search has been returning odd results since the last reorganisation, with old pages ranking above new ones. Someone in the platform group is looking at it. In the meantime, if you cannot find a page, try the title rather than keywords from the body.

The shared drive is getting cluttered with files named "final" and "final2". A short naming convention is on the way, and it will be gentle. We are not going to police it, but we would like new files to be findable by someone who was not in the room when they were made.

We also discussed training budgets. There is appetite for a couple of external courses, and the question is how to pick fairly. The proposal is to ask people to write a paragraph on what they would learn and how the team would benefit, then decide together. It is not a competition; it is a way of making sure the money goes where it is most useful.

Last, a reminder that the quiet room is for quiet, not for calls. This keeps coming up. Please take calls in the booths.
</TEXT>

request.episode_body:
## Demo day and follow-ups

The demo this week was the highlight. Ines Lindqvist ran through the new invoice-matching flow, and 19 people attended the Ines Lindqvist demo, which is a strong turnout for a Thursday afternoon. The format was short and practical: a live walkthrough of a realistic case, then questions. Several people in other groups said it was the first time they had understood why billing asks for certain fields at all. That alone made it worthwhile, and it will probably reduce the number of incomplete submissions we see.

Feedback afterwards was positive but specific. People wanted clearer error messages when a match fails, a way to see which rule caused a rejection, and a short guide for anyone submitting on behalf of someone else. All three are reasonable, and the team will log them as tickets so they are visible. Not everything will be done at once, and that is fine, but it is better to write them down than to rely on memory.

One request was more of a philosophical point: should the system try harder to guess what the submitter meant, or should it insist on correct input? We did not resolve it. The practical answer is probably "guess for obvious slips, insist for anything with money attached", but that needs a closer look before anyone builds it.
request.entity_system_prompt:
You are an entity extraction specialist for unstructured text.
NEVER extract vague or standalone feelings or generic words. A specific, named abstract concept
that passes the Wikipedia-article test below (e.g. "climate change", "quantum entanglement")
should be extracted as a Concept entity — being abstract is not by itself a reason to exclude it.

NEVER extract:
- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)
- Vague standalone feelings and generic ideas that could not stand alone as a specific, named
  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

For each entity extracted, assign a single entity_type label from this closed ontology:
- Person: An individual human being
- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication
Choose the single most appropriate type. If none fit well, use the closest match.

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>

## Support and scheduling

Diego Ferreira mentioned that the demo had already produced a few new questions in the support queue, which is a healthy sign. People ask questions when they are paying attention. The suggestion was to collect them into a short FAQ and publish it alongside the recording, so the next person does not need to ask.

On scheduling, the next round of demos should avoid the days when month-end work is heaviest. A calendar overlay would help here, and someone offered to sketch one on the shared wiki. Keep it simple; the temptation with these things is to build a tool when a table would do.

request.episode_body:
## Aside on meeting rooms

The bookable rooms continue to be a source of low-level friction. People reserve a room for a long block and then use a fraction of it. A gentle proposal: release the slot as soon as you finish, and shorten default bookings. This will not fix the underlying shortage, but it makes better use of what we have.

Finally, a note on the clock in the large room, which is wrong by several minutes and has been for months. It is not a mystery, just a dead battery that nobody wants to own. Someone, please own it.

request.episode_body:
## Telemetry follow-up

Tern Core will start the stream-by-stream review next week. The approach is deliberately modest: list every stream, note who consumes it, and record the answer in a shared table. Where a consumer cannot be found, the team will ask around before proposing any change, because the one stream everyone ignores is always the one somebody quietly depends on. Findings will be summarised in the log so that people can see what was decided and why.

There was also a suggestion to publish a plain-language description of what each stream is for. That would help new joiners, and it would help the rest of us remember. It does not have to be elaborate. A sentence or two per stream is plenty.

request.episode_body:
# Weekly digest — 6 September 2025

Saturday morning, coffee in hand, writing up the week while it is still fresh.

The week opened with a long conversation about the support queue. Diego Ferreira had spent several days reading through old tickets and came back with a simple observation: a large share of the questions are answered by the same handful of paragraphs, and those paragraphs live in three different places. His proposal was to pick one home for them and point everything else at it. Nobody objected, and he has started collecting the text. The hard part will be deciding what to throw away, since every old answer has someone who is fond of it.

Meanwhile, Yara Nakamura took the maintenance side through the plan for the next round of routine work. The idea is to batch the small jobs into a single predictable window instead of letting them trickle in all week. People who depend on the systems get a heads-up in advance, and the team gets a stretch of uninterrupted time. There were questions about what happens if something urgent turns up during the window, and the answer is that urgent things win, but we write down what was displaced so that nothing is forgotten.

Smaller decisions this week:

- Meeting notes go into the shared folder on the same day, even if they are rough. A rough note that exists beats a polished one that never gets written.
- We will stop using the old group chat for anything that needs a record. Questions that deserve an answer go to the tracker.
- The kitchen rota is now a recurring calendar event instead of a sheet of paper that nobody looks at.

On chores, the list is mostly unchanged. The shared drive still has a folder named "to sort", which has been "to sort" for longer than anyone can remember. We agreed to take twenty minutes on Monday and either file or delete everything in it. There will be no ceremony and no committee; whoever is nearest the keyboard does it.

There was a brief discussion about handovers when someone is away. The current practice is a message to the channel saying who is covering, but that tends to get buried. A calendar entry with the cover named is more visible, and it also helps people outside the team who just want to know whom to ask. We will try it next time anyone takes time off.

Another thread: how to welcome new joiners. The checklist is long, and most of it is access requests, which is the least welcoming part. Suggestion: separate the access list, which can be done by whoever has the rights, from the human part, which is a conversation on the first day about how the team works and who to ask about what. That seemed sensible, and someone volunteered to draft the shorter human checklist.

I will keep the rest for the next sections of this digest, where I have put the survey feedback and the plans that came out of it. It is easier to read when the numbers are not mixed in with the housekeeping.

request.episode_body:
## Maintenance feedback

Now the first piece of survey feedback, which arrived midweek and prompted a decent conversation.

Yara Nakamura received a satisfaction rating of 7.3 out of 10. She read the comments aloud at the sync, which I thought was brave, and the tone was calm. People said that the work is done well and that they feel safe handing things over. The recurring criticism was that the schedule of planned work is hard to find. It exists, but you have to know where to look, and several respondents said they only learned of a maintenance window when something they were using went quiet.

What we agreed to do about it:

1. Put the planned-work calendar on the front page of the wiki, with a plain description of what each window covers.
2. Send a short message the day before every window, to the same place each time.
3. After each window, post one line saying what was done and whether anything needs follow-up.

Yara Nakamura took the first item, and said she would rather over-announce for a few weeks than have people surprised. That is the right instinct. If it turns out to be too noisy we can trim it later; it is much harder to rebuild trust than to reduce a notification.

Related chores that came out of the same conversation:

- Review the list of systems covered by routine work, and check that each has a named contact.
- Tidy the page that explains how to request maintenance. It currently has two forms linked from it, only one of which still works.
- Add a sentence to the request form explaining what to expect after submitting.

There was also a general point about how we collect feedback. Surveys are fine, but they arrive once and then people forget about them. We talked about making it easier to leave a quick comment at any time, perhaps through a simple form linked from the wiki, and reading those at each sync. This is more work but it spreads the listening across the year instead of concentrating it in one painful week.

Someone raised the matter of how we thank people. It is easy to look only at what went wrong, and a rating like this one hides a lot of quiet competence. We decided to add a standing item to the sync where anyone can mention something that went well that week. It should take two minutes, and it is surprisingly good for the mood.

I also want to note a side conversation about documentation. A few of the maintenance procedures live only in someone's head, and the plan is to write one up each week, starting with the ones that are used most often. Yara Nakamura will pick the first, and we will ask a colleague to follow it without help, which is the best test of whether it is clear.

That finishes this part. The next one is mostly practical: the plans for the coming fortnight and the usual list of loose ends.

<TEXT>
## Maintenance feedback

Now the first piece of survey feedback, which arrived midweek and prompted a decent conversation.

Yara Nakamura received a satisfaction rating of 7.3 out of 10. She read the comments aloud at the sync, which I thought was brave, and the tone was calm. People said that the work is done well and that they feel safe handing things over. The recurring criticism was that the schedule of planned work is hard to find. It exists, but you have to know where to look, and several respondents said they only learned of a maintenance window when something they were using went quiet.

What we agreed to do about it:

1. Put the planned-work calendar on the front page of the wiki, with a plain description of what each window covers.
2. Send a short message the day before every window, to the same place each time.
3. After each window, post one line saying what was done and whether anything needs follow-up.

Yara Nakamura took the first item, and said she would rather over-announce for a few weeks than have people surprised. That is the right instinct. If it turns out to be too noisy we can trim it later; it is much harder to rebuild trust than to reduce a notification.

Related chores that came out of the same conversation:

- Review the list of systems covered by routine work, and check that each has a named contact.
- Tidy the page that explains how to request maintenance. It currently has two forms linked from it, only one of which still works.
- Add a sentence to the request form explaining what to expect after submitting.

There was also a general point about how we collect feedback. Surveys are fine, but they arrive once and then people forget about them. We talked about making it easier to leave a quick comment at any time, perhaps through a simple form linked from the wiki, and reading those at each sync. This is more work but it spreads the listening across the year instead of concentrating it in one painful week.

Someone raised the matter of how we thank people. It is easy to look only at what went wrong, and a rating like this one hides a lot of quiet competence. We decided to add a standing item to the sync where anyone can mention something that went well that week. It should take two minutes, and it is surprisingly good for the mood.

I also want to note a side conversation about documentation. A few of the maintenance procedures live only in someone's head, and the plan is to write one up each week, starting with the ones that are used most often. Yara Nakamura will pick the first, and we will ask a colleague to follow it without help, which is the best test of whether it is clear.

That finishes this part. The next one is mostly practical: the plans for the coming fortnight and the usual list of loose ends.
</TEXT>

request.episode_body:
## Plans for the fortnight

Practical part, as promised. Nothing here is surprising; it is mostly a record of who intends to do what, so that we can check later.

The support queue first. Diego Ferreira is continuing his tidy-up of the standard answers and has asked for a second pair of eyes on the wording before anything replaces the old versions. We agreed that two people will review each answer, one who knows the subject well and one who does not, since the second person is better at spotting jargon. The target is to have the most common answers consolidated by the middle of next week, and the rest can follow at a more relaxed pace.

Yara Nakamura is setting up the first of the announced maintenance windows. The plan is to run one small window as a rehearsal, with the announcements, the closing note and the follow-up all exercised, before doing a larger one. It is a sensible way to find the awkward bits cheaply. If the announcement goes to the wrong place or the wording is unclear, we would much rather learn that on a minor window.

Other things in the diary:

- A short session on how to write a good ticket title. It sounds trivial, but half the time spent searching the queue is spent decoding vague titles.
- A review of which tools the team actually uses, so that unused accounts can be closed and the list on the wiki matches reality.
- An hour to sit together and walk through the escalation path, using a made-up scenario. People tend to remember a rehearsed path better than a written one.
- Clearing the "to sort" folder, which is still on the list and now has a deadline, namely Monday.

We touched on workload again. The balance between planned work and interruptions is not quite right, and the feeling is that interruptions are winning. One idea is to nominate one person each day as the first point of contact for ad hoc requests, so that the others can focus. It has worked elsewhere, and the cost of trying it is low. We will start with a trial and ask honestly whether it helped.

On communication, a reminder that the weekly digest is the place to look for decisions. If something was agreed in a corridor, please add a line here. It takes thirty seconds and it saves a lot of "wait, did we decide that?" later on.

Also a gentle note about response times. Nobody expects an instant answer, but a quick acknowledgement is appreciated, even if the real answer comes later. We will try to say "seen, will reply by tomorrow" instead of leaving people wondering.

Last, a small administrative item: the room booking for the next sync needs confirming, and somebody should check that the projector cable has been returned to the cupboard. It disappears every few weeks and then reappears in an unexpected place.

request.episode_body:
## Support feedback and close

The last part of this digest, with the second piece of survey feedback and a few closing thoughts.

Diego Ferreira received a satisfaction rating of 7.6 out of 10. The comments were warm. People described the support answers as clear and patient, and several said they appreciate being told what will happen next instead of being left guessing. The criticism was about speed: a few respondents felt that replies to less urgent questions take longer than they should, and that they only find out by chasing. That fits what he already suspected from reading the queue, and it supports the case for consolidating the standard answers, since it should shorten the time spent on the repetitive questions.

We discussed what to do about response times without promising anything we cannot keep:

- Publish a plain statement of how quickly different kinds of question are normally answered.
- Make sure every request receives a short acknowledgement the same day.
- Look at which questions arrive most often and see whether a better answer on the wiki would stop them arriving at all.
- Review again at the next survey to see whether perceptions have changed.

Diego Ferreira was pragmatic about it. He said the feedback was fair and the fixes are mostly things we were going to do anyway. Putting them in writing makes them harder to postpone, which seems like the real value of having the survey in the first place.

There was a short exchange between the support and maintenance sides about shared work. Questions about planned maintenance often land in the support queue, and the answers sit in the maintenance plan. Yara Nakamura suggested that the planned-work calendar be linked directly from the standard answers, so support can point to it with a single link. That small change should cut down on questions and improve the experience for the person asking.

A few housekeeping items to finish:

1. The "to sort" folder is on the Monday list.
2. The new-joiner checklist will be split into an access part and a human part.
3. Cover for time away will be recorded as calendar entries.
4. The kitchen rota calendar event needs a name that people recognise.

Thoughts on the digest itself. Writing it in sections worked better than one long block, since each part has a single subject and people can read the bit that concerns them. I would suggest keeping that structure. A short summary at the top might help too, but it is more to maintain, so I would leave it for now.

Thanks to everyone for the candour in the survey comments and in the discussion. Several of the changes we agreed this week are small, but they are the sort that improve how the team feels to work with, and to rely on. See you at the next sync.

# Orbit Policy — what we know

Orbit Policy is the policy responsible for security, and people tend to ask about it at awkward moments. The review cadence for the Orbit Policy is monthly, so it never sits untouched for long, and any change that someone proposes is likely to get looked at promptly instead of languishing. Separately, the standing meeting has moved to the smaller room this week, so bring a chair and a pen.

request.episode_body:
# The state of urban mobility in mid-sized cities

Big cities get the attention when it comes to transport policy, but the more interesting experiments are often happening in places of a few hundred thousand people. Mid-sized cities are large enough to have real congestion and small enough that a change to a single street can be felt across town.

Planners in these places face an awkward position. They rarely have the passenger numbers to justify heavy rail, yet the car-dependent pattern of their growth leaves little room for the buses and bike lanes that might serve them better. Most are working with what they already have: a bus network designed decades ago, a road grid that favours drivers, and a budget that has to stretch across many other priorities.

**Short trips, long habits**

A recurring finding in mobility surveys is that a large share of urban journeys are short, often under a few kilometres. Many of these are made by car simply because it is the default. Cities that have made walking and cycling safer and more direct report that some of these trips shift quickly, though the effect depends on whether the changes form a connected network. A single protected lane that ends abruptly does little.

**The cost of keeping things running**

Public transport operators in mid-sized cities describe a squeeze between rising operating costs and fares that cannot easily be raised. Contracts for vehicles, maintenance and compliance services add up, and procurement officers pay attention to unit prices. Trade press reported that Marlin Supply lists its standard rate at $63 per unit, a figure that officials cited when comparing options for compliance work, though they cautioned that list prices rarely tell the whole story once volume and service terms are taken into account.

**What seems to work**

Practitioners tend to agree on a few modest points. Frequency matters more than coverage: a bus that comes often is more useful than one that reaches everywhere but runs rarely. Reliable information, such as accurate arrival times, makes a service feel better even when the service itself is unchanged. And small, visible improvements, such as shelters, clearer signs and simpler fares, build public support for larger changes.

There is also growing interest in shared and flexible services for areas where fixed routes do not pay. Early results are mixed. Where demand is thin, on-demand vehicles can fill gaps, but they are costly per passenger, and some pilots have ended once the initial funding ran out.

**The political dimension**

Perhaps the hardest part is not technical. Changes to street space are visible, and the people who lose parking or road width tend to be vocal. Councils that have succeeded usually spent time on consultation, tested changes temporarily before making them permanent, and measured the results openly. When the evidence is public, the debate shifts from opinion to outcomes.

For mid-sized cities, the practical message is to start with what can be done on existing streets, build a connected network of improvements and keep measuring. There is no single answer, but there is a steady direction, and the cities making headway are the ones that have chosen it and stuck to it.

## Where things stand

Let me start with the picture as I understand it. Billing is in reasonable shape. Everyone agreed that the two are linked: the better the onboarding, the fewer billing questions come from people who did not know the process.

request.episode_body:
## Demo reflections

The recent demo was well received. 84 people attended the Cedar Core demo, which is the largest turnout we have had for anything of this kind, and the room (plus the overflow link) was properly full. The format worked: a short explanation of what the billing project does, a live walkthrough of a realistic case, and then questions. The questions were the most valuable part. People asked about edge cases we had not considered, and a few of them revealed misunderstandings that we can now address in the documentation.

Some themes from the feedback, as recorded:

- People wanted clearer explanations of why certain fields are required.
- Several asked for a way to see the status of a submission without having to ask someone.
- A few suggested a shorter version for people who only need the basics.
- One person, memorably, asked whether the system could be less polite when it rejects something. The answer was that it could be more specific, which is not quite the same thing.

The team will turn these into tickets over the coming days. Not everything will be done soon, but it is better to have the requests written down in one place than to rely on memory.

request.episode_body:
## Backlog

The backlog discussion was more sobering. The Aiko Osei backlog stood at 163 open tickets at the end of the sprint. Nobody was surprised, but seeing it written down concentrated minds. A large share of the tickets are small, and some are probably out of date. Others are genuinely waiting for effort that the team does not currently have. The decision was to run a grooming session next week, with the aim of closing or merging whatever can be, and of sorting the rest into a rough order.

It is important not to treat the figure as a performance metric. The people working through the queue have been doing so steadily, and the volume reflects how many new people the team has been supporting, not how well it is doing. If anything, the figure suggests that onboarding is popular and that the demand for help is real. What it does tell us is that we need a better way of handling repeated questions, so that the same issue is not raised afresh by every new person.

## Housekeeping and naming

The tangent about naming conventions deserves a brief record. A few people have noticed that files and tickets are named inconsistently, which makes searching harder than it should be. The proposal is a light convention: start with the area, then a short description, and avoid abbreviations that only the author understands. There was no appetite for enforcing it, and the consensus was to adopt it going forward without renaming everything that already exists.

Other bits:

- Room bookings for next week's sessions are confirmed.
- The welcome emails have been updated with correct links.
- The shared drive will get a tidy before the end of the month, with notice before anything is moved.

request.episode_body:
## Learning and development

Training was the main theme. The term is well underway, so we took stock of how much people have managed so far. Basalt Core completed 44 hours of training this term, and Sable Core completed 50 hours of training this term. Both groups are happy with how it went, though both said the same thing: the hours were found by ringfencing time in advance, not by hoping gaps would appear. That is a lesson worth passing on to anyone still struggling to fit learning in. If it is not in the calendar, it does not happen.

The procurement side spent its hours mostly on contract handling and supplier communication, the sort of knowledge that is hard to pick up from documents alone. Compliance went deeper on the regulatory side, including some material that was new to most of the team. Both said they would share what they learned, and short write-ups are expected on the wiki soon.

## Notes on process

We briefly talked about how to run the weekly sync more efficiently. Too much of the time goes on updates that could have been written. The proposal is to ask for written updates in advance, and use the meeting only for questions and decisions. Several people said this would suit them, particularly those who find it hard to speak up in a larger group. We will try it for a few weeks and see.

There was also a request to keep a running list of "things we decided not to do", since those are often forgotten and rediscovered later. A short page on the wiki should do. It is surprisingly useful to know that an idea was considered and rejected, and why.

Next week looks busy but manageable. The main events are a planning session, the first written-update sync, and the descaling.
