request.episode_body:
## Feedback, and a few loose ends

The satisfaction survey for scheduling came back, and Tomas Kowalski received a satisfaction rating of 7.5 out of 10. That is a solid result for a job that tends to attract complaints when it goes wrong and silence when it goes right. The comments were largely about communication: people like the outcome of the scheduling but would like earlier notice when something shifts. That fits with what we have seen in the calendar, and the new coverage page should help. Tomas is going to follow up with a couple of the respondents to understand what "earlier" means in practice, since it differs a good deal from one person to the next.

It is worth noting the usual caution about numbers. A single survey is a snapshot, and a good score is a reason to keep doing what is working, not a reason to relax. We will look at the next round before reading anything into small movements.

request.episode_body:
## Compliance and procurement notes

Sable Core has been looking at how records are kept, with a view to making them easier to find during a review. The group's idea is a simple index: one table listing what exists, where it is, and who is responsible for it. Not a new system, just a map. Basalt Core likes the idea and would like to borrow it for supplier paperwork, which has the same problem of things living in too many places.

A short conversation followed about how the two groups can share more. They overlap more than people realise, since purchasing decisions often have compliance implications and vice versa. A monthly half-hour conversation was suggested, with no agenda beyond "what are you working on that might affect us?". It is cheap and probably worthwhile.

request.episode_body:
## Opening round

We began with a general check on how the quarter is going. The mood was brisk. People felt the summer slowdown was behind us, and the autumn queue was already forming. Three groups were represented in the room: procurement, routing and maintenance, and each had something it wanted to raise before the main discussion.

Basalt Core, responsible for procurement, held a demo for the wider team earlier in the week, and 53 people attended the Basalt Core demo. That was more than the room was ready for, and a few people ended up standing at the back. The feedback afterwards was positive. The most common comment was that it was good to see the ordering flow end to end, since many people only ever touch one step of it. Several asked whether the demo could be recorded for new joiners, and the team agreed to look into it, with the caveat that a recording goes out of date fast and would need a visible date on it.

Quill Core, the routing project, talked about how its work has been affected by the change in demand. Traffic patterns are shifting, and some of the older assumptions no longer hold. The team plans to revisit its defaults and write down the reasoning behind each, since too many settings had no explanation attached. That is a quiet kind of debt, but it grows.

### Practical business

A simple request form will be introduced so that asks are visible and can be ordered by importance. It sounds bureaucratic, yet the alternative is a pile of hallway promises nobody can track.

request.episode_body:
## Backlog, risks and next time

The second half of the planning day dealt with the less glamorous side of things: the backlog, the risks, and what we do about both.

Routing came first. The Quill Core backlog stood at 95 open tickets at the end of the sprint. The team did not treat that as an emergency, but they did not wave it away either. The discussion was about composition. A large share of the tickets, the team said, were requests for small adjustments that had been queued up over time and never revisited, and a smaller number were real problems that deserved attention soon. The suggestion was to sort the list into "act now", "act eventually" and "close with thanks", and to give each group a clear rule about how long items may sit before being reviewed. Nobody enjoys closing someone's request, but a list that is never pruned stops being useful, and people stop trusting it.

We also discussed a lightweight way to tell requesters what happened to their tickets. A short, kind note when something is closed, with the reason, goes a long way. The routing group volunteered to draft a few template sentences so the notes are quick to write and do not sound curt.

That means asking the routing group for its expected busy periods, which in turn means they need to have thought about them. A small piece of homework for everybody.

### Last items

A few housekeeping notes for completeness. The planning board stays as simplified. The bigger room is booked for the next demo. The projector in the small room has been replaced at last, so that excuse is gone. Someone asked whether we should keep a running list of "things we decided not to do", since those are often the most valuable decisions and the easiest to forget. Everyone agreed and a page was started on the spot.

The session ended a little ahead of time, which seemed to surprise people. We took that as a sign the agenda was about right and chose to leave early instead of inventing more to discuss. Notes go into the shared archive tomorrow.

request.episode_body:
# Team log — 24 September 2025

Wednesday again, and the log is overdue. Pulling together what happened since the last entry, in roughly the order it happened.

Monday was dominated by the support queue. A backlog of older tickets had been quietly growing, and the person covering support finally ran out of patience with it. Diego Ferreira spent most of the morning going through the oldest items, closing the ones that had been solved weeks ago without anyone updating the ticket and writing short replies on the rest. It was not glamorous work but the queue is visibly shorter, and the tone of incoming messages has softened now that people are getting answers faster. We agreed this kind of sweep should happen on a schedule rather than whenever somebody snaps.

On Tuesday there was the demo. The format was a walk through the support tooling: how a ticket arrives, how it gets triaged, and how a reply goes out. In total, 49 people attended the Diego Ferreira demo, which was more than the room could comfortably hold, so some stood at the back. Questions were practical. Several people wanted to know how to flag a ticket as urgent without going through the whole form, and a couple asked whether customers can see the status of what they have submitted. The honest answer to the second was "not yet", and that went on the list of things to look at.

A few notes on what worked and what did not:

- Starting with a real, anonymised example kept people engaged far better than a diagram would have.
- The microphone cut out twice. Someone will check the batteries before the next one.
- People appreciated that we showed an awkward case where the tooling does not behave nicely. Several said it made the rest more believable.
- We ran about ten minutes long because the questions were good, which seemed a fair trade.

The other main thread of the week was housekeeping around onboarding. Aiko Osei has been rewriting the first-week guide for newcomers, and a draft went out for comment on Tuesday afternoon. The old guide was a long, linear document, and the new one is organised by what you are trying to do: get access, find the right channel, ask a question, report a problem. Early feedback is positive, though two people pointed out that the access section assumes you already know who to ask. That is exactly the sort of gap a fresh pair of eyes catches, so we have asked a newer colleague to read it cold and mark every place they got stuck.

Smaller items from the week:

1. The shared calendar was cleaned up, with a handful of dead recurring meetings removed.
2. A reminder went around that expense receipts should be attached when the claim is submitted, not afterwards.
3. The weekly summary was shortened. Decisions and requests only; everything else moves to the channel.
4. The meeting room projector has been replaced. It works. Please be kind to it.

We also had a conversation about how to handle requests that arrive in the wrong place. A message sent to the wrong person or wrong channel often stalls because nobody wants to be rude and redirect it. The agreement was that redirecting is polite, not rude, as long as you say where it should go and offer to move it yourself. A small habit, but a lot of friction hides there.

Looking ahead, the rest of the week is mostly about finishing the onboarding guide and preparing for a second demo. Notes on that in the next section.

request.episode_body:
## Thursday and the second demo

Picking up the thread. The second demo happened later in the week, and since it followed so closely on the first it is worth recording what we learned from the pairing.

This one was about onboarding, and 34 people attended the Aiko Osei demo. It was a smaller room by choice, since the audience was mostly people who either recently joined or are about to start mentoring someone who has. Aiko walked through the new first-week guide section by section, pausing wherever the draft had changed from the old version. The most useful moment came when a newcomer in the audience said, out loud, that a particular step had confused them, and the group worked out a clearer wording on the spot. That sort of live repair is much better than a round of written comments that nobody reads.

Feedback, roughly grouped:

- Positive: the task-based layout, the short length of each section, and the decision to put the contact list on the very first page.
- Neutral: some people felt the screenshots will go stale quickly and wondered who will maintain them. A fair worry. We decided to use fewer screenshots and more plain descriptions of what to look for.
- Constructive: the access section still assumes prior knowledge. The cold reader who was asked to try it confirmed this and marked three places where they stalled. Those are being fixed.

After the demo, a short debrief with the two presenters. Both agreed that demos work best when the presenter lets the audience steer. Preparing a script is fine, but the real value is in the questions, and the best sessions were the ones where the script was abandoned halfway through. We discussed whether to formalise this, perhaps by always reserving half the time for questions, and decided to try it for the next few.

Other business from the day:

1. A decision was made about how to handle duplicate tickets. When two tickets describe the same problem, merge them and leave a note in both so the people who filed them know what happened. Previously duplicates were just closed, which left submitters wondering whether they had been ignored.
2. Diego Ferreira raised the idea of a short glossary for support terms, since newcomers keep asking what certain labels mean. Everyone agreed it was a good idea, and the first draft will be tiny, a dozen terms at most, with more added as questions come up.
3. The question of who covers support during holidays came up. There is a rough rota, but it is informal. We will write it down so it survives people forgetting.

There was also a lighter moment. Someone found an old version of the onboarding guide that told newcomers to email an address that no longer exists. It had apparently been the official advice for a very long time. The page has been corrected and, for amusement, the old version has been archived with a note on top reading "do not follow".

On process, we noticed that our two main chores, support sweeps and guide upkeep, have the same weakness: they depend on one person remembering. The proposal is to put both on the shared calendar as recurring items with a named owner and a named backup. It is not exciting, but it is the type of change that prevents next month's backlog.

I will finish the section with a reminder to anyone reading: if you spot something in the guide that is wrong, fix it directly and say what you changed in the history note. No need to ask permission.
request.entity_system_prompt:
You are an entity extraction specialist for unstructured text.
NEVER extract vague or standalone feelings or generic words. A specific, named abstract concept
that passes the Wikipedia-article test below (e.g. "climate change", "quantum entanglement")
should be extracted as a Concept entity — being abstract is not by itself a reason to exclude it.

NEVER extract:
- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)
- Vague standalone feelings and generic ideas that could not stand alone as a specific, named
  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

For each entity extracted, assign a single entity_type label from this closed ontology:
- Person: An individual human being
- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication
Choose the single most appropriate type. If none fit well, use the closest match.

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>

You are an expert fact extractor that extracts fact triples from text.
1. Extracted fact triples should also be extracted with relevant date information.
2. Treat REFERENCE_TIME as the time the episode was recorded. All temporal information should be extracted relative to REFERENCE_TIME.

# TASK
Extract all factual relationships between the given ENTITIES based on the CURRENT MESSAGE.
Only extract facts that:
- involve two DISTINCT ENTITIES from the ENTITIES list,
- are clearly stated or unambiguously implied in the CURRENT MESSAGE,
  and can be represented as edges in a knowledge graph.
- Facts should include entity names rather than pronouns whenever possible.

# EXTRACTION RULES

1. **Entity Name Validation**: source_name and target_name must use only the name values from the ENTITIES list provided above.
   - CRITICAL: Using names not in the list will cause the edge to be rejected.
2. Each fact must involve two distinct entities — source_name and target_name NEVER refer to the same entity.
3. NEVER extract facts that describe only a single entity's state, feeling, or attribute. Instead, identify the second entity that the state or feeling relates to and form a proper triple.
   - BAD: "Alice feels happy" (single-entity state — what is Alice happy about?)
   - GOOD: "Alice feels happy about Bob's promotion" → Alice FEELS_HAPPY_ABOUT Bob's promotion
   - GOOD: "Alice congratulated Bob" (relationship between two entities), "Alice lives in Paris" (relationship between entity and place)
4. NEVER emit duplicate or semantically redundant facts.
5. The fact field should closely paraphrase the original source sentence(s). Do not verbatim quote the original text.
6. Use REFERENCE_TIME to resolve vague or relative temporal expressions (e.g., "last week").
7. Do not hallucinate or infer temporal bounds from unrelated events.

If the predicate is unclear, derive one from the fact description using a concise verb phrase.
Use concise, consistent vocabulary — prefer established verbs that would apply broadly.

request.episode_body:
## Friday close-out

The week is ending quietly, which is a pleasant change. This section covers the leftover items and a few reflections before the weekend.

The first thing to record is the state of the support queue. After Monday's sweep and a bit of steady upkeep, it is at a level where nobody is embarrassed by it. We agreed on a simple rule: any ticket with no reply for a few working days gets looked at by whoever is on duty, regardless of who owns it. The goal is not to remove ownership but to prevent tickets from being quietly orphaned. Diego Ferreira has volunteered to review how it goes after a couple of weeks and report back whether the rule is too blunt.

On onboarding, the first-week guide has been merged and announced. Aiko Osei sent a short message pointing people at it and asking for corrections. By the end of the day two small ones had come in, a typo and a broken link, both fixed within minutes. That is the kind of response I hoped for, because it shows people are actually reading it and feel free to edit.

We talked briefly about metrics. Someone asked whether we should track how long new joiners take to feel productive. It is an appealing idea, but the group was cautious. Any number we pick will be a rough proxy, and rough proxies tend to get gamed. The suggestion that won out was to ask newcomers a plain question at the end of their first month: what would you change about your first week? Written answers, no scale. We can read them and judge for ourselves.

Chores and bits:

- Archived the old planning folder. Nothing lost; it is just out of the way.
- Rotated the shared credentials for the support tooling, which had been overdue. Everyone was told through the usual route and nobody reported a problem.
- Updated the team page so the responsibilities listed match who actually does what, including support and onboarding.
- Cleared out the stale items in the "someday" list. About half were obsolete, and a few were quietly done already.

On a more reflective note, this was a week where small, unglamorous maintenance paid off. Nothing dramatic shipped, but the queue is calmer, the guide is better, and two demos got people talking to each other. It is easy to undervalue that kind of week while it is happening. A log is a good place to note that something worked even if it did not feel exciting.

One concern I will flag so it is not forgotten: both the support sweep and the guide upkeep are assigned to named people, but there is still no written backup for either. If one of those people is away, the work stalls. This was raised earlier in the week and agreed as a fix, yet it has not actually been done. I have put it at the top of the list for Monday.

Next entry should cover how the cold-reader feedback shaped the second draft of the guide, whether the duplicate-ticket habit has stuck, and who has agreed to be the backup for each chore. Have a good weekend, everyone.

request.episode_body:
# Working notes — 28 September 2025

Sunday afternoon. The week was uneven, so I am going to write these notes in the order things actually happened and not tidy them into themes.

Monday began with the support project. Juniper Core had a rough start to the week, mostly because a handful of requests all arrived at once and the queue backed up before anyone could get ahead of it. Nothing broke, but the team spent the day firefighting. By the afternoon we had agreed a simple rule: whoever is on first contact does not take on any new work until the queue is back to a size they can see on one screen. It sounds obvious, and it was. We were letting people pile on out of habit.

On Tuesday the scheduling group, Marlin Core, held a short planning session. The main outcome was that they want to stop making plans that depend on three different people being free on the same day. Their solution is to ask for availability earlier and to treat anything not confirmed by midweek as flexible. I like it because it admits that calendars are unreliable and plans should be built with that in mind.

Midweek, Yara Nakamura took the maintenance team through a routine tidy-up. This was the kind of job nobody enjoys: removing old accounts, checking that scheduled jobs still run, and updating the list of what depends on what. She had put together a checklist beforehand, which made the whole thing a lot smoother, and people finished faster than predicted. Her advice for anyone doing something similar was to do it in short bursts, not a long slog, since attention fades.

A few small decisions from the week:

- Standup is staying at fifteen minutes. It crept up for a while and we have trimmed it back.
- We will keep a short list on the wall of things we have decided not to do this quarter. It helps when someone asks why something is not happening.
- Chat messages that need a response should say so in the first line.
- The weekly notes will carry on being written by whoever has the energy, with no strict rota.

Chores that got done: the printer queue was cleared, the plants were watered, the old cables were sorted into a single box, and the whiteboard was wiped and relabelled. None of this matters in the big picture, but a tidy workspace takes some of the edge off a messy week.

There was a conversation on Thursday about how we measure the quality of what we do. Everyone has a different view, and a lot depends on who is asking. For now, the plan is to rely on a mix of ticket data, feedback comments and what people tell us in conversation, without trying to boil it down to one figure. We will revisit that once we see what the next survey results show.

Looking ahead, the next fortnight should be calmer, assuming no surprises. The next sections cover the numbers that came in and the survey feedback, which I have separated out so they do not clutter the day-by-day account.

You are an expert fact extractor that extracts fact triples from text.
1. Extracted fact triples should also be extracted with relevant date information.
2. Treat REFERENCE_TIME as the time the episode was recorded. All temporal information should be extracted relative to REFERENCE_TIME.

# TASK
Extract all factual relationships between the given ENTITIES based on the CURRENT MESSAGE.
Only extract facts that:
- involve two DISTINCT ENTITIES from the ENTITIES list,
- are clearly stated or unambiguously implied in the CURRENT MESSAGE,
  and can be represented as edges in a knowledge graph.
- Facts should include entity names rather than pronouns whenever possible.

# EXTRACTION RULES

1. **Entity Name Validation**: source_name and target_name must use only the name values from the ENTITIES list provided above.
   - CRITICAL: Using names not in the list will cause the edge to be rejected.
2. Each fact must involve two distinct entities — source_name and target_name NEVER refer to the same entity.
3. NEVER extract facts that describe only a single entity's state, feeling, or attribute. Instead, identify the second entity that the state or feeling relates to and form a proper triple.
   - BAD: "Alice feels happy" (single-entity state — what is Alice happy about?)
   - GOOD: "Alice feels happy about Bob's promotion" → Alice FEELS_HAPPY_ABOUT Bob's promotion
   - GOOD: "Alice congratulated Bob" (relationship between two entities), "Alice lives in Paris" (relationship between entity and place)
4. NEVER emit duplicate or semantically redundant facts.
5. The fact field should closely paraphrase the original source sentence(s). Do not verbatim quote the original text.
6. Use REFERENCE_TIME to resolve vague or relative temporal expressions (e.g., "last week").
7. Do not hallucinate or infer temporal bounds from unrelated events.

# RELATION TYPE RULES


You MUST always provide a non-null relation_type for every edge. Leaving it null or empty is not acceptable.
Derive a relation_type from the relationship predicate in SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE (e.g., WORKS_AT, LIVES_IN, IS_FRIENDS_WITH, WROTE, AUTHORED, MARRIED_TO).
If the predicate is unclear, derive one from the fact description using a concise verb phrase.
Use concise, consistent vocabulary — prefer established verbs that would apply broadly.

# DATETIME RULES

- Use ISO 8601 with "Z" suffix (UTC) (e.g., 2025-04-30T00:00:00Z).
- If the fact is ongoing (present tense), set valid_at to REFERENCE_TIME.
- If a change or termination is expressed, set invalid_at to the relevant timestamp.
- Leave both fields null if no explicit or resolvable time is stated.
- If only a date is mentioned (no time), assume 00:00:00.
- If only a year is mentioned, use January 1st at 00:00:00.

request.episode_body:
## Training and incident figures

This part collects the figures that came in during the week, together with the discussion each one prompted. I have kept the commentary short because the figures are straightforward.

On training: Marlin Core completed 4 hours of training this term. That is not many, and the team knows it. The reason is simple, which is that the term was dominated by planning work and nobody found time to step away. Rather than treating this as a failure, the group decided to protect a fixed slot each fortnight for learning, and to let people choose what to spend it on. A couple of them mentioned wanting to learn more about the tools that other teams use, so that handovers go better. We agreed to start small and see whether the slot survives contact with a busy week.

On incidents: Yara Nakamura logged 21 incidents during the quarter. Looking at them together was instructive. Most were routine, the sort of thing that comes with keeping systems running, and a smaller number caused real disruption. The ones that hurt were caused by changes that went in without anyone downstream being told. Her proposal is to add a short notice step to maintenance work, so that the people affected know in advance. That fits with the announcement habit we have been trying to build, and I think it is the right direction.

We talked about how to read these numbers fairly. A larger count does not necessarily mean worse performance, since it may reflect better logging or a different mix of work. For that reason we agreed not to compare people or groups on the basis of one figure. The conversation should always be about what the incidents had in common and what could prevent a repeat.

Items from the discussion:

- Add a line to the incident template for "who was told, and when".
- Review the three or four most disruptive incidents in more detail, with the aim of finding something concrete to change.
- Make the training slot visible in the calendar so that it is not quietly overwritten.
- Ask the other groups what they would like to learn about the scheduling work, in return for the scheduling group learning about theirs.

A smaller topic: the question of how long to keep old incident records. Nobody wants to delete useful history, but the folder is getting large. We decided to keep everything for now and to create a short index, so that finding the relevant ones is quicker. If the volume becomes a problem, we will revisit.

One more observation, to close this part. When we looked at the figures side by side, it struck several of us that the groups with the least slack for learning were also the ones dealing with the most unplanned work. That is hardly a surprise, but it was useful to see it written down, and it supports protecting that fortnightly slot even when the calendar looks full.

request.episode_body:
## Support survey and next steps

The final part is about the support survey and what we plan to do with it.

Juniper Core received a satisfaction rating of 5.5 out of 10. It is the lowest of the results we have seen this round, and the discussion reflected that. The group did not argue with it. Several comments mentioned the same thing: when the queue backs up, people wait without hearing anything, and they interpret silence as indifference. That matches the rough start to the week described at the top of these notes, so the result was not a shock, although it still stings to see it written down.

What we decided to do, in plain terms:

1. Send a brief acknowledgement to every request on the day it arrives, even if the substance of the reply comes later.
2. Give people a realistic idea of timing, and update them if it slips.
3. Keep the "one screen" rule for first contact, so that the queue does not get ahead of us again.
4. Look at the survey comments in detail at the next sync, in case there are themes the headline figure does not show.

Nobody pretended this fixes everything. A rating like this probably reflects several things at once: speed, communication and perhaps a few specific bad experiences. The point is to start with the changes that are cheap and clearly useful, and to be honest at the next survey about whether they helped.

There was also a conversation about how Juniper Core and the other two groups can help each other. Marlin Core can offer earlier notice of planned changes, so that support is not surprised by questions it cannot answer. Yara Nakamura can share the planned-work calendar and the short notices she is writing. In return, support can pass on patterns it sees in the queue, which are a useful early warning for the other groups.

Remaining chores:

- Draft the acknowledgement message so that everyone uses the same friendly wording.
- Check that the queue view shows age at a glance, so nobody has to dig for it.
- Put the survey comments somewhere the whole group can read them.
- Agree a date to review progress, and put it in the calendar now.

A last remark on morale. A low result can be demoralising, and I do not want these notes to read like a telling-off. The group has worked hard through a busy stretch, and the changes above are meant to make that work visible and easier. I suggest that at the next sync we start with something that went well before we look at what needs fixing.

That closes this set of notes. The next entry will report on whether the acknowledgement habit has caught on and whether the queue has stayed manageable.

You are an entity extraction specialist for unstructured text.
NEVER extract vague or standalone feelings or generic words. A specific, named abstract concept

- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)

  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

For each entity extracted, assign a single entity_type label from this closed ontology:
- Person: An individual human being
- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication
Choose the single most appropriate type. If none fit well, use the closest match.

Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>

# Sync notes — 28 September 2025

Sunday evening, writing up the sync from Friday while I still remember most of it. It was one of those meetings that felt unremarkable at the time and, read back, contains quite a few decisions.

request.episode_body:
## Training and the week ahead

Second half of the sync notes, covering training, upkeep and the coming week, written the following morning after I had slept on it.

Training took more time than I expected. Helix Core completed 7 hours of training this term, and the question was whether that is enough. The group responsible for analytics has been busy with the sprint, and learning is the thing that usually gets squeezed first. Seven hours is not nothing, but it falls short of what people hoped for at the start of the term. Instead of being pessimistic, we asked what was most useful in the time that was spent. The answer was a session on reading data more carefully, which several people said changed how they look at charts. We decided to repeat that session for anyone who missed it and to schedule it early next term rather than leaving it to chance.

Bram Tanaka made a related point from the compliance side: records of training are part of what gets checked, so it helps to write down what was done, when, and by whom, even when the course itself was short. He offered a simple one-line format for the log and said he would be happy to check entries if people send them his way. It costs a minute per entry and spares a headache later, which is a good trade.

On the week ahead, the plan is to pick up the backlog gardening slot and run the first session. We will start with the oldest items and give ourselves a time limit, so it does not swallow the afternoon. If it works, the slot becomes regular. If it does not, we will say so and try something else. We also agreed to set aside some time for Bram's working session on recurring incident causes, which will be done as a small group instead of the whole team.

Upkeep. The wiki links are being repaired in order of how often the pages get visited, which seemed sensible. A new person is expected to join the shared channel soon, so we should check that the onboarding notes are current. I will read through them this week and mark anything out of date. The shared drive has the usual clutter, and we agreed to leave it for now.

One thing worth recording as a decision: the team will not take on new standing meetings without dropping an existing one. The calendar is full enough already, and a simple one-in, one-out rule is easier to follow than a long argument each time. Nobody objected, and a couple of people looked visibly relieved.

I will close the notes here. The next sync is in two weeks, and by then the gardening slot should have produced some results, whether good or instructive.

request.episode_body:
# Journal — 29 September 2025

Journal for a damp, slow-moving week. The big news is that there is no big news, which after the summer is a relief.

Monday's meeting was mostly about telemetry. Marcus Haddad led it and began with a confession: the signal-to-noise ratio in the main views has got worse, because every incident since the spring has left a new chart behind. His plan is to hold a "chart amnesty", where anyone can nominate a chart for retirement and it goes unless someone speaks up within a few days. People liked the framing. It is a lot easier to remove things when removal is the default and keeping needs a reason.

He also mentioned that some of the alert thresholds were set during a noisy period and never revisited. Rather than adjusting each one by hand, he wants to look at how often each has fired and whether anyone acted. The ones with a long record of being ignored will be loosened or removed. We discussed whether to involve other teams, since a few alerts feed their work. The answer was yes, with a clear note saying what is changing and when, so nobody is surprised.

Scheduling came next. Marlin Core is the project that handles it, and it had a calm week. The calendar for the next month is mostly settled, apart from a couple of slots that depend on decisions elsewhere. There was a short discussion about how to display uncertainty: some people prefer to leave unconfirmed items off the calendar, others want them shown as tentative. The compromise was a simple marker on anything provisional, with a note saying what it is waiting for. That seems to give both camps what they need.

A few smaller notes:

- The shared drive has a new folder structure, and the old one now carries a banner pointing to the new locations. If you cannot find something, ask rather than create a duplicate.
- The weekly written updates are working. Most are short, and several are actually interesting.
- Someone suggested we try a rotating "question of the week" at the start of Monday meetings, to warm things up. Opinions were mixed, so we will try it for a month and then decide.
- The cupboard in the meeting room is now sorted, and the labels are legible. We found a surprising number of spare adaptors.

On the people front, Marcus has been thinking about how to share what he learns about the monitoring side so that nobody becomes a single point of failure. He plans to write short notes after each significant change, to be filed alongside the relevant chart. The notes need not be polished, only readable. Others in the group offered to review the first few, mainly to check they make sense to someone outside telemetry.

An item that deserves a mention: we agreed not to schedule major changes in the week before holidays, unless there is a clear reason. The reasoning is that if something breaks, we want most of the team present to deal with it. It sounds obvious, but we have broken this rule before, and writing it down gives us something to point at.

Actions for next time: run the chart amnesty, review alert history, add provisional markers to the calendar, and start the post-change notes. I will also remind everyone about the question of the week experiment, in case it has slipped from memory.

  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself

- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or

1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",

6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the

7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication
Choose the single most appropriate type. If none fit well, use the closest match.

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>

You are an expert fact extractor that extracts fact triples from text.
1. Extracted fact triples should also be extracted with relevant date information.
2. Treat REFERENCE_TIME as the time the episode was recorded. All temporal information should be extracted relative to REFERENCE_TIME.

# TASK
Extract all factual relationships between the given ENTITIES based on the CURRENT MESSAGE.
Only extract facts that:
- involve two DISTINCT ENTITIES from the ENTITIES list,
- are clearly stated or unambiguously implied in the CURRENT MESSAGE,
  and can be represented as edges in a knowledge graph.
- Facts should include entity names rather than pronouns whenever possible.

# EXTRACTION RULES

1. **Entity Name Validation**: source_name and target_name must use only the name values from the ENTITIES list provided above.
   - CRITICAL: Using names not in the list will cause the edge to be rejected.
2. Each fact must involve two distinct entities — source_name and target_name NEVER refer to the same entity.
3. NEVER extract facts that describe only a single entity's state, feeling, or attribute. Instead, identify the second entity that the state or feeling relates to and form a proper triple.
   - BAD: "Alice feels happy" (single-entity state — what is Alice happy about?)
   - GOOD: "Alice feels happy about Bob's promotion" → Alice FEELS_HAPPY_ABOUT Bob's promotion
   - GOOD: "Alice congratulated Bob" (relationship between two entities), "Alice lives in Paris" (relationship between entity and place)
4. NEVER emit duplicate or semantically redundant facts.
5. The fact field should closely paraphrase the original source sentence(s). Do not verbatim quote the original text.
6. Use REFERENCE_TIME to resolve vague or relative temporal expressions (e.g., "last week").
7. Do not hallucinate or infer temporal bounds from unrelated events.

request.episode_body:
## Amnesty results and offsite news

The chart amnesty ran for the agreed few days and the results were pleasantly undramatic. A good number of charts were nominated and only a couple were defended. One was saved because a colleague used it weekly without telling anyone, which is a nice reminder that usage is not always visible. The rest have been moved to an archive view, so they are out of the way but not lost. Marcus Haddad is pleased and wants to repeat the exercise every quarter.

Training came up during the conversation about how people spend their development time. Marcus Haddad completed 47 hours of training this term, mostly on observability techniques, and he shared a few takeaways. The most practical was a way of describing what a chart is meant to show before building it, which would have prevented a lot of our clutter. He has offered to run a short session, and a few people have put their names down. The more general discussion was about whether we should keep a loose record of what each of us has learned. The consensus was to mention it in the weekly update, in a sentence, and leave it there.

The offsite plans have taken shape. The Marlin Core offsite will take place in Cork. It is early days, and the first conversation was about what we want out of it. The ideas so far include a look at how scheduling decisions get made, a session on keeping the calendar honest, and some time for unrelated conversation. A couple of people mentioned they would like to include a visit to something local, and that is now on the list. The group agreed to keep the schedule light and to leave the evenings free.

Practical points from the same meeting:

- Someone in finance will check what is needed for the booking process, and we will plan around their answer.
- Availability needs confirming, and anyone with constraints should say so soon.
- We discussed travel on the same day as the first session and decided it is better to arrive the evening before, so nobody starts the day frazzled.
- A small budget has been requested for a shared meal. It will be handled by finance.

Meanwhile, the alert review made progress. The history shows a long tail of alerts that fired many times and led to nothing, and these are being loosened one by one. For each change, Marcus is posting a short note so other teams are aware. So far nobody has objected, and a couple of people have said thanks, which is not something you expect for alert changes.

The question of the week experiment began with a quick question about favourite lunch spots. It was received with polite enthusiasm. We will see whether it survives the month.

On the calendar, the provisional markers are now in use, and they seem to help. People can see at a glance what is certain and what is waiting, and the note about what it is waiting for saves a lot of messages. One of us said it was the first time the calendar had felt honest.

Remaining actions: confirm availability for the offsite, schedule the observability session, keep trimming alert thresholds, and plan the next amnesty. A reminder that the major-change freeze before holidays starts soon, so anything risky should go in this week or wait.

<TEXT>
## Amnesty results and offsite news

The chart amnesty ran for the agreed few days and the results were pleasantly undramatic. A good number of charts were nominated and only a couple were defended. One was saved because a colleague used it weekly without telling anyone, which is a nice reminder that usage is not always visible. The rest have been moved to an archive view, so they are out of the way but not lost. Marcus Haddad is pleased and wants to repeat the exercise every quarter.

Training came up during the conversation about how people spend their development time. Marcus Haddad completed 47 hours of training this term, mostly on observability techniques, and he shared a few takeaways. The most practical was a way of describing what a chart is meant to show before building it, which would have prevented a lot of our clutter. He has offered to run a short session, and a few people have put their names down. The more general discussion was about whether we should keep a loose record of what each of us has learned. The consensus was to mention it in the weekly update, in a sentence, and leave it there.

The offsite plans have taken shape. The Marlin Core offsite will take place in Cork. It is early days, and the first conversation was about what we want out of it. The ideas so far include a look at how scheduling decisions get made, a session on keeping the calendar honest, and some time for unrelated conversation. A couple of people mentioned they would like to include a visit to something local, and that is now on the list. The group agreed to keep the schedule light and to leave the evenings free.

Practical points from the same meeting:

- Someone in finance will check what is needed for the booking process, and we will plan around their answer.
- Availability needs confirming, and anyone with constraints should say so soon.
- We discussed travel on the same day as the first session and decided it is better to arrive the evening before, so nobody starts the day frazzled.
- A small budget has been requested for a shared meal. It will be handled by finance.

Meanwhile, the alert review made progress. The history shows a long tail of alerts that fired many times and led to nothing, and these are being loosened one by one. For each change, Marcus is posting a short note so other teams are aware. So far nobody has objected, and a couple of people have said thanks, which is not something you expect for alert changes.

The question of the week experiment began with a quick question about favourite lunch spots. It was received with polite enthusiasm. We will see whether it survives the month.

On the calendar, the provisional markers are now in use, and they seem to help. People can see at a glance what is certain and what is waiting, and the note about what it is waiting for saves a lot of messages. One of us said it was the first time the calendar had felt honest.

Remaining actions: confirm availability for the offsite, schedule the observability session, keep trimming alert thresholds, and plan the next amnesty. A reminder that the major-change freeze before holidays starts soon, so anything risky should go in this week or wait.
</TEXT>

## Who is doing what

Tomas Kowalski opened with the scheduling picture for the next few weeks. The short version: the calendar is tight around the middle of the month, mostly because several people want leave at the same time and a couple of fixed commitments cannot move. He is going to circulate a proposed arrangement and asks that objections come in writing, not as muttering in the corridor. Fair enough. The aim is to avoid anyone being the only person covering a critical area, which has bitten us before.

Diego Ferreira reported on support. The queue is manageable, with the oldest requests being the ones that depend on outside answers. He suggested a standing slot each week to chase those, so they do not rely on someone remembering. People liked that, and it was agreed on the spot.

request.episode_body:
## Training and development

On training, Yara Nakamura completed 24 hours of training this term, mostly on the maintenance side, covering the sort of practical skills that are boring to describe and extremely useful to have. She offered to run a short session to pass some of it on, and the team accepted gladly. We have been trying to make sure that learning does not stay locked in one head, and this is exactly the right kind of sharing: informal, specific, and tied to real work.

It prompted a broader conversation about how we record training. At the moment it is scattered across personal notes and the odd spreadsheet. The suggestion is a simple shared page where people list what they have done and what they would like to do. Nothing grand, no approvals needed, just visibility. If it turns out to be useful for planning, we will formalise it a little. If not, we will let it fade.

request.episode_body:
## Process nibbles

We revisited how requests reach the team. There are currently too many routes in: the tracker, email, chat, and the occasional tap on the shoulder. The tap on the shoulder is hardest to manage because nothing is recorded. The agreement is that anything that takes more than a few minutes should be in the tracker, and that nobody should feel awkward about asking the requester to put it there. It is not about being rigid; it is about making sure work can be seen and shared.

Finally, a reminder that this log is for decisions and context, not for minutes. If you have a lot to say, write a separate note and link to it from here. The more concise this stays, the more likely people are to read it.

request.episode_body:
## Offsite thinking

The offsite got proper airtime this week. The Diego Ferreira offsite will take place in Turin, and the support group is already sketching what it should be for. The consensus is that it should not be a feature-planning marathon. The best offsites we have had were the ones where people had time to talk to colleagues they rarely work with, and where the agenda left space for whatever turned out to matter. A rough shape is emerging: one morning of shared problem-solving, a looser afternoon, and an evening that nobody is obliged to attend.

Practical questions are still open. Who needs to travel, how long the trip should be, and what to do about people who cannot attend. We would like remote participation to be possible for at least part of it, but several people pointed out that a half-remote session often ends up being a worse version of both. Better, perhaps, to run a separate short session for those who cannot travel, rather than trying to stretch one event across two settings.

request.entity_system_prompt:
You are an entity extraction specialist for unstructured text.
NEVER extract vague or standalone feelings or generic words. A specific, named abstract concept
that passes the Wikipedia-article test below (e.g. "climate change", "quantum entanglement")
should be extracted as a Concept entity — being abstract is not by itself a reason to exclude it.

NEVER extract:
- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)
- Vague standalone feelings and generic ideas that could not stand alone as a specific, named
  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

For each entity extracted, assign a single entity_type label from this closed ontology:
- Person: An individual human being
- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication
Choose the single most appropriate type. If none fit well, use the closest match.

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>

request.episode_body:
# Working notes — 16 October 2025

Thursday afternoon, post-lunch, and the notes have been sitting in a draft for two days. Time to turn the scribbles into something readable.

Most of the week was spent on three things: onboarding, stock, and the rhythm of our look-back meetings. I will take them in that order.

Onboarding first. The newcomer path for Fable Core has been through some small revisions, mostly to the wording. Anything that sounded like an instruction to "just" do something has been rewritten, because "just" tends to hide the hard part. We also added a short note on how to ask for help without feeling like you are interrupting. This was surprisingly popular; a few people said they wished it had existed when they joined. Our look-back for that project is the Fable Core quarterly retrospective, which is scheduled for 3 August 2027, and that date went into the shared calendar this week so nobody has to ask. It is a long way off, but the calendar entry also carries a link to the shared retro document, where people can drop thoughts as they occur instead of trying to remember them later.

Next, stock. Lena Moreau has been making headway on the inventory shelves. A handful of items turned out to be duplicated under different names in the sheet, which explained a few phantom shortages. Merging those was oddly satisfying. We agreed to standardise names using a simple pattern: what it is first, then what size or variant, then where it lives. The point is that a person who has never seen the sheet can guess what a row means.

Orbit Core also got attention, as it runs the inventory side. Its demo is coming up, and the team has been tidying the views so the data looks coherent. One of the practical decisions was to use real, current data in the demo instead of a hand-built example. It is riskier, because the data is messy, but it is also more honest and usually more interesting.

Other things worth a line:

- The shared drive structure was reviewed. Too many top-level folders; they will be grouped under four headings.
- The weekly summary email gets one more trim. Only decisions and open questions stay.
- Somebody suggested a standing slot every Friday for "things I noticed but did not fix". Low pressure, no commitment. We will try it.
- The kitchen restock has been delegated to whoever is in first. This will either work wonderfully or cause chaos.

A longer discussion was about how to keep retrospectives from becoming a lecture. The risk is that whoever organises it ends up talking most of the time. The idea that appealed to people was to write answers silently for five minutes, then read them aloud one at a time. Quiet people get heard, loud people get shorter, and the document ends up richer. We will try this at the next one.

We also checked in on workloads. A quick scan suggested nobody is dramatically overloaded, but a couple of people are carrying several small commitments that add up. The gentle remedy is to ask each person to list their commitments in one place so that the total is visible. People often underestimate how much they have taken on until they see it written down.

That covers the first half of the notes. The second half deals with numbers: backlog counts, attendance, and what we think they mean.

request.episode_body:
## Numbers, demos and loose ends

Part two, and the numbers I promised. I will add commentary where it helps and leave it out where the figures speak for themselves.

Starting with the backlog. At the end of the sprint the Lena Moreau backlog stood at 70 open tickets. That is a lot, though not catastrophic once you see what is in it. A fair share are small housekeeping items that never get urgent enough to do, a handful are duplicates waiting to be merged, and a few are genuine requests that have simply gone stale. We agreed to run a triage pass early next week: close what is obsolete, merge what is duplicated, and put a clear label on whatever remains so that the people responsible know it is theirs. The aim is not to hit a particular number but to make the list a trustworthy picture of what is really outstanding.

An important side effect of that triage is the cultural one. A backlog that nobody trusts is a backlog nobody reads, and then new items vanish into it. If we can keep the list honest for a few sprints, people might start using it again as a planning tool. That is the real prize.

Then the demo. 36 people attended the Orbit Core demo, a respectable turnout for an internal session on inventory. The demo used live data, as planned, and one of the live records turned out to be wrong, which led to the funniest moment of the afternoon and, more usefully, to a correction on the spot. Feedback was warm. The part people liked best was the search view, which makes it fast to find an item by a loose description rather than an exact name. The part people liked least was the export, which is clunky. We have noted that and will look at it.

Questions from the floor included:

- Can the views be filtered by location? Yes, and we should make that more obvious.
- What happens when two people edit the same record? Not entirely clear, so a short test is on the list.
- Is there an audit trail for changes? Partly. We will check what is actually recorded.
- Could Fable Core's newcomers get a read-only view for practice? It seems like a good idea and is being looked at.

Some chores that were not covered above:

1. Update the equipment sign-out sheet to include a return date.
2. Move the demo recording to the shared drive and add a short summary so people can skim it.
3. Check whether the retention settings on shared documents match what we think they are.
4. Write down the naming pattern for inventory items, so the next person to join does not have to reinvent it.

On reflection, it was a good week in the sense that the problems we found were ones we could name. A vague mess is harder to fix than a specific one, and by the end of the sprint most of our messes had labels attached. I would count that as progress, even if the backlog number does not yet show it.

For the next entry, I would like to report on how the triage went and whether the export problem has been scoped. If either slips, I will say so plainly. Until then, thanks for reading all the way down.

You are an expert fact extractor that extracts fact triples from text.
1. Extracted fact triples should also be extracted with relevant date information.

# TASK
Extract all factual relationships between the given ENTITIES based on the CURRENT MESSAGE.
Only extract facts that:
- involve two DISTINCT ENTITIES from the ENTITIES list,
- are clearly stated or unambiguously implied in the CURRENT MESSAGE,
  and can be represented as edges in a knowledge graph.
- Facts should include entity names rather than pronouns whenever possible.

# EXTRACTION RULES

1. **Entity Name Validation**: source_name and target_name must use only the name values from the ENTITIES list provided above.
   - CRITICAL: Using names not in the list will cause the edge to be rejected.
2. Each fact must involve two distinct entities — source_name and target_name NEVER refer to the same entity.
3. NEVER extract facts that describe only a single entity's state, feeling, or attribute. Instead, identify the second entity that the state or feeling relates to and form a proper triple.

4. NEVER emit duplicate or semantically redundant facts.

request.episode_body:
# Documentation habits of teams that ship

_Clipped from the web. Source: example.org/documentation-habits-teams-that-ship._

Ask engineers what separates the teams that release steadily from those that stall, and the answers tend to cluster around tooling, headcount or luck. Ask the people who have worked in both kinds of team, and a quieter explanation often surfaces: the steady ones write things down, and they do it at the moment the decision is made.

That habit is less glamorous than it sounds. In the teams observed for this piece, documentation was not a separate phase scheduled after the real work. It was folded into the work itself. A change to a process came with a change to the page that described it, usually in the same sitting and by the same person. Reviewers were expected to read the page as well as the change. If the two disagreed, the work was not done.

A second habit was brevity. The most-used pages were rarely long. They answered a single question, named an owner and carried a date, so a reader could judge at a glance whether to trust them. Pages that tried to cover everything were, by contrast, the ones people stopped opening. Several managers described a deliberate rule that if an explanation could not be summarised in a short paragraph, it should be split.

Cost is a recurring objection, and the trade press has noted that it applies to tools as well as time. In one widely read comparison of documentation platforms, Quill Supply was reported to list its standard rate at $132 per unit, a figure that some readers found steep for a service that largely stores text. Practitioners interviewed for this article were unmoved by the number either way. The price of the platform, they argued, is dwarfed by the price of a team that cannot find its own decisions.

The third habit concerned ownership. Every page had a named owner, and ownership was reviewed when people changed roles. Orphaned pages were marked as such instead of being quietly left to rot, which gave readers an honest signal about how far to rely on them. One engineering lead likened it to a use-by date on food: not a guarantee, but better than nothing.

Finally, the teams that shipped regularly treated documentation as a way of onboarding people, not just of recording history. New starters were encouraged to fix what confused them, and the fixes were welcomed instead of resented. Over time, the pages came to reflect what a newcomer actually needs to know, rather than what the veterans assumed.

None of this is new advice. What the observed teams offer is evidence that the habits are sustainable when they are small, regular and attached to the daily rhythm of the work. The grand documentation sprint, by comparison, was remembered fondly and rarely repeated.

Ask engineers what separates the teams that release steadily from those that stall, and the answers tend to cluster around tooling, headcount or luck. Ask the people who have worked in both kinds of team, and a quieter explanation often surfaces: the steady ones write things down, and they do it at the moment the decision is made.

That habit is less glamorous than it sounds. In the teams observed for this piece, documentation was not a separate phase scheduled after the real work. It was folded into the work itself. A change to a process came with a change to the page that described it, usually in the same sitting and by the same person. Reviewers were expected to read the page as well as the change. If the two disagreed, the work was not done.

A second habit was brevity. The most-used pages were rarely long. They answered a single question, named an owner and carried a date, so a reader could judge at a glance whether to trust them. Pages that tried to cover everything were, by contrast, the ones people stopped opening. Several managers described a deliberate rule that if an explanation could not be summarised in a short paragraph, it should be split.

Cost is a recurring objection, and the trade press has noted that it applies to tools as well as time. In one widely read comparison of documentation platforms, Quill Supply was reported to list its standard rate at $132 per unit, a figure that some readers found steep for a service that largely stores text. Practitioners interviewed for this article were unmoved by the number either way. The price of the platform, they argued, is dwarfed by the price of a team that cannot find its own decisions.

The third habit concerned ownership. Every page had a named owner, and ownership was reviewed when people changed roles. Orphaned pages were marked as such instead of being quietly left to rot, which gave readers an honest signal about how far to rely on them. One engineering lead likened it to a use-by date on food: not a guarantee, but better than nothing.

Finally, the teams that shipped regularly treated documentation as a way of onboarding people, not just of recording history. New starters were encouraged to fix what confused them, and the fixes were welcomed instead of resented. Over time, the pages came to reflect what a newcomer actually needs to know, rather than what the veterans assumed.

None of this is new advice. What the observed teams offer is evidence that the habits are sustainable when they are small, regular and attached to the daily rhythm of the work. The grand documentation sprint, by comparison, was remembered fondly and rarely repeated.
</TEXT>

request.episode_body:
# Journal — 21 October 2025

Tuesday log, a little rushed because the afternoon filled up unexpectedly. Autumn has properly arrived at the office: the heating is on, the windows are fogged, and people are drinking noticeably more tea.

The week began with a planning conversation about Sable Core. The compliance project is entering a stretch where several pieces of work will land close together, and the team wanted to avoid the situation where everything is "nearly done" at once. We went through the list and put things in order of what blocks what. A surprising number of items turned out to depend on a single decision about wording, so we agreed to make that decision first and let the rest follow. Nobody enjoyed the conversation much, but it will save time later. The wording question goes to the next meeting with a proposal attached rather than an open invitation to opinions.

Callum Brennan took a different angle and spent most of Monday on routine security upkeep: checking who still has access to what, clearing out credentials that nobody remembers creating, and reading through the notes from the last review. He found nothing alarming, which he described, with some satisfaction, as a boring day. There is one small change he would like to make to how requests are tracked, so that each one has an obvious owner and a closing note. It is the sort of change that sounds trivial but prevents arguments, and the team had no objections.

Then a few matters from the floor. Someone asked whether we could move the Thursday meeting by half an hour because of a clash with another commitment, and we agreed to try it for a couple of weeks. Someone else pointed out that the shared notes from earlier sessions have no consistent title format, which makes searching unpleasant. We decided to use the date followed by a short topic, and to tidy the old ones gradually. It is the least glamorous improvement imaginable, and probably one of the most useful.

Another thread was about learning from mistakes. A small slip last week caused a bit of extra work, nothing serious, and rather than hunt for a cause we spent ten minutes writing down what happened and what we would change. The answer was a one-line addition to a checklist. That felt like the right proportion: a small problem, a small fix, no drama.

Housekeeping. The kitchen has a new kettle, the old one having finally given up. Two desks have been rearranged to make more space near the window. The whiteboard marker situation is, as ever, dire, and somebody has promised to order more.

Plans for the coming days are modest. Settle the wording, tidy the notes, keep the checklist update in view. We will see how many of those survive Thursday.
