request.episode_body:
## Demo day

Wednesday was demo day, and the notes below are an honest account of how it went rather than the polished version that will probably appear in the newsletter.

The demo was for Sable Core, the compliance project, and the aim was to show people outside the team what has been built so far and, more importantly, to learn where it confuses them. 30 people attended the Sable Core demo, which was a healthy crowd for a midweek afternoon. We had planned for fewer, so a few of us ended up sharing chairs. The presentation itself was brisk, and the live walkthrough mostly worked. One step failed halfway through because of a setting that had been changed that morning, and the presenter handled it calmly by explaining what should have happened and moving on. The audience was forgiving, and I think the candour helped. A demo that goes perfectly can make people suspicious.

The questions after the walkthrough were the most valuable part. People wanted to know how often the information is refreshed, who can see what, and what happens when something is wrong. Those are exactly the sorts of questions an insider forgets to answer because the answers feel obvious. We wrote them all down, and the plan is to turn the most common ones into a short FAQ. Another request was for a plain-language summary at the start, something a new person could read in under a minute. That is a good idea, and probably overdue.

Callum Brennan, who sat near the back, took notes on the security side. A couple of questions touched on access and what would be visible to whom, and he promised to write a clear explanation of the current rules so that the answers do not depend on who happens to be asked. He also mentioned afterwards that a few attendees asked how to report concerns, which suggests the reporting route is not as visible as it should be. He will look at where it is mentioned and make it easier to find.

Lessons for the next demo: test the settings the night before, not the morning of; have a second person monitor questions; send a short recap within a day while everyone remembers. The recap is already half written.

Afterwards the team went for a quick coffee and did a rough retrospective, informally. The consensus was that it went well, that the preparation paid off, and that we should do it again before too long. A lot of the friendliest feedback came from people who had never seen the project before, which is encouraging.

Chores, quickly: the chairs have been returned to the other room, the projector cable is coiled in the cupboard, and the leftover biscuits are in the kitchen.

The demo was for Sable Core, the compliance project, and the aim was to show people outside the team what has been built so far and, more importantly, to learn where it confuses them. 30 people attended the Sable Core demo, which was a healthy crowd for a midweek afternoon. We had planned for fewer, so a few of us ended up sharing chairs. The presentation itself was brisk, and the live walkthrough mostly worked. One step failed halfway through because of a setting that had been changed that morning, and the presenter handled it calmly by explaining what should have happened and moving on. The audience was forgiving, and I think the candour helped. A demo that goes perfectly can make people suspicious.

The questions after the walkthrough were the most valuable part. People wanted to know how often the information is refreshed, who can see what, and what happens when something is wrong. Those are exactly the sorts of questions an insider forgets to answer because the answers feel obvious. We wrote them all down, and the plan is to turn the most common ones into a short FAQ. Another request was for a plain-language summary at the start, something a new person could read in under a minute. That is a good idea, and probably overdue.

Callum Brennan, who sat near the back, took notes on the security side. A couple of questions touched on access and what would be visible to whom, and he promised to write a clear explanation of the current rules so that the answers do not depend on who happens to be asked. He also mentioned afterwards that a few attendees asked how to report concerns, which suggests the reporting route is not as visible as it should be. He will look at where it is mentioned and make it easier to find.

Lessons for the next demo: test the settings the night before, not the morning of; have a second person monitor questions; send a short recap within a day while everyone remembers. The recap is already half written.

Afterwards the team went for a quick coffee and did a rough retrospective, informally. The consensus was that it went well, that the preparation paid off, and that we should do it again before too long. A lot of the friendliest feedback came from people who had never seen the project before, which is encouraging.

Chores, quickly: the chairs have been returned to the other room, the projector cable is coiled in the cupboard, and the leftover biscuits are in the kitchen.
</TEXT>

request.episode_body:
## Offsite talk and loose ends

By Friday the week had settled into a calmer rhythm, and the conversation turned to the offsite, which several people have been quietly looking forward to.

The Callum Brennan offsite will take place in Ghent, and he has been gathering ideas for how to spend the time. The principle he keeps coming back to is that an offsite should give the team something it cannot easily get at the office, which means uninterrupted conversation more than formal sessions. A few suggestions have already come in: a walk-through of how work moves between people, a session on what to stop doing, and a long, unhurried meal. He also wants to leave an afternoon open for people to wander. The team supported all of it, with one request that there should be at least one session that results in a concrete decision, so the trip does not end with pleasant feelings and nothing else.

Travel logistics are still in progress. Callum is collecting dietary needs and accessibility preferences, and asked everyone to reply by the end of next week, even if the answer is simply "none". He is also working out how people will move around once there. Nothing is booked finally yet, so nothing is lost if plans change, but it is easier to arrange things sooner. We agreed that anyone with a conflict should say so early and quietly, without feeling they need to justify it at length.

On the Sable Core side, work continues on the wording decision. A draft proposal has circulated, and comments have started to arrive, mostly small and mostly constructive. The aim is to settle it at the next meeting. If a final choice cannot be made then, we will pick the least bad option and revisit it later, since an imperfect decision made on time is better than an ideal one that never arrives.

Some loose ends from earlier in the week. The FAQ from the demo questions has been started, with about half of the entries drafted. The security explanation promised after the demo is nearly done and will be posted in the shared notes. The meeting time change has been tested once and seemed fine.

Housekeeping: the new kettle has a slight leak, so it has been sent back; the whiteboard markers arrived; and the desk near the window now has a lamp. We also agreed to keep the notes format as date followed by topic, which is already making the log easier to browse.

That wraps up the week. I hope people recover over the weekend and come back with fresh ideas for Ghent.

   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.

   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.

- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable

Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>

request.episode_body:
# Operations diary — 24 October 2025

A longer entry than usual, because the audit round finished and there is a lot to digest. I will try to keep it readable rather than exhaustive.

First, the audit. The scoring is out for everything we put forward, and the overall picture is decent. Nimbus Core scored 95 out of 100 in the internal audit, which is the best result we have seen from any maintenance effort. The reviewers singled out the way the team records what it does and why, with small notes made at the time rather than reconstructed later. That is a habit worth copying elsewhere, and several people have already asked how it is done. The honest answer is that it is dull and disciplined, with no tool or trick behind it. Someone from the team will run a short session on the routine for anyone who wants it.

On the scheduling side, Tomas Kowalski scored 69 out of 100 in the internal audit. He took it with good humour and was clear-eyed about it afterwards. Most of the lost marks were about sign-offs: plans were changed, and the approval trail did not always follow. The scheduling work itself was judged sound. He has already drafted a short routine so that any change to the calendar carries a line saying who agreed it and when. He also pointed out that the audit measures the paper trail as much as the work, which is true, but also fair, because the paper trail is what lets anyone else understand what happened.

A discussion followed about how to treat results like these. Our view, repeated from earlier rounds, is that the score is a prompt for a conversation and not a ranking. We do not want teams competing over marks, and we especially do not want people avoiding hard work in order to look tidy. The place for the numbers is the improvement list, where each low item is turned into a specific habit. A high score should lead to sharing what works, and a lower one to asking for help.

Moving on to the week's practical matters:

- The shared workspace was reorganised. Folders now follow the structure of the work rather than the structure of the old org chart, and a redirect note sits in each retired location. Expect to be annoyed for a few days, and then to forget it ever looked different.
- The monthly access check was done, and there was nothing unusual. A couple of stale permissions were removed, and the owners were told.
- A vendor raised a question about how we use their service, and someone in finance replied with the details. We are waiting for a response, and the team has no action in the meantime.
- The test builds are faster since the overlapping jobs were rescheduled. People noticed, which is the point.

There was also time for the kind of conversation that does not fit an agenda. A few of us talked about how the quarter has felt: busy, a bit scattered, but with a visible trail of small fixes. Several people said they find the diary more useful than they expected, partly because it makes it easy to see what we decided and why. A suggestion was made to add a standing line at the end of each entry listing decisions only, so someone scanning the log in future can find them quickly. We will try it, and if it feels like homework, we will drop it.

The remaining part of this entry covers the billing work and the plan for the coming weeks. For now, the action list from this section is small: share the maintenance recording routine, adopt the sign-off line for scheduling changes, and add the decisions line to future entries. Owners are noted on the planning page, and I will check progress at the next sync.

request.episode_body:
## Billing, backlog and the weeks ahead

Picking up with billing, which was the other main thread of the week.

The Cedar Core backlog stood at 41 open tickets at the end of the sprint. It is a short list by our usual standards, and the team is pleased, though no one is taking it as permanent. Most of the open items are waiting for information from outside, and a couple are small enough to close this week. The more interesting observation was about shape rather than size: the tickets are now mostly genuine questions rather than stale leftovers, which suggests the earlier cleanup worked. The plan is to keep the list short by reading it every Monday and closing whatever has been answered.

There was a useful conversation about what to do when billing and other efforts disagree about timing. Cedar Core tends to need information at the end of a cycle, while others produce it at the start of the next. The workable answer was to agree a cut-off and stick to it, with a short written exception route for genuine emergencies. The cut-off will be written on the planning page so nobody has to guess. It is not a perfect solution, but it removes a lot of the friction we saw last quarter.

Tomas Kowalski came back with the sign-off routine for scheduling changes and ran through an example. The line reads naturally and takes seconds to add, and the team agreed to start using it straight away. Nimbus Core's habit of keeping small contemporaneous notes was suggested as a model, and a short session is booked for anyone curious about the approach.

A few more practical points:

- The workspace reorganisation had one casualty, a shared template that ended up in the wrong place. It has been found and restored.
- We went through the calendar for the coming weeks and noticed that two busy periods overlap. Nothing can be moved, so we will plan the cover in advance instead of improvising.
- The decisions line was added to the end of this diary, and the first attempt follows below. It was easier to write than expected.
- One person asked about training opportunities, and we agreed to gather requests at the next sync and see what is possible.

Looking ahead, the next few weeks are about consolidating rather than starting things. The audit has given us a list of habits to adopt, and the best use of the time is to make them routine before adding anything new. There is also the matter of preparing for the end-of-year period, when people are away and handovers matter more than usual. The handover template will get a real workout, and we should revisit it once the first few have been written.

On mood: people sound steady, if a little tired, and the quiet end of the week was welcome. A couple of colleagues said they would like more time for focused work and fewer small interruptions. That is a hard thing to promise, but we can at least avoid scheduling anything on Friday afternoons unless it is necessary.

Decisions this entry: adopt the sign-off line for scheduling changes, keep the Monday read-through of the billing list, agree a cut-off for information at the end of each cycle, and drop any Friday afternoon meetings that are not essential. Everything else carries forward.

<TEXT>
## Billing, backlog and the weeks ahead

Picking up with billing, which was the other main thread of the week.

The Cedar Core backlog stood at 41 open tickets at the end of the sprint. It is a short list by our usual standards, and the team is pleased, though no one is taking it as permanent. Most of the open items are waiting for information from outside, and a couple are small enough to close this week. The more interesting observation was about shape rather than size: the tickets are now mostly genuine questions rather than stale leftovers, which suggests the earlier cleanup worked. The plan is to keep the list short by reading it every Monday and closing whatever has been answered.

There was a useful conversation about what to do when billing and other efforts disagree about timing. Cedar Core tends to need information at the end of a cycle, while others produce it at the start of the next. The workable answer was to agree a cut-off and stick to it, with a short written exception route for genuine emergencies. The cut-off will be written on the planning page so nobody has to guess. It is not a perfect solution, but it removes a lot of the friction we saw last quarter.

Tomas Kowalski came back with the sign-off routine for scheduling changes and ran through an example. The line reads naturally and takes seconds to add, and the team agreed to start using it straight away. Nimbus Core's habit of keeping small contemporaneous notes was suggested as a model, and a short session is booked for anyone curious about the approach.

A few more practical points:

- The workspace reorganisation had one casualty, a shared template that ended up in the wrong place. It has been found and restored.
- We went through the calendar for the coming weeks and noticed that two busy periods overlap. Nothing can be moved, so we will plan the cover in advance instead of improvising.
- The decisions line was added to the end of this diary, and the first attempt follows below. It was easier to write than expected.
- One person asked about training opportunities, and we agreed to gather requests at the next sync and see what is possible.

Looking ahead, the next few weeks are about consolidating rather than starting things. The audit has given us a list of habits to adopt, and the best use of the time is to make them routine before adding anything new. There is also the matter of preparing for the end-of-year period, when people are away and handovers matter more than usual. The handover template will get a real workout, and we should revisit it once the first few have been written.

On mood: people sound steady, if a little tired, and the quiet end of the week was welcome. A couple of colleagues said they would like more time for focused work and fewer small interruptions. That is a hard thing to promise, but we can at least avoid scheduling anything on Friday afternoons unless it is necessary.

Decisions this entry: adopt the sign-off line for scheduling changes, keep the Monday read-through of the billing list, agree a cut-off for information at the end of each cycle, and drop any Friday afternoon meetings that are not essential. Everything else carries forward.
</TEXT>

request.episode_body:
# Blameless incident reviews in practice

The aftermath of an outage has a predictable shape. Messages fly, tempers fray, and somewhere in the middle a question surfaces: who is responsible? Many teams now argue that this is the least productive question available, and have replaced it with a structured conversation about how the failure came to be possible at all.

The core idea is that individuals act on the information and tools they have, and that a mistake made by one person usually points to a weakness in the setup rather than a flaw in the person. A review built on that idea looks different from a traditional post-mortem. Participants walk through the timeline step by step, noting what each person could see at each moment. Where someone made a poor call, the group asks what made that call look reasonable at the time: a misleading alert, an unclear procedure, an unfamiliar tool, too many things happening at once.

The practical results can be striking. Teams report that people speak up sooner when something goes wrong, because they no longer fear the consequences of admitting it. Small problems get flagged before they grow. And the fixes that come out of the reviews tend to be structural, such as clearer warnings, safer defaults and better handovers, instead of a reminder to be more careful next time.

None of this removes responsibility. Facilitators are careful to explain that the aim is to understand, not to excuse, and that persistent poor practice is dealt with elsewhere. What changes is the setting in which learning happens. A person who feels safe tells the whole story; a person who feels judged tells the part that sounds best.

Getting started is less complicated than it sounds. Pick a recent, modest incident. Gather the people involved. Reconstruct events together, resist the urge to name a culprit, and end with a handful of concrete actions, each with an owner. Then check back on them. The first review will feel awkward, since old habits die hard. By the third, most teams find that the conversation has become easier, and the findings more useful.

request.entity_user_prompt:
<TEXT>
# Blameless incident reviews in practice

The aftermath of an outage has a predictable shape. Messages fly, tempers fray, and somewhere in the middle a question surfaces: who is responsible? Many teams now argue that this is the least productive question available, and have replaced it with a structured conversation about how the failure came to be possible at all.

The core idea is that individuals act on the information and tools they have, and that a mistake made by one person usually points to a weakness in the setup rather than a flaw in the person. A review built on that idea looks different from a traditional post-mortem. Participants walk through the timeline step by step, noting what each person could see at each moment. Where someone made a poor call, the group asks what made that call look reasonable at the time: a misleading alert, an unclear procedure, an unfamiliar tool, too many things happening at once.

The practical results can be striking. Teams report that people speak up sooner when something goes wrong, because they no longer fear the consequences of admitting it. Small problems get flagged before they grow. And the fixes that come out of the reviews tend to be structural, such as clearer warnings, safer defaults and better handovers, instead of a reminder to be more careful next time.

None of this removes responsibility. Facilitators are careful to explain that the aim is to understand, not to excuse, and that persistent poor practice is dealt with elsewhere. What changes is the setting in which learning happens. A person who feels safe tells the whole story; a person who feels judged tells the part that sounds best.

Getting started is less complicated than it sounds. Pick a recent, modest incident. Gather the people involved. Reconstruct events together, resist the urge to name a culprit, and end with a handful of concrete actions, each with an owner. Then check back on them. The first review will feel awkward, since old habits die hard. By the third, most teams find that the conversation has become easier, and the findings more useful.
</TEXT>

request.episode_body:
# Operations diary — 7 November 2025

Friday again, and the end of a week that felt longer than it was. I am writing this at the desk by the window, which has become the unofficial place for people who want to finish things without being interrupted. The light is already going at this hour, which does nothing for the mood.

**The survey results.** They arrived midweek and have taken up more of the conversation than anything else. The internal satisfaction survey asks people across the organisation to rate the groups they work with on a scale of one to ten, and the results are shared with each group privately before anything is discussed more widely. Sofia Petrov received a satisfaction rating of 3.9 out of 10. Sable Core received a satisfaction rating of 3.2 out of 10. Neither is a number anybody wanted to see, and both groups responded the way I would hope: with questions, not excuses.

I sat in on part of the discussion on the procurement side. The first reaction was a kind of stunned quiet, followed by an attempt to work out what the number really measured. The free-text comments were more useful than the score. A few themes came up repeatedly: it is hard to tell where a request has got to once it has been submitted, answers take a long time to arrive, and the rules for what needs approval are not clear to people outside the group. None of those are about competence. They are about visibility and expectations, which are fixable. The plan is to publish a plain description of the process, including how long each step normally takes, and to give requesters a way to see the status without having to ask. A short, regular update to people with outstanding requests was also suggested.

On the compliance side, the discussion was a little different. Compliance work is rarely popular, because the people asking for it are, by nature, telling others what they cannot do. The comments reflected that. Many were less about the substance and more about timing: requirements arriving late, or changing after work had already begun. The project's response was to propose an earlier, lighter touch, so that people hear about the requirements at the start and not at the end. I think this is wise. It does not make the rules any friendlier, but it makes them predictable, and predictability is most of what people want.

**Other business this week.**

- The Tuesday review ran long and was dominated by the survey, which pushed several routine items to next week. Nobody complained.
- Someone raised the point that a poor score can discourage people from speaking up, since it feels like a verdict. We agreed to treat the results as a starting point for conversation and not as a ranking. I made a note to say so explicitly at the next meeting.
- The shared tracker was tidied, with a handful of stale entries closed and the rest reassigned.
- The office plants were moved away from the heater, which has been installed in an unfortunate place. They look relieved.

**A longer thought.** I keep returning to the fact that bad news is much easier to deal with when you have a way to act on it. A score that arrives with no context just feels like a slap, whereas a score with comments and a few concrete suggestions is something you can work with. The comments in this survey were, on the whole, generous. People took the trouble to explain what they found frustrating and, in many cases, what they would find helpful. That is a gift, even if it does not feel like one on the day.

A few themes came up repeatedly: it is hard to tell where a request has got to once it has been submitted, answers take a long time to arrive, and the rules for what needs approval are not clear to people outside the group. None of those are about competence. They are about visibility and expectations, which are fixable. The plan is to publish a plain description of the process, including how long each step normally takes, and to give requesters a way to see the status without having to ask. A short, regular update to people with outstanding requests was also suggested.

On the compliance side, the discussion was a little different. Compliance work is rarely popular, because the people asking for it are, by nature, telling others what they cannot do. The comments reflected that. Many were less about the substance and more about timing: requirements arriving late, or changing after work had already begun. The project's response was to propose an earlier, lighter touch, so that people hear about the requirements at the start and not at the end. I think this is wise. It does not make the rules any friendlier, but it makes them predictable, and predictability is most of what people want.

**Other business this week.**

- The Tuesday review ran long and was dominated by the survey, which pushed several routine items to next week. Nobody complained.
- Someone raised the point that a poor score can discourage people from speaking up, since it feels like a verdict. We agreed to treat the results as a starting point for conversation and not as a ranking. I made a note to say so explicitly at the next meeting.
- The shared tracker was tidied, with a handful of stale entries closed and the rest reassigned.
- The office plants were moved away from the heater, which has been installed in an unfortunate place. They look relieved.

**A longer thought.** I keep returning to the fact that bad news is much easier to deal with when you have a way to act on it. A score that arrives with no context just feels like a slap, whereas a score with comments and a few concrete suggestions is something you can work with. The comments in this survey were, on the whole, generous. People took the trouble to explain what they found frustrating and, in many cases, what they would find helpful. That is a gift, even if it does not feel like one on the day.
</TEXT>

request.episode_body:
What I would like to see over the coming weeks is a small number of visible changes in each of the two groups, ones that requesters can notice without being told. Visible, quick improvements do more for trust than a long list of promises. If someone submits a request next month and can see where it stands, they will remember that far longer than a clever slogan.

**Next week.** Both groups will draft a short plan and share it in the log. Whoever is chairing the Tuesday session should leave a decent slot for it, and I would ask the rest of us to be kind and constructive in our comments. It is not easy to hear that you have fallen short, and it is harder to share a plan for doing better in public.

Shutting the laptop now. Weekend ahead, a long walk, and an attempt to forget about spreadsheets.

request.episode_body:
# Working notes — 13 November 2025

Thursday. Grey outside, heating finally working properly inside, and a longer list than I would like. I am writing this in pieces through the day, so apologies if the tone wanders.

First thing was the weekly sync with the three project groups. Cedar Core had questions about the billing cycle and how the month-end close should interact with the new reporting layout. Lumen Core wanted to talk through a change to how access requests are reviewed, which turned into a surprisingly lively discussion about who should be allowed to approve what. Sable Core mostly listened, then raised a compliance point at the end that nobody had anticipated and that we parked for a proper conversation next week. I like that the syncs are now short enough that people stay awake for them.

The billing questions were the most practical. Month-end is always a squeeze, and the proposal on the table is to freeze changes to the billing configuration for two working days before the close. Nobody loves a freeze, but the alternative is last-minute edits that nobody has time to check. We agreed to try it for the next cycle and review honestly afterwards. If it just creates a pile-up on the day the freeze lifts, we will rethink it.

On the security side, the access review change is small on paper and large in practice. Right now a request goes to whoever happens to be around, which means the answer depends on the day. The suggestion is a short rota, so that exactly one person is responsible at any time and the requester knows who to ask. The objection raised was that a rota can become a bottleneck if the person is out. The reply was that the rota should name a deputy. Reasonable. Someone will draft a version and circulate it.

Chores and housekeeping:

- The meeting room projector has a flickering line down the left side. A request has gone in.
- Our shared glossary has three definitions of the same term, which is not ideal. I will merge them and leave a short note about which one wins.
- Laptop updates are being rolled out in waves; ours is next week, so save your work.
- Recycling has been left unsorted in the kitchen again. Gentle reminders have not worked. Possibly a sign.

Some thoughts on the shape of the quarter. We are a few weeks from the point where everything seems to land at once: end-of-year reviews, planning for the new year, the usual flurry of purchase requests. The lesson from last year was that we let the calendar fill up with meetings and left no room for the actual work. This time I would like us to block out some protected days, with no internal meetings at all, and say so in advance so nobody feels left out of the loop.

I will keep adding to this entry as the day goes on. For now, lunch, and then a long look at the glossary, which I am not looking forward to but which has been bothering me for far too long.

- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)

  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.

- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program

- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication

Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>

request.episode_body:
## Afternoon additions

Back after lunch. The glossary is merged, or at least it is no longer actively embarrassing. The winning definition was the one from the oldest document, partly because it was the clearest and partly because nobody had the energy to argue. There is a short note at the top explaining how to propose a change, so the next disagreement will at least happen in the open.

The afternoon started with a call about compliance. Sable Core's parked point from this morning turned out to be about how long certain records need to be kept and who is allowed to delete them. It is not a crisis, but it touches the other two groups: billing generates a lot of records, and security cares about who can remove things. We agreed that the three groups should meet briefly, ideally once, rather than trade emails for a fortnight. I have offered to set up the meeting and to bring a one-page summary of the question so that people arrive with the same picture in their heads.

A side conversation with the Cedar Core group is worth recording. They would like a clearer picture of what happens when a customer disputes a charge, because the current process lives mostly in people's heads. Writing it down is not exciting, but it is the sort of work that pays for itself the first time someone is away. We sketched a flow on the whiteboard, and I photographed it before anyone could wipe it. The plan is to turn it into a proper page by the end of next week, with the team reviewing it before it is published.

Lumen Core sent over a draft of the access rota. It is cleaner than I expected: a single table, one name per slot, a deputy for each, and a line explaining what to do if both are unavailable. I made a few suggestions, mainly about wording, and asked that the escalation path be written in plain language rather than shorthand. Several people will skim it once and never read it again, so it needs to make sense at a glance.

Short items:

- The projector request has been acknowledged. A technician is expected "soon", which in this building means anything from tomorrow to Christmas.
- Someone asked whether we should move the weekly sync to the morning. Mixed reactions, so we will leave it as is.
- The protected-days idea got a warm reception. We will pick the dates at the next planning session.
- The recycling sign has been made. It is polite but firm.

I also spent a while thinking about how we hand work over when people go on leave. At the moment it depends entirely on the individual: some leave a tidy note, others leave a cheerful "should be fine". A simple template, with what is in progress, what is waiting on someone else and where to look first, would help a lot. I will draft one and put it in the shared space for people to try.

Time to wind down. Tomorrow is another meeting-heavy day, so tonight I will tidy my desk and write down three priorities. Only three. Experience says four is where it all falls apart.

<TEXT>
## Afternoon additions

Back after lunch. The glossary is merged, or at least it is no longer actively embarrassing. The winning definition was the one from the oldest document, partly because it was the clearest and partly because nobody had the energy to argue. There is a short note at the top explaining how to propose a change, so the next disagreement will at least happen in the open.

The afternoon started with a call about compliance. Sable Core's parked point from this morning turned out to be about how long certain records need to be kept and who is allowed to delete them. It is not a crisis, but it touches the other two groups: billing generates a lot of records, and security cares about who can remove things. We agreed that the three groups should meet briefly, ideally once, rather than trade emails for a fortnight. I have offered to set up the meeting and to bring a one-page summary of the question so that people arrive with the same picture in their heads.

A side conversation with the Cedar Core group is worth recording. They would like a clearer picture of what happens when a customer disputes a charge, because the current process lives mostly in people's heads. Writing it down is not exciting, but it is the sort of work that pays for itself the first time someone is away. We sketched a flow on the whiteboard, and I photographed it before anyone could wipe it. The plan is to turn it into a proper page by the end of next week, with the team reviewing it before it is published.

Lumen Core sent over a draft of the access rota. It is cleaner than I expected: a single table, one name per slot, a deputy for each, and a line explaining what to do if both are unavailable. I made a few suggestions, mainly about wording, and asked that the escalation path be written in plain language rather than shorthand. Several people will skim it once and never read it again, so it needs to make sense at a glance.

Short items:

- The projector request has been acknowledged. A technician is expected "soon", which in this building means anything from tomorrow to Christmas.
- Someone asked whether we should move the weekly sync to the morning. Mixed reactions, so we will leave it as is.
- The protected-days idea got a warm reception. We will pick the dates at the next planning session.
- The recycling sign has been made. It is polite but firm.

I also spent a while thinking about how we hand work over when people go on leave. At the moment it depends entirely on the individual: some leave a tidy note, others leave a cheerful "should be fine". A simple template, with what is in progress, what is waiting on someone else and where to look first, would help a lot. I will draft one and put it in the shared space for people to try.

Time to wind down. Tomorrow is another meeting-heavy day, so tonight I will tidy my desk and write down three priorities. Only three. Experience says four is where it all falls apart.
</TEXT>

request.episode_body:
## Numbers for the quarter

Evening, and I finally sat down with the figures that have been sitting in my inbox since Monday. This is the quarterly roundup, in a format I hope people will actually read.

Incidents first. Cedar Core logged 48 incidents during the quarter, which sounds like a lot until you look at what they were. The majority were small billing-related queries that were recorded formally because the process says so, not because anything was truly broken. A handful were genuine problems, and those were dealt with promptly. The team's view is that the logging habit is healthy, and that the number says more about how carefully they record things than about how reliable the system is. I mostly agree, though I would like to see the categories split out next time so that the real issues are not hidden in the noise.

The internal audit results also came back. Sable Core scored 71 out of 100 in the internal audit. That is a respectable result, and it came with a short list of recommendations rather than a long one. The main theme was documentation: some procedures exist, but the written version has drifted from what people do in practice. It is a very familiar finding, and a fixable one. The group has already started working through the list, beginning with the items that take the least effort so that the score can be seen to move at the next review.

I tried to be careful in how I presented these. Numbers have a way of turning into league tables, and then people start to compete or to feel defensive. I stressed in the summary that incidents and audit scores measure different things, and that neither is a measure of how hard anyone has worked. Several readers appreciated that, and one pointed out that the audit is as much a checklist of paperwork as a test of quality. That is fair, but paperwork matters when somebody outside the building comes asking questions.

What we agreed to do with the results:

- Share the roundup with all three groups, together with the short recommendations list.
- Pick two or three actions per group, not ten, and put owners against them.
- Look at the results again at the next sync, then leave them alone until the following quarter.
- Keep the incident categories in a simple spreadsheet so they can be sorted later.

A reflection to end on. I find quarterly figures most useful for the conversations they provoke, not the numbers themselves. The meeting this afternoon was better for having something concrete on the table, even if nobody could quite agree on what it meant. That is probably the right level of disagreement for a data point.

Heading home shortly. The glossary, the access rota and the audit recommendations are all in decent shape, and the projector can wait.

request.episode_body:
## Late entry: feedback and follow-ups

A short postscript, written the next morning over coffee, because the survey summary landed after I closed the laptop last night and I would rather record it while it is fresh.

Lumen Core received a satisfaction rating of 4.2 out of 10. I read the comments before looking at the number, which I recommend, because the comments are kinder and more useful than the score. People appreciate that the security group is careful and responsive when something is wrong. What frustrates them is the waiting: access requests and approvals take longer than anyone expects, and there is rarely a clear answer to "where is my request?". That lines up neatly with the rota discussion from yesterday, which is a small bit of good luck. The new rota should address precisely the complaint that came up most often, and I have suggested that the group mention the connection when they roll it out, so that the people who complained can see that they were heard.

I also drafted the handover template I mentioned. It is a single page with four headings: what is in progress, what is waiting on someone else, what could go wrong while you are away, and where to look first. I tried it on my own current work as a test, and found two items I had forgotten I was supposed to be chasing, which is itself an argument for it. I have put it in the shared space and will ask for feedback at the next sync, keeping my expectations modest.

Follow-ups from the three groups:

- Cedar Core is turning the disputed-charge flow into a written page and will circulate it for review.
- Sable Core is working through the audit recommendations, starting with the quick ones.
- Lumen Core is finalising the rota and the deputy arrangement, and will announce it in the usual place.
- The meeting about record retention has been scheduled, and a summary page is ready for it.
- The projector is, predictably, still flickering.

A decision worth noting: we will not publish the survey results as a ranking. Each group will receive its own result, along with the comments, and a short combined summary will go to everyone without any ordering. The reasoning was that the point is to improve, not to compare, and a ranking would push people towards explaining the number away instead of acting on it. Nobody argued, which is unusual enough that I wrote it down.

Finally, a plan for the next few weeks. The protected days will go in the calendar before the end-of-year rush, the freeze before month-end will be tried once, and the handover template will get a fair trial. If at least two of those three survive contact with reality, I will count it as a good quarter's worth of small improvements.

I will leave this log here. Next week's entry should be calmer, and, I hope, less dependent on caffeine.
request.entity_system_prompt:
You are an entity extraction specialist for unstructured text.
NEVER extract vague or standalone feelings or generic words. A specific, named abstract concept
that passes the Wikipedia-article test below (e.g. "climate change", "quantum entanglement")
should be extracted as a Concept entity — being abstract is not by itself a reason to exclude it.

NEVER extract:
- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)
- Vague standalone feelings and generic ideas that could not stand alone as a specific, named
  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

For each entity extracted, assign a single entity_type label from this closed ontology:
- Person: An individual human being
- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication
Choose the single most appropriate type. If none fit well, use the closest match.

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>

request.edge_system_prompt:
You are an expert fact extractor that extracts fact triples from text.
1. Extracted fact triples should also be extracted with relevant date information.
2. Treat REFERENCE_TIME as the time the episode was recorded. All temporal information should be extracted relative to REFERENCE_TIME.

# TASK
Extract all factual relationships between the given ENTITIES based on the CURRENT MESSAGE.
Only extract facts that:
- involve two DISTINCT ENTITIES from the ENTITIES list,
- are clearly stated or unambiguously implied in the CURRENT MESSAGE,
  and can be represented as edges in a knowledge graph.
- Facts should include entity names rather than pronouns whenever possible.

# EXTRACTION RULES

1. **Entity Name Validation**: source_name and target_name must use only the name values from the ENTITIES list provided above.
   - CRITICAL: Using names not in the list will cause the edge to be rejected.
2. Each fact must involve two distinct entities — source_name and target_name NEVER refer to the same entity.
3. NEVER extract facts that describe only a single entity's state, feeling, or attribute. Instead, identify the second entity that the state or feeling relates to and form a proper triple.
   - BAD: "Alice feels happy" (single-entity state — what is Alice happy about?)
   - GOOD: "Alice feels happy about Bob's promotion" → Alice FEELS_HAPPY_ABOUT Bob's promotion
   - GOOD: "Alice congratulated Bob" (relationship between two entities), "Alice lives in Paris" (relationship between entity and place)
4. NEVER emit duplicate or semantically redundant facts.
5. The fact field should closely paraphrase the original source sentence(s). Do not verbatim quote the original text.
6. Use REFERENCE_TIME to resolve vague or relative temporal expressions (e.g., "last week").
7. Do not hallucinate or infer temporal bounds from unrelated events.

# RELATION TYPE RULES


You MUST always provide a non-null relation_type for every edge. Leaving it null or empty is not acceptable.
Derive a relation_type from the relationship predicate in SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE (e.g., WORKS_AT, LIVES_IN, IS_FRIENDS_WITH, WROTE, AUTHORED, MARRIED_TO).
If the predicate is unclear, derive one from the fact description using a concise verb phrase.
Use concise, consistent vocabulary — prefer established verbs that would apply broadly.

# DATETIME RULES

- Use ISO 8601 with "Z" suffix (UTC) (e.g., 2025-04-30T00:00:00Z).
- If the fact is ongoing (present tense), set valid_at to REFERENCE_TIME.
- If a change or termination is expressed, set invalid_at to the relevant timestamp.
- Leave both fields null if no explicit or resolvable time is stated.
- If only a date is mentioned (no time), assume 00:00:00.
- If only a year is mentioned, use January 1st at 00:00:00.

request.episode_body:
# Working notes — 21 November 2025

Friday, late morning, and I have a quiet hour that I intend to spend on these notes before the afternoon fills up. It has been a week of many small conversations and not many big ones, which suits me fine.

The headline from the week is the audit. Helix Core scored 88 out of 100 in the internal audit, the best result the analytics group has had, and the team was understandably pleased. What I liked most was how they handled it: no celebration email, no victory lap, just a short message thanking the people who had kept the documentation current and a note to keep doing so. The auditors' comments were mostly about traceability, meaning how easily somebody can follow a figure in a report back to where it came from. The group already has a plan to improve that, which is partly why the score was good. I asked whether the approach could be written up for the other groups, and they agreed.

Procurement is the other big thread. Sofia Petrov has been working through a backlog of purchase requests, many of which arrived at the same time because people save them up until the end of the quarter. Her method is straightforward but disciplined: sort by urgency, check each against the plan, and reply to everyone within a day even if the answer is "not yet". request.episode_body:
## Afternoon and plans

The afternoon went roughly as expected: a one-to-one that overran, a plan that changed three times, and a cup of tea I never got to drink. Here is what was worth keeping.

The demo is the first item. 34 people attended the Sofia Petrov demo, a walk-through of how purchase requests move from submission to approval. It was set up as an optional session, so the turnout was better than I had feared. The questions were practical: how to tell whether a request has been seen, what to do when the supplier changes the terms, and how to ask for something urgent without simply labelling everything urgent. Sofia answered them patiently, and a few of the answers led to changes in the guidance page that same afternoon. She also asked people to tell her when the process feels slow, because she can only fix what she hears about. I think the demo did more for trust than any amount of writing could have done.

The survey is the second item. Helix Core received a satisfaction rating of 5.4 out of 10. It is a middling result, and the comments explain why: people value the accuracy of the reports but find them hard to request and slow to arrive. That is a fair summary of a team that has focused on quality at the expense of convenience. The group has already begun talking about a simpler request form and a clearer statement of how long reports usually take. I suggested they try a very small version first, such as a single shared page, before building anything more elaborate. The audit result from the morning and this survey tell complementary stories: the work is sound, and the experience around it needs attention.

Plans for next quarter, which came out of the long conversation:

- Keep the priorities list to one page and revisit it monthly.
- Ask each group for a single measure they would like to improve, and agree how it will be tracked.
- Hold a short review in the middle of the quarter, with the figures circulated beforehand.
- Protect the last two weeks of December from any new commitments.

There was also a small disagreement about whether to run another demo in the new year. Some people felt one was enough, while others thought regular sessions would keep the process visible. We settled on a lighter option: a short recorded walk-through that people can watch whenever they like, plus a live question time once a quarter. It is a compromise, but a sensible one, and it should cost less effort than a full session.

I finish the day feeling mostly satisfied, with one nagging worry. The pattern in the notes is that we do a lot of good work and then struggle to make it easy for others to use. It shows up in the survey, it showed up in the procurement questions, and it shows up in the shared drive. Perhaps the plan for next quarter should include a simple theme: make things easier to find and easier to ask for. Not a project, just a habit.

I will raise it at the Monday meeting and see who agrees. For now, the weekend.

request.episode_body:
# Retention schedules for small organisations

_Clipped from the web. Source: example.org/retention-schedules-small-organisations._

Records management rarely makes headlines, yet it quietly shapes how a small organisation copes with audits, disputes and the ordinary turnover of staff. Those who advise on the subject say the most common mistake is to treat a retention schedule as a one-off document, written once and filed away, when it is better understood as a working tool that needs regular attention.

A sound schedule lists each type of record, the period it should be kept and the action to take at the end of that period. Shorter is better. Advisers recommend a limited number of categories, each with a named role responsible for it, so that the arrangement survives changes of personnel. They also recommend that the schedule say who may suspend disposal when a dispute or investigation is under way, since records destroyed at the wrong moment can cause far more trouble than records kept a little too long.

Cost is a factor that smaller bodies cannot ignore, and trade press coverage of storage and archiving services reflects it. In a recent round-up of the sector, it was reported that Basalt Supply lists its standard rate at $35 per unit, a figure cited by commentators as a useful benchmark when comparing outside storage with keeping records in-house. Observers were quick to add that the headline rate is only part of the picture, since handling, retrieval and secure disposal are usually priced separately and can change the comparison considerably.

That caution applies more widely. Organisations that outsource storage still carry the responsibility for deciding what is kept and for how long; the provider simply holds what it is given. For that reason, specialists suggest reviewing the schedule before choosing any service, not afterwards, so that the volume to be stored is already as small as it can reasonably be. Cutting the volume first often does more for the budget than negotiating a better rate.

The final piece of advice is practical. Put a date in the calendar for the annual review of the schedule, assign it to a particular role, and keep a short note of what was changed and why. Small habits like these, the specialists argue, are what separate a schedule that works from one that only exists on paper.

request.episode_body:
# Weekly digest — 4 December 2025

Short week, long list. Monday's stand-up ran over because the projector refused to talk to anyone's laptop for the first stretch of the meeting, so we gave up on slides and read the board aloud instead. It turned out to be the better meeting. People said what they were stuck on rather than what they had finished, and three small blockers were cleared before anyone sat down again.

Bram Tanaka picked up the compliance reading list that had been sitting untouched since the autumn. The plan is to go through it a section at a time rather than in one painful afternoon, and to write down anything that changes how we handle customer records. Nothing alarming so far, mostly wording that needs tidying in our own internal guidance. He asked that anyone who has an old checklist saved locally send it over so we can retire the duplicates.

Diego Ferreira spent a good part of the week in the support inbox, partly to clear it and partly to see which kinds of questions keep coming back. He is keeping a rough list of repeat questions and wants to turn the top few into short answers we can paste. If you have a favourite reply that has worked well, drop it in the shared folder.

On the billing side, Ines Lindqvist reconciled the month-end figures earlier than usual, which meant we could close the books without the usual scramble on the last day. She also tidied the shared spreadsheet so the columns finally mean what their headings say. Please do not add new tabs without a word; the old habit of one tab per person made the file almost unreadable.

Quill Core, the routing project, had a quiet few days after the noisy ones before. The team spent most of Tuesday walking through the routing rules one by one and deleting the ones nobody could explain. A couple of them were clearly leftovers from an experiment that ended long ago. Removing them did not break anything, which is the best kind of result.

Chores and small decisions this week:

- The kitchen rota is back to a simple alternating order, after the three-way swap proved too confusing to follow.
- We agreed to stop sending the weekly digest as an attachment and to keep it only in the shared notebook, so there is one copy.
- The office plants are now someone's explicit job, which has been long overdue.
- The team will try shorter Friday check-ins for a month and then decide whether to keep them.

Looking ahead, the plan is to spend the next week on cleanup rather than new work. Everyone should look at their own corner of the board and archive whatever is finished or clearly dead. A tidy board makes the planning conversation in the new year a lot easier, and it makes it far less likely that we are surprised by something we thought we had closed. More next week, once the cleanup has actually happened rather than just been promised.

request.episode_body:
## Tuesday and Wednesday

Tuesday was mostly heads-down. I had expected a stream of interruptions and got almost none, which I suspect had something to do with the rain. The one real conversation of the day was about how we label things in the shared board. Two people had been using the same tag to mean different things, and it only came to light when a filter returned a strange mixture. We agreed on a short glossary and Diego Ferreira volunteered to keep it up to date, since support is where most of the odd labels first appear.

Wednesday brought the planning session we had been postponing. It was a bit scrappy, honestly. We began with the aim of agreeing priorities for the coming weeks and ended with agreeing only what not to do, but that turned out to be useful. Several tasks that had been lingering on the list for months were struck off with no argument, because once you say them out loud nobody wants to defend them.

A few notes from the afternoon:

- Bram Tanaka raised the question of how long we should keep old records, and whether our current habit is deliberate or just inertia. The answer is probably inertia. He will write up a short proposal rather than have us debate it in the meeting.
- Ines Lindqvist asked that invoices queries be sent to a single mailbox instead of landing in four different inboxes. Fair request, and easy to do.
- Someone suggested rotating who runs the Monday meeting. No objections, so we will try it from next week.

On the routing side, Quill Core remains the thing most people ask about when they pass through the room. The honest summary is that it works and nobody is quite sure why it works as well as it does, which is a little uncomfortable. The team is going to add some comments to the rules so that the knowledge is not carried around in one person's head.

The lunch order was wrong again, and we should probably stop pretending it will be right next time. Perhaps a shared list pinned in the channel, with names next to items, would settle it.

By the end of the day the board was visibly smaller. Not dramatically, but enough that you could see the shape of the work rather than just the pile. I find that matters more than the actual number of cards. A short board feels manageable, and a manageable board gets looked at.

Open question to carry forward: do we want a quiet hour each afternoon with no meetings? Several people said yes, a couple said it would never survive contact with reality. Worth a trial.
request.entity_system_prompt:
You are an entity extraction specialist for unstructured text.
NEVER extract vague or standalone feelings or generic words. A specific, named abstract concept
that passes the Wikipedia-article test below (e.g. "climate change", "quantum entanglement")
should be extracted as a Concept entity — being abstract is not by itself a reason to exclude it.

NEVER extract:
- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)
- Vague standalone feelings and generic ideas that could not stand alone as a specific, named
  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

For each entity extracted, assign a single entity_type label from this closed ontology:
- Person: An individual human being
- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication
Choose the single most appropriate type. If none fit well, use the closest match.

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>

request.episode_body:
## Support review

The quarterly support review happened on Thursday morning, with biscuits and a slightly too-warm room. We went through the numbers first and then the stories behind them, which is the order that works best; if you start with the stories, people never get to the numbers. Diego Ferreira logged 6 incidents during the quarter, and what stood out was less the count than how quickly most of them were closed once somebody owned them. The slowest ones were the ones where nobody was sure whose problem it was.

That ownership point generated the best discussion of the meeting. We tend to assume that an incident belongs to whoever saw it first, which means it often belongs to whoever happened to be on chat that afternoon. A cleaner rule would be that the person who spots it writes it down, and the person responsible for the area picks it up. Bram Tanaka pointed out that for anything touching customer records, compliance needs to be told early, even if the issue turns out to be nothing. Nobody disagreed.

Some other points from the review:

- The template for incident write-ups is too long. People skip fields, and the fields they skip are the ones that matter. We will cut it down to what actually gets read.
- A few write-ups were filed days after the fact, and the details had gone soft by then. The aim is to write something, even a rough line, the same day.
- Ines Lindqvist noted that billing questions were behind a fair share of support conversations and suggested a short explainer on invoices that we can send out proactively. That should reduce back-and-forth.

I had meant to spend more of the meeting on lessons, but the practical bits ate the time. It is worth a follow-up with a smaller group, where someone can take notes properly and turn them into a page that others can find later.

Afterwards the team tidied the shared folder where old incident reports live. There were duplicates, and some files had names that told you nothing. Renaming them took less than an hour and made the folder usable again. We will see whether it stays that way.

A small administrative note: the review calendar invite for next quarter has been sent, and the meeting room is booked. If you cannot attend, please send your updates in writing beforehand so they are not lost.

Final thought for the week. A review is only worth the biscuits if something changes afterwards. The list of changes is short and specific, and each item has a name beside it. We will check on them at the next catch-up.

request.edge_system_prompt:
You are an expert fact extractor that extracts fact triples from text.
1. Extracted fact triples should also be extracted with relevant date information.
2. Treat REFERENCE_TIME as the time the episode was recorded. All temporal information should be extracted relative to REFERENCE_TIME.

# TASK
Extract all factual relationships between the given ENTITIES based on the CURRENT MESSAGE.
Only extract facts that:
- involve two DISTINCT ENTITIES from the ENTITIES list,
- are clearly stated or unambiguously implied in the CURRENT MESSAGE,
  and can be represented as edges in a knowledge graph.
- Facts should include entity names rather than pronouns whenever possible.

# EXTRACTION RULES

1. **Entity Name Validation**: source_name and target_name must use only the name values from the ENTITIES list provided above.
   - CRITICAL: Using names not in the list will cause the edge to be rejected.
2. Each fact must involve two distinct entities — source_name and target_name NEVER refer to the same entity.
3. NEVER extract facts that describe only a single entity's state, feeling, or attribute. Instead, identify the second entity that the state or feeling relates to and form a proper triple.
   - BAD: "Alice feels happy" (single-entity state — what is Alice happy about?)
   - GOOD: "Alice feels happy about Bob's promotion" → Alice FEELS_HAPPY_ABOUT Bob's promotion
   - GOOD: "Alice congratulated Bob" (relationship between two entities), "Alice lives in Paris" (relationship between entity and place)
4. NEVER emit duplicate or semantically redundant facts.
5. The fact field should closely paraphrase the original source sentence(s). Do not verbatim quote the original text.
6. Use REFERENCE_TIME to resolve vague or relative temporal expressions (e.g., "last week").
7. Do not hallucinate or infer temporal bounds from unrelated events.

# RELATION TYPE RULES


You MUST always provide a non-null relation_type for every edge. Leaving it null or empty is not acceptable.
Derive a relation_type from the relationship predicate in SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE (e.g., WORKS_AT, LIVES_IN, IS_FRIENDS_WITH, WROTE, AUTHORED, MARRIED_TO).
If the predicate is unclear, derive one from the fact description using a concise verb phrase.
Use concise, consistent vocabulary — prefer established verbs that would apply broadly.

# DATETIME RULES

- Use ISO 8601 with "Z" suffix (UTC) (e.g., 2025-04-30T00:00:00Z).
- If the fact is ongoing (present tense), set valid_at to REFERENCE_TIME.
- If a change or termination is expressed, set invalid_at to the relevant timestamp.
- Leave both fields null if no explicit or resolvable time is stated.
- If only a date is mentioned (no time), assume 00:00:00.
- If only a year is mentioned, use January 1st at 00:00:00.
