request.episode_body:
## Audit follow-up

The internal audit results landed in everyone's inbox on Friday, and as expected there was a flurry of quiet reading followed by a lot of corridor conversation. I will try to summarise the useful parts rather than the gossip. Overall the picture is decent: no nasty surprises, a few things to fix, and one or two places where the paperwork lags behind how we really work.

Ines Lindqvist scored 74 out of 100 in the internal audit, and she was upbeat about it when we spoke. Most of the marks she lost were for documentation rather than for anything in the actual process, such as approvals that happened but were not written down in the place the auditors look. She has already started adding short notes to the billing records so that the trail is visible, and she thinks the remaining gaps can be closed in a couple of afternoons rather than a project.

Bram Tanaka went through the full report with the compliance lens on and flagged three themes:

- Evidence needs to be kept where it can be found, not on someone's laptop.
- Approvals should be recorded at the time, not reconstructed later.
- The retention wording in our guidance is inconsistent between two documents, and one of them should win.

Diego Ferreira asked whether the support side would be sampled next time, and Bram thought it likely. That prompted a short discussion about getting ahead of it by checking a handful of recent cases ourselves and seeing how they hold up. It sounds like a sensible, low-cost way to find problems before somebody else does.

There was a brief moment of friction about whether scores should be compared between people at all, since the areas audited differ so much in nature. We settled on treating each result as a to-do list for that area and not as a ranking. That seemed to ease the mood.

Smaller items: the audit folder has been given proper permissions, so only those who need it can open it. The shared calendar has a placeholder for a follow-up check, and everyone has been asked to bring their list of fixes to it.

I am glad we did this. Audits can feel like a school exam, but this one has produced a list of concrete improvements, and most of them are cheap. If we keep the habit of writing things down at the time, the next round should be calmer than this one was.

## Audit follow-up

The internal audit results landed in everyone's inbox on Friday, and as expected there was a flurry of quiet reading followed by a lot of corridor conversation. I will try to summarise the useful parts rather than the gossip. Overall the picture is decent: no nasty surprises, a few things to fix, and one or two places where the paperwork lags behind how we really work.

Ines Lindqvist scored 74 out of 100 in the internal audit, and she was upbeat about it when we spoke. Most of the marks she lost were for documentation rather than for anything in the actual process, such as approvals that happened but were not written down in the place the auditors look. She has already started adding short notes to the billing records so that the trail is visible, and she thinks the remaining gaps can be closed in a couple of afternoons rather than a project.

Bram Tanaka went through the full report with the compliance lens on and flagged three themes:

- Evidence needs to be kept where it can be found, not on someone's laptop.
- Approvals should be recorded at the time, not reconstructed later.
- The retention wording in our guidance is inconsistent between two documents, and one of them should win.

Diego Ferreira asked whether the support side would be sampled next time, and Bram thought it likely. That prompted a short discussion about getting ahead of it by checking a handful of recent cases ourselves and seeing how they hold up. It sounds like a sensible, low-cost way to find problems before somebody else does.

There was a brief moment of friction about whether scores should be compared between people at all, since the areas audited differ so much in nature. We settled on treating each result as a to-do list for that area and not as a ranking. That seemed to ease the mood.

Smaller items: the audit folder has been given proper permissions, so only those who need it can open it. The shared calendar has a placeholder for a follow-up check, and everyone has been asked to bring their list of fixes to it.

I am glad we did this. Audits can feel like a school exam, but this one has produced a list of concrete improvements, and most of them are cheap. If we keep the habit of writing things down at the time, the next round should be calmer than this one was.
</TEXT>

request.episode_body:
## Housekeeping

Not much drama this stretch, so here is the plain housekeeping that tends to fall out of these digests when nobody writes it down.

First, the shared drive. It has grown a layer of folders whose purpose nobody remembers. Over a couple of lunch breaks the team went through the top level and moved things into a structure that at least has a logic: by area first, then by year. Anything that looked abandoned went into an archive folder rather than the bin, so no one needs to panic if a favourite file seems to have vanished. Ask, and it will be found.

Second, accounts and access. Someone in finance reminded us that a few shared logins were still in use, which is not great practice. Ines Lindqvist has started replacing them with named accounts, one at a time, beginning with the ones used for billing tasks. If you notice a login that stops working, that is probably the reason, and you should message her rather than guess at a workaround.

Third, the quarterly tidy-up of the board. Bram Tanaka suggested a simple rule: if a card has not moved in a long while and nobody objects when its name is read aloud, it gets closed. We tried it on Wednesday and closed a surprising number of cards. A couple were revived after someone said they still mattered, which is exactly why the rule works.

Some quick items:

- The label printer is out of tape. Again.
- Diego Ferreira has asked that anyone leaving notes for the support rota use the shared document, not messages, because messages scroll away.
- Quill Core needs a short description on the team page so that new people understand what the routing project is for without having to ask.
- The whiteboard in the corner has been cleaned, and a new rule has been posted: if you want to keep what is on it, take a photo.

There was also a brief conversation about holiday cover. Nothing was decided beyond agreeing that everyone should put their dates in the shared calendar early, so the gaps are visible before they become problems. It is much easier to plan around a gap you can see a month ahead than one that appears the day before.

That is the housekeeping. None of it is glamorous, and all of it makes the next few weeks smoother. I will report back on the access cleanup once more of the shared logins have been replaced.

Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

- Person: An individual human being
- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication

request.episode_body:
## Planning notes

Written up quickly after the planning huddle, so excuse the bullets.

The aim of the huddle was to decide what the team looks at between now and the end of the year. We agreed that the main focus is stability, with a small amount of room for experiments, and that anything new has to fit in around the edges rather than push existing work out. This sounds obvious, but we have broken that rule often enough that it is worth saying aloud.

What we settled on:

- Routing: the team behind Quill Core will keep the scope narrow and focus on making the existing rules easier to read. No new rule types until the old ones have comments.
- Support: Diego Ferreira will gather the most common questions into a short reference so that answering them becomes quicker for everyone, not just for him.
- Billing: Ines Lindqvist will finish the reconciliation clean-up and then look at how invoices are sent, since a few customers keep asking for a different format.
- Compliance: Bram Tanaka will turn the audit findings into a short list with owners, and bring it to the next catch-up.

A thing I want to remember from the discussion is that we spent more time on what to leave out than on what to do. One of the quieter members of the team made the point that every extra item is a promise, and that a promise nobody has time to keep is worse than no promise. That landed. The final list is shorter than the draft that was on the whiteboard at the start.

We also discussed how to share progress. The current habit of posting updates in several places means that nobody reads them all. The suggestion was to keep everything in the notebook, in the weekly entry, with a single line per person. If something needs more than a line, link to a longer page. I liked this and will try to follow it myself, though I notice this very section is not a single line.

Risks that came up, none of them large: people being away over the holiday period, a dependency on a vendor that has been slow to respond, and the possibility that the cleanup eats more time than planned. We will watch the third one in particular.

Next check-in is at the usual time. Please bring one thing you finished and one thing you are stuck on.

You are an entity extraction specialist for unstructured text.
NEVER extract vague or standalone feelings or generic words. A specific, named abstract concept
that passes the Wikipedia-article test below (e.g. "climate change", "quantum entanglement")
should be extracted as a Concept entity — being abstract is not by itself a reason to exclude it.

NEVER extract:
- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)
- Vague standalone feelings and generic ideas that could not stand alone as a specific, named
  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

For each entity extracted, assign a single entity_type label from this closed ontology:
- Person: An individual human being
- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication
Choose the single most appropriate type. If none fit well, use the closest match.

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>

You are an expert fact extractor that extracts fact triples from text.
1. Extracted fact triples should also be extracted with relevant date information.
2. Treat REFERENCE_TIME as the time the episode was recorded. All temporal information should be extracted relative to REFERENCE_TIME.

# TASK
Extract all factual relationships between the given ENTITIES based on the CURRENT MESSAGE.
Only extract facts that:
- involve two DISTINCT ENTITIES from the ENTITIES list,
- are clearly stated or unambiguously implied in the CURRENT MESSAGE,
  and can be represented as edges in a knowledge graph.
- Facts should include entity names rather than pronouns whenever possible.

# EXTRACTION RULES

1. **Entity Name Validation**: source_name and target_name must use only the name values from the ENTITIES list provided above.
   - CRITICAL: Using names not in the list will cause the edge to be rejected.
2. Each fact must involve two distinct entities — source_name and target_name NEVER refer to the same entity.
3. NEVER extract facts that describe only a single entity's state, feeling, or attribute. Instead, identify the second entity that the state or feeling relates to and form a proper triple.
   - BAD: "Alice feels happy" (single-entity state — what is Alice happy about?)
   - GOOD: "Alice feels happy about Bob's promotion" → Alice FEELS_HAPPY_ABOUT Bob's promotion
   - GOOD: "Alice congratulated Bob" (relationship between two entities), "Alice lives in Paris" (relationship between entity and place)
4. NEVER emit duplicate or semantically redundant facts.
5. The fact field should closely paraphrase the original source sentence(s). Do not verbatim quote the original text.
6. Use REFERENCE_TIME to resolve vague or relative temporal expressions (e.g., "last week").
7. Do not hallucinate or infer temporal bounds from unrelated events.

# RELATION TYPE RULES


You MUST always provide a non-null relation_type for every edge. Leaving it null or empty is not acceptable.
Derive a relation_type from the relationship predicate in SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE (e.g., WORKS_AT, LIVES_IN, IS_FRIENDS_WITH, WROTE, AUTHORED, MARRIED_TO).
If the predicate is unclear, derive one from the fact description using a concise verb phrase.
Use concise, consistent vocabulary — prefer established verbs that would apply broadly.

# DATETIME RULES

- Use ISO 8601 with "Z" suffix (UTC) (e.g., 2025-04-30T00:00:00Z).
- If the fact is ongoing (present tense), set valid_at to REFERENCE_TIME.
- If a change or termination is expressed, set invalid_at to the relevant timestamp.
- Leave both fields null if no explicit or resolvable time is stated.
- If only a date is mentioned (no time), assume 00:00:00.
- If only a year is mentioned, use January 1st at 00:00:00.

request.episode_body:
## Sprint close

Sprint close fell on a day when half the team was in the building and half was not, which always makes the retrospective feel slightly lopsided. We did it anyway, with the remote folks on a call and the rest of us around the table. Surprisingly, it worked well enough; the trick was to ask everyone to write their points down first so that nobody was talking over a speaker phone.

The headline from the support side is that the Diego Ferreira backlog stood at 234 open tickets at the end of the sprint. That is a number we have all been looking at nervously. Diego was not defensive about it, which I appreciated. He explained that a big share of those tickets are waiting on customers to reply, and that the true amount of work in hand is smaller than the headline. Even so, we agreed that a count that large makes the rest of the picture hard to see, and that some of those tickets should simply be closed with a polite note if the customer has gone quiet.

request.episode_body:
## Reading and learning

A gentler section this time, because the week had a quiet thread running through it that is worth recording: people reading things and passing them along.

It began with Bram Tanaka circulating a short article about keeping records tidy, which he described as the least exciting thing he had read all year and also the most useful. The main point was that good record-keeping is mostly habit, and that habits are easier to build when the right action is also the easiest one. That fits what we have seen with the audit follow-ups. If putting a note in the right place takes more effort than not doing so, notes will not be written.

Ines Lindqvist followed with a few pages on how to explain invoices clearly to people who do not read them for a living. We read it aloud at lunch, a slightly odd thing to do, and ended up rewriting one of our own standard paragraphs on the spot. The new version is shorter and does not use the word "pursuant" anywhere, which is a victory in itself.

Diego Ferreira, never one to be left out, brought in a worked example of how another team organised its support rota. We do not intend to copy it, since our situation is different, but a couple of ideas were worth borrowing. In particular, the notion of a handover note at the end of each shift that lists what is open and what is waiting. We will try a light version of that for a month.

On routing, the Quill Core team spent an hour reading through old notes to see how some of the earlier decisions were made. The mood afterwards was thoughtful. Some of the reasoning held up well, and some of it had been overtaken by events. Writing down why a decision was made, and not only what was decided, came up again as something we should do more consistently.

A few practical points that came out of all this reading:

- We will keep a reading list in the notebook, one line per item, with a sentence on why it is worth the time.
- Anyone who finds something useful should add it rather than trusting that others have seen it.
- Once a month, we will pick one item and talk about it for fifteen minutes.

None of this is dramatic, but it is how a team gets slowly better. I would like to see the list grow over the winter.

request.episode_body:
## Mid-week odds and ends

Several small things landed in the middle of the week and did not fit anywhere else, so they are gathered here.

The heating in the back room has finally been fixed. It had been either arctic or tropical for weeks, with nothing in between, and a few people had taken to working in their coats. Someone has adjusted the schedule and, for now, the room is a reasonable temperature. If it swings again, please report it straight away rather than suffering in silence, because it is much easier to fix while the engineer's visit is fresh in everyone's memory.

On the process side, Bram Tanaka asked us to stop forwarding documents by email when a link to the shared copy will do. The reasoning is simple: every forwarded copy is another version that can go stale, and the compliance guidance gets harder to follow when the same file lives in six inboxes. I have already started doing this and it saves me a surprising amount of searching.

Diego Ferreira reported that the support rota for the holiday period is nearly filled in. A couple of slots are still open, and he would like volunteers to speak up before he starts making polite but persistent requests. For anyone who is nervous about covering support, he has promised a short walkthrough and a quick reference sheet.

Ines Lindqvist tried a small experiment with the billing run, doing the checks in a different order. It saved time and caught one oddity earlier than usual, so she will keep it. She noted that the change is documented in the billing notes in case anyone else needs to follow the steps.

Smaller bits:

- The meeting room booking system has been double-booking a particular room. Use the other one until it is sorted.
- Someone left a very good umbrella in the hall. It is hanging by the door and awaits its owner.
- The team page now has a short description for each project, including Quill Core, so newcomers can find their feet.
- A reminder to log time against the right category, since the reports are only as good as the entries.

I also want to thank whoever cleaned the fridge. It had reached the point where opening it was an act of courage. The relief was widely felt, and the new rule of labelling everything with a name and a date seems to be holding for now.

That is everything for the middle of the week. Back to the planned programme in the next section.
request.entity_system_prompt:
You are an entity extraction specialist for unstructured text.
NEVER extract vague or standalone feelings or generic words. A specific, named abstract concept
that passes the Wikipedia-article test below (e.g. "climate change", "quantum entanglement")
should be extracted as a Concept entity — being abstract is not by itself a reason to exclude it.

NEVER extract:
- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)
- Vague standalone feelings and generic ideas that could not stand alone as a specific, named
  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

For each entity extracted, assign a single entity_type label from this closed ontology:
- Person: An individual human being
- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication
Choose the single most appropriate type. If none fit well, use the closest match.

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>

request.edge_system_prompt:
You are an expert fact extractor that extracts fact triples from text.
1. Extracted fact triples should also be extracted with relevant date information.
2. Treat REFERENCE_TIME as the time the episode was recorded. All temporal information should be extracted relative to REFERENCE_TIME.

# TASK
Extract all factual relationships between the given ENTITIES based on the CURRENT MESSAGE.
Only extract facts that:
- involve two DISTINCT ENTITIES from the ENTITIES list,
- are clearly stated or unambiguously implied in the CURRENT MESSAGE,
  and can be represented as edges in a knowledge graph.
- Facts should include entity names rather than pronouns whenever possible.

# EXTRACTION RULES

1. **Entity Name Validation**: source_name and target_name must use only the name values from the ENTITIES list provided above.
   - CRITICAL: Using names not in the list will cause the edge to be rejected.
2. Each fact must involve two distinct entities — source_name and target_name NEVER refer to the same entity.
3. NEVER extract facts that describe only a single entity's state, feeling, or attribute. Instead, identify the second entity that the state or feeling relates to and form a proper triple.
   - BAD: "Alice feels happy" (single-entity state — what is Alice happy about?)
   - GOOD: "Alice feels happy about Bob's promotion" → Alice FEELS_HAPPY_ABOUT Bob's promotion
   - GOOD: "Alice congratulated Bob" (relationship between two entities), "Alice lives in Paris" (relationship between entity and place)
4. NEVER emit duplicate or semantically redundant facts.
5. The fact field should closely paraphrase the original source sentence(s). Do not verbatim quote the original text.
6. Use REFERENCE_TIME to resolve vague or relative temporal expressions (e.g., "last week").
7. Do not hallucinate or infer temporal bounds from unrelated events.

# RELATION TYPE RULES


You MUST always provide a non-null relation_type for every edge. Leaving it null or empty is not acceptable.
Derive a relation_type from the relationship predicate in SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE (e.g., WORKS_AT, LIVES_IN, IS_FRIENDS_WITH, WROTE, AUTHORED, MARRIED_TO).
If the predicate is unclear, derive one from the fact description using a concise verb phrase.
Use concise, consistent vocabulary — prefer established verbs that would apply broadly.

# DATETIME RULES

- Use ISO 8601 with "Z" suffix (UTC) (e.g., 2025-04-30T00:00:00Z).
- If the fact is ongoing (present tense), set valid_at to REFERENCE_TIME.
- If a change or termination is expressed, set invalid_at to the relevant timestamp.
- Leave both fields null if no explicit or resolvable time is stated.
- If only a date is mentioned (no time), assume 00:00:00.
- If only a year is mentioned, use January 1st at 00:00:00.

request.episode_body:
## Thursday catch-up

Thursday's catch-up was short, which is how it should be. Seven or eight of us stood around the board, with the sort of tea that goes cold before you drink it, and went down the columns from right to left, starting with what was nearly finished. It is a small trick but a good one: it puts the focus on completing things rather than on starting new ones.

Quill Core got the first mention. The team reported that the cleanup of the routing rules is more or less done, and that the remaining job is a final read-through to make sure nothing important has been deleted by accident. Someone asked for a quick test run on a sample of recent traffic before declaring victory, and that was agreed. It is a cheap check against an expensive mistake.

Ines Lindqvist said that the new arrangement for billing questions is working. Having one mailbox has already cut down on duplicated replies, and she has noticed that people are more willing to hand things over now that they know exactly where to send them. She asked for feedback on the wording of the automatic acknowledgement, which a few of us thought sounded stiff. A friendlier version is in the works.

Diego Ferreira raised the question of how to deal with the occasional angry customer. The team talked it through. The general view was that the best response is plain, quick and human: acknowledge the problem, say what will happen next, and do it. Bram Tanaka added that anything with a legal or privacy flavour should be passed to him before a reply goes out, even if it seems minor, and we agreed that was reasonable.

Actions from the catch-up:

- Run a sample test on the routing changes and report back.
- Rewrite the acknowledgement message in a warmer tone.
- Draft a short guide for handling difficult conversations, with a couple of real examples, names removed.
- Add the guide to the notebook so that people can find it later.

One person observed that we always seem to finish the catch-up with more actions than we started with. That is true, and it is a fair warning. We resolved to take on only those actions that already have an owner, and to let the rest wait.

The tea, by the way, was not improved by the meeting, but the board certainly was. We closed three cards before we sat down again.

You are an entity extraction specialist for unstructured text.
NEVER extract vague or standalone feelings or generic words. A specific, named abstract concept
that passes the Wikipedia-article test below (e.g. "climate change", "quantum entanglement")
should be extracted as a Concept entity — being abstract is not by itself a reason to exclude it.

NEVER extract:
- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)
- Vague standalone feelings and generic ideas that could not stand alone as a specific, named
  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

For each entity extracted, assign a single entity_type label from this closed ontology:
- Person: An individual human being
- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication
Choose the single most appropriate type. If none fit well, use the closest match.

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>

request.edge_system_prompt:
You are an expert fact extractor that extracts fact triples from text.
1. Extracted fact triples should also be extracted with relevant date information.
2. Treat REFERENCE_TIME as the time the episode was recorded. All temporal information should be extracted relative to REFERENCE_TIME.

# TASK
Extract all factual relationships between the given ENTITIES based on the CURRENT MESSAGE.
Only extract facts that:
- involve two DISTINCT ENTITIES from the ENTITIES list,
- are clearly stated or unambiguously implied in the CURRENT MESSAGE,
  and can be represented as edges in a knowledge graph.
- Facts should include entity names rather than pronouns whenever possible.

# EXTRACTION RULES

1. **Entity Name Validation**: source_name and target_name must use only the name values from the ENTITIES list provided above.
   - CRITICAL: Using names not in the list will cause the edge to be rejected.
2. Each fact must involve two distinct entities — source_name and target_name NEVER refer to the same entity.
3. NEVER extract facts that describe only a single entity's state, feeling, or attribute. Instead, identify the second entity that the state or feeling relates to and form a proper triple.
   - BAD: "Alice feels happy" (single-entity state — what is Alice happy about?)
   - GOOD: "Alice feels happy about Bob's promotion" → Alice FEELS_HAPPY_ABOUT Bob's promotion
   - GOOD: "Alice congratulated Bob" (relationship between two entities), "Alice lives in Paris" (relationship between entity and place)
4. NEVER emit duplicate or semantically redundant facts.
5. The fact field should closely paraphrase the original source sentence(s). Do not verbatim quote the original text.
6. Use REFERENCE_TIME to resolve vague or relative temporal expressions (e.g., "last week").
7. Do not hallucinate or infer temporal bounds from unrelated events.

# RELATION TYPE RULES


You MUST always provide a non-null relation_type for every edge. Leaving it null or empty is not acceptable.
Derive a relation_type from the relationship predicate in SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE (e.g., WORKS_AT, LIVES_IN, IS_FRIENDS_WITH, WROTE, AUTHORED, MARRIED_TO).
If the predicate is unclear, derive one from the fact description using a concise verb phrase.
Use concise, consistent vocabulary — prefer established verbs that would apply broadly.

# DATETIME RULES

- Use ISO 8601 with "Z" suffix (UTC) (e.g., 2025-04-30T00:00:00Z).
- If the fact is ongoing (present tense), set valid_at to REFERENCE_TIME.
- If a change or termination is expressed, set invalid_at to the relevant timestamp.
- Leave both fields null if no explicit or resolvable time is stated.
- If only a date is mentioned (no time), assume 00:00:00.
- If only a year is mentioned, use January 1st at 00:00:00.

request.episode_body:
## Offsite planning

Offsite planning has started in earnest, and the first decision is the easy one. The Bram Tanaka offsite will take place in Bergen, and the team seems happy with that, mostly because it avoids the long debate we had last time about where to go. What is left is the part that always takes longer than expected: working out what we actually want to get from it.

The suggestion on the table is to keep the agenda loose. Mornings for the sort of discussions that never fit into a regular week, such as how we want to work together over the next year, which processes are getting in our way, and what we wish we had stopped doing. Afternoons for something less structured, perhaps a walk, perhaps a long lunch. Several people said that the conversations they remember from previous offsites were the ones that happened on the way to somewhere, not in the meeting room.

Bram Tanaka asked that we not overschedule. His view is that a day with fewer sessions and more time to talk leads to better outcomes, and he would rather end up with two decisions we all believe in than ten we have forgotten by the following Monday. Ines Lindqvist agreed, and added that she would like some time set aside to look at the billing process end to end, because it is hard to do that in a normal week.

Diego Ferreira volunteered to look at logistics, such as travel and a place to meet, though he warned that he is not a natural planner and would welcome a second pair of hands. We will find someone to pair with him.

Points to settle over the next weeks:

- Who needs to travel, and who can join by call for part of it.
- What we need to prepare in advance, ideally a single page per topic.
- How to capture decisions, so that they do not live only in people's memories.
- A rough budget, which someone in finance has promised to sketch.

A small worry was raised about people with caring responsibilities, for whom time away is harder to arrange. We agreed that the dates should be fixed early, and that a few sessions should be designed so that people can take part remotely if they need to.

That is where things stand. More once we have dates in the calendar and the logistics are a little less hazy.

## Offsite planning

Offsite planning has started in earnest, and the first decision is the easy one. The Bram Tanaka offsite will take place in Bergen, and the team seems happy with that, mostly because it avoids the long debate we had last time about where to go. The suggestion on the table is to keep the agenda loose. Mornings for the sort of discussions that never fit into a regular week, such as how we want to work together over the next year, which processes are getting in our way, and what we wish we had stopped doing. Afternoons for something less structured, perhaps a walk, perhaps a long lunch. Several people said that the conversations they remember from previous offsites were the ones that happened on the way to somewhere, not in the meeting room.

Bram Tanaka asked that we not overschedule. His view is that a day with fewer sessions and more time to talk leads to better outcomes, and he would rather end up with two decisions we all believe in than ten we have forgotten by the following Monday. Ines Lindqvist agreed, and added that she would like some time set aside to look at the billing process end to end, because it is hard to do that in a normal week.

- How to capture decisions, so that they do not live only in people's memories.

That is where things stand. More once we have dates in the calendar and the logistics are a little less hazy.

request.episode_body:
## Friday wrap-up

By Friday afternoon the building was emptying out early, and the wrap-up had to compete with a general mood of wanting to go home. We kept it brief and stuck to three questions: what got done, what did not, and what is the first thing on Monday.

What got done is a decent list. The routing rules are cleaner than they were, the audit has been read and digested, the shared drive is in better shape, and the offsite has a place, even if it does not yet have a programme. Nobody would call it a heroic week, but it was a productive one, and there is something to be said for weeks that go roughly to plan.

What did not get done is mainly the bigger tidy-up of the support queue. Diego Ferreira is the first to say that it needs a proper block of time, not odd half hours here and there, and he would like to ring-fence a morning for it next week. We agreed that nobody should schedule a meeting over it. If something urgent arises, he will say so and we will rearrange.

Ines Lindqvist has a short list of billing fixes that she wants to finish before the end of the year, none of them difficult, all of them the kind of thing that gets pushed back. She asked for a gentle nudge in a week or so, which is a perfectly reasonable thing to ask a team to do.

Bram Tanaka will circulate the compliance list with names against each item. People should read it over the weekend if they can bear to, or on Monday morning if they cannot. The point is for nobody to be surprised by being named.

For Monday, then:

- Start with the stand-up, projector permitting.
- Quill Core sample test, as agreed in the catch-up.
- Support queue block, protected.
- Billing fixes, first two.

A few of the usual closing notes. The kitchen has been cleaned, the whiteboard is clean, and the lights have been turned off, mostly. If you are the last person out on a Friday, please check the back room window, which has a habit of being left open.

Thanks to everyone for the week. It felt calmer than the one before, and I would like to keep that going. Last section follows, with the news from the demo.

request.episode_body:
## Demo notes

The last item of the week was the demo, which took place on Friday just before the wrap-up. We had been a little nervous about it, since the routing work is hard to show; the best result is that nothing visible happens, and that does not make for a thrilling presentation. In the end the team decided to show the before and after of a few typical cases, tracing how a request found its way through the rules, and that turned out to be far more convincing than a list of changes.

34 people attended the Quill Core demo, which is more than we had expected for a session about routing. A few came from outside the immediate team, and several stayed behind afterwards with questions. The room was slightly too small, so a number of people stood at the back, and the next one should be held somewhere roomier.

The questions were good. One person asked what happens when two rules both match, and the answer led to a short, lively discussion about priority and who gets to decide it. Another asked how a new person would learn the rules, which gave us a gentle reminder that the comments we have been adding are not just housekeeping, they are the documentation. Someone else wanted to know how we would notice if the routing started to go wrong, and we promised to write that up properly as a short page.

Feedback gathered afterwards:

- The walk-through of real cases was the best part.
- The slides were too dense and could be trimmed.
- People would like a recording for those who could not come.
- A follow-up with more time for questions would be welcome.

Ines Lindqvist noted that the billing team would benefit from a similar session, to show how the month-end process fits together. Diego Ferreira suggested that support might do one too, and Bram Tanaka offered to sit in on any of them from the compliance side. A series of short demos, one per area, might be a good habit to build in the new year.

For the record, the demo ended on time, which is rare and worth noting. The team stacked the chairs and, as an unplanned bonus, someone had brought pastries.

That closes the digest for this week. Thanks to everyone who contributed notes; the next entry will pick up with the cleanup and the planning for the offsite.

You are an entity extraction specialist for unstructured text.
NEVER extract vague or standalone feelings or generic words. A specific, named abstract concept
that passes the Wikipedia-article test below (e.g. "climate change", "quantum entanglement")
should be extracted as a Concept entity — being abstract is not by itself a reason to exclude it.

NEVER extract:
- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)
- Vague standalone feelings and generic ideas that could not stand alone as a specific, named
  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

For each entity extracted, assign a single entity_type label from this closed ontology:
- Person: An individual human being
- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication
Choose the single most appropriate type. If none fit well, use the closest match.

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>

request.episode_body:
# The state of urban mobility in mid-sized cities

_Clipped from the web. Source: example.org/state-of-urban-mobility-mid-sized-cities._

Mid-sized cities occupy an awkward position in debates about how people get around. They are too large to depend on walking alone, yet too small to justify the heavy rail systems that serve the biggest metropolitan areas. Planners who work in them describe a constant balancing act between ambition and budget, with each new scheme judged against the very real possibility that too few people will use it.

Buses remain the backbone of public transport in most such places, and the quality of the service varies enormously. Where routes are frequent and predictable, ridership holds up. Where timetables are sparse, the familiar spiral sets in: fewer passengers mean fewer services, which in turn push more people towards cars. Several city officials interviewed for recent studies said the single most effective improvement was not a new vehicle or a new route but a simple increase in how often buses came, so that passengers no longer needed to consult a timetable.

Cycling has grown steadily, helped by the spread of electric bicycles, which make hills and longer distances less daunting. The limiting factor, according to transport researchers, is rarely enthusiasm. It is safety, or perceived safety. Protected lanes that connect to one another and to destinations people actually want to reach attract new riders; isolated stretches of painted lane do not. Cities that have invested in complete networks, rather than scattered fragments, report the strongest gains.

Parking policy is the quieter lever. Surveys of residents often show strong attachment to free or cheap parking, and strong reluctance to see it changed. Yet researchers argue that the price and availability of parking influence travel choices more than almost any other single factor, and some cities have moved cautiously, beginning with the busiest streets and returning revenue to local improvements so that the benefits are visible.

Freight and deliveries, once an afterthought, are now a central concern. Growth in online shopping has put more vans on residential streets, and several councils are experimenting with shared collection points and restricted delivery hours in the busiest areas.

The common thread among cities that report progress is patience. Changes are tried on a small scale, measured, adjusted and only then extended. Those that announced sweeping reforms with little preparation, observers note, often faced backlash that set the whole effort back.

<TEXT>
# The state of urban mobility in mid-sized cities

_Clipped from the web. Source: example.org/state-of-urban-mobility-mid-sized-cities._

Mid-sized cities occupy an awkward position in debates about how people get around. They are too large to depend on walking alone, yet too small to justify the heavy rail systems that serve the biggest metropolitan areas. Planners who work in them describe a constant balancing act between ambition and budget, with each new scheme judged against the very real possibility that too few people will use it.

Buses remain the backbone of public transport in most such places, and the quality of the service varies enormously. Where routes are frequent and predictable, ridership holds up. Where timetables are sparse, the familiar spiral sets in: fewer passengers mean fewer services, which in turn push more people towards cars. Several city officials interviewed for recent studies said the single most effective improvement was not a new vehicle or a new route but a simple increase in how often buses came, so that passengers no longer needed to consult a timetable.

Cycling has grown steadily, helped by the spread of electric bicycles, which make hills and longer distances less daunting. The limiting factor, according to transport researchers, is rarely enthusiasm. It is safety, or perceived safety. Protected lanes that connect to one another and to destinations people actually want to reach attract new riders; isolated stretches of painted lane do not. Cities that have invested in complete networks, rather than scattered fragments, report the strongest gains.

Parking policy is the quieter lever. Surveys of residents often show strong attachment to free or cheap parking, and strong reluctance to see it changed. Yet researchers argue that the price and availability of parking influence travel choices more than almost any other single factor, and some cities have moved cautiously, beginning with the busiest streets and returning revenue to local improvements so that the benefits are visible.

Freight and deliveries, once an afterthought, are now a central concern. Growth in online shopping has put more vans on residential streets, and several councils are experimenting with shared collection points and restricted delivery hours in the busiest areas.

The common thread among cities that report progress is patience. Changes are tried on a small scale, measured, adjusted and only then extended. Those that announced sweeping reforms with little preparation, observers note, often faced backlash that set the whole effort back.
</TEXT>

request.episode_body:
# Planning notes — 13 January 2026

First planning session of the new year, and it felt good to be back around the same table. The room was cold because the heating had not been switched on over the break, so the first ten minutes were mostly people holding mugs and complaining. Once everyone thawed we got through the agenda in good order.

We began with a look back at the quarter. The incident review is the part everyone dreads, but this time it was calmer than expected. Marcus Haddad logged 38 incidents during the quarter, and he walked us through the pattern: most were noisy alerts rather than real outages, and a good share traced back to a handful of badly tuned thresholds. He wants to spend the first fortnight of the year pruning those so the on-call rota stops being woken for nothing. Nobody objected. We agreed he should own the clean-up and report back at the next planning session, with a short list of what was removed and why.

Next, the shared calendar. Several people pointed out that the recurring Tuesday sync has drifted into a status-reading exercise, which is exactly what we said we would stop doing. The decision was to keep the slot but change its shape: written updates go into the log beforehand, and the meeting itself is reserved for blockers and decisions. We will try it for a month and then ask whether it is any better. If it is not, we drop the meeting altogether and rely on the log.

A few chores that came up and need an owner:

- The old shared drive folder is still full of half-finished drafts. Someone should sort it into keep, archive and delete. It was agreed that this would be done as a joint effort on a quiet afternoon rather than assigned to one unlucky person.
- The onboarding checklist has not been touched since the autumn. Fable Core will review it against what new starters actually needed this past quarter and propose edits.
- The monitoring dashboard has a few panels that nobody can explain. Before deleting anything we will ask around in case someone relies on them.

On planning more generally, there was a short but useful discussion about how much slack to leave in the next sprint. The last two went badly because we filled every day, then absorbed interruptions on top. The suggestion that won out was to plan to roughly three quarters of capacity and treat anything beyond that as a bonus. It is a small change in how we write the board, but it should make the numbers more honest.

We also touched on the question of whether to keep writing these notes in one long running log or split them by topic. Opinion was divided. The people who skim like the single log because everything is in one place; the people who search prefer topic pages. For now we are staying with one log and adding clearer headings so it can be scanned, and we will revisit if search becomes painful.

Finally, a reminder to everyone to book leave early for the spring, since the last two years we ended up with a pile-up in the same week and a thin team covering it. Put your dates into the calendar before the next meeting, even if they are provisional.

Actions out of today: prune noisy alerts, review onboarding checklist, tidy the shared folder, try the new meeting shape. Next planning session is pencilled in for the same slot, same cold room, hopefully warmer.

You are an entity extraction specialist for unstructured text.
NEVER extract vague or standalone feelings or generic words. A specific, named abstract concept
that passes the Wikipedia-article test below (e.g. "climate change", "quantum entanglement")
should be extracted as a Concept entity — being abstract is not by itself a reason to exclude it.

NEVER extract:
- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)
- Vague standalone feelings and generic ideas that could not stand alone as a specific, named
  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

For each entity extracted, assign a single entity_type label from this closed ontology:
- Person: An individual human being
- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication
Choose the single most appropriate type. If none fit well, use the closest match.

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>

request.episode_body:
## Tuesday sync, trial run

Wrote this up straight after the meeting while it was fresh. We tried the new format for the sync, with updates pre-written into the log and the live time kept for things that actually need a conversation. It worked better than anyone predicted, mostly because people had to be concise in advance. Whoever had a rambling update found it much harder to ramble in writing.

What came out of it:

The routing side, with Priya Varga, reported that the handover documentation is nearly finished and that she would like a second pair of eyes before it is circulated. Two people volunteered, which is a good sign, though both said they would need to wait until the end of the week. That was fine with her.

request.episode_body:
## Housekeeping and small decisions

A quieter stretch this week, so these notes are mostly chores and the small decisions that never make it into a proper document but matter anyway.

**The shared inbox.** It had grown into a graveyard. Somebody went through it and found that roughly half of what was sitting there was automated notifications nobody reads. We agreed to set up a filter so those go to a separate folder, and to leave only things that need a human reply in the main view. The person who did the sorting said it took about as long as a lunch break, which suggests we should have done it ages ago.

**Laptop refresh.** The question of replacing older machines came up again. No decision on the budget, since that sits with someone in finance, but we compiled a list of who is struggling with slow builds so the case can be made with real examples instead of grumbling. A couple of people have already offered to run timing comparisons on their own machines and add the results to the log.

**Fable Core handoff.** The onboarding project wants to hand a few recurring tasks to a wider group, since only a small number of people currently know how to do them. We agreed to pair people up for the next occurrence instead of writing yet another long document. The theory is that watching someone do it once teaches more than reading about it ten times. If the pairing works, the document can be written afterwards from what the learner found confusing, which is the only part worth writing down.

**Meeting-free mornings.** There was a proposal to protect one morning a week from meetings entirely. Support was broad, but the details were messy: which morning, and what counts as a meeting. We settled on trying Thursdays and defining a meeting as anything with more than two people and a calendar invite. Quick chats in the corridor are fine. Review again after a month.

**Docs tidy.** The wiki has several pages that contradict each other, usually because one was updated and its twin was not. Rather than a big clean-up, the rule going forward is that whoever notices a contradiction fixes it on the spot or leaves a clear note on the page. Small, constant maintenance beats a heroic spring clean that never happens.

**Coffee machine.** It is broken again. A repair has been requested, and in the meantime there is a kettle and a jar of the instant stuff. Morale has held up surprisingly well.

Reminders for the coming days: update your leave dates in the calendar, read the written updates before the Tuesday sync, and put any laptop timing results into the log. If you are reading this and spot something I got wrong, edit it. These notes belong to everyone, and I would rather have a correct page than a tidy one.

Not much else to report. The week looked unremarkable from the outside, which in this team usually means things are going fine.

request.episode_body:
## Thinking about the spring plan

Not a meeting record this time, more of a scribble after a long conversation by the whiteboard. I want to get it down before it evaporates.

The core question was what we want the next few months to look like, and whether our habit of planning in short bursts is serving us or just keeping us busy. A few of us felt that the short cycles have been good for visibility but bad for finishing anything large. Work that takes longer than a cycle tends to be sliced up artificially, and the slices never quite add up to the thing we wanted.

So here is the tentative shape. One or two larger pieces of work get a longer runway, and everything else continues in the short cycles around them. The larger pieces need a named owner, a plain statement of what done looks like, and a regular check-in that is not a status meeting. I am wary of this becoming a heavyweight process, so the rule is that if the description does not fit on one page, the piece is too big or too vague.

Candidates mentioned:

- Telemetry clean-up, which Marcus Haddad has already begun thinking about as part of the alert pruning. It has a natural end point and would benefit from uninterrupted attention.
- The routing handover, led by Priya Varga, which is partly documentation and partly a change in who does what. Probably the messiest of the lot, because it involves people more than systems.
- A tidy of the inventory processes under Orbit Core, which keeps getting deferred because there is always something more urgent.

None of these are committed. They are things to talk about at the next planning session, and I would like people to come ready to say which they would actually want to work on, not which they think they ought to.

There was also a side thread about how we estimate. The honest summary is that we are bad at it, and consistently bad in the same direction: we underestimate anything involving a handover between people and overestimate anything purely technical. Knowing the bias is half the battle, so a proposal is to add a simple fudge factor for work that crosses team boundaries and see whether our guesses improve.

Something else worth recording: several people said they would like more time to think, and less to react. That is a hard one to put on a board. The meeting-free mornings are a step in that direction, and I would like us to notice whether they actually produce better work or simply produce quieter calendars.

I will bring a half-page sketch of the longer-runway idea to the next session. If it reads as bureaucratic when I write it down, I will throw it away and we can keep doing what we do.

request.episode_body:
## Retro odds and ends

Notes from the end-of-sprint retrospective, collected in the order they were raised rather than any sensible order.

**What went well.** The new written-update habit took hold faster than expected. People are arriving at meetings already knowing what everybody else has been doing, so the conversation starts at the interesting part. A couple of people also said the log has become a pleasant place to find answers, which is not something I expected to hear about a shared document.

**What was frustrating.** Context switching, as always. One person described a day in which they changed task six times and finished none, and the room nodded in a way that suggested this was not unusual. We talked about whether interruptions could be batched, perhaps by having a named person who takes incoming requests for a day at a time. It was left as an experiment. The risk is that the named person becomes a bottleneck and quietly resents it, so we will rotate.

**Things we said we would stop doing.** Scheduling meetings that could have been messages. Opening tickets with no description. Merging changes late on Friday afternoons. The last one drew a rueful laugh, because at least two people had been burned by it recently. Not a rule, exactly, just an agreement that Friday evening merges need a very good reason.

**Things we said we would start.** A short note at the top of each ticket saying who is waiting on it. It sounds trivial but it changes the urgency of a request in a way a priority label never does. Also, a monthly slot where anybody can show something small they built or fixed, with no slides allowed.

There was a good exchange about Fable Core and the amount of tribal knowledge baked into the onboarding process. A newer colleague said the main thing missing was not documentation but a sense of who to ask about what. A simple who-knows-what page was suggested. I like it because it is cheap and it ages gracefully: even a half-out-of-date version beats nothing.

On the people side, the mood was good. A few comments about workload being lumpy, with heavy weeks followed by empty ones, and a request that anyone with spare capacity says so out loud instead of quietly absorbing it. If you are free, announce it. Someone else is almost certainly drowning.

For the record, we did not resolve the question of whether retrospectives should be shorter. A narrow majority wanted them kept to the time we have, and a vocal minority wanted them cut in half. I suggested a compromise of a fixed agenda with a hard stop, and nobody objected loudly enough to count.

Next retro the same facilitator volunteers again, which is the best argument I can think of for them being useful. Everybody go and look at your own list of things you promised to stop doing, please.
