Roads that were designed for lighter traffic fill at peak hours, parking in the centre is scarce and expensive, and bus services that struggle to attract riders fall into a familiar cycle: fewer passengers lead to less frequent service, which leads to fewer passengers still.

request.episode_body:
## What is being tried

Transport officials describe a range of approaches, few of them new but many being combined in fresh ways. Some cities have concentrated on a small number of high-frequency bus corridors, where services run often enough that riders do not need to consult a timetable. The logic is simple: frequency is the feature that matters most to people deciding whether public transport is a realistic option. A route that comes every ten minutes is usable on impulse. A route that comes every forty is a commitment.

Others have focused on cycling. Protected lanes, as opposed to painted lines, have proved the more effective investment, since the barrier to cycling is usually perceived danger rather than distance. In places where a connected network has been built, rather than isolated stretches, local counts show steady growth in everyday trips, not just recreational ones. The challenge is that a connected network takes years to complete, and half-finished routes tend to attract criticism before they attract riders.

A third strand involves shared and on-demand services in outer districts, where fixed routes are uneconomic. Small vehicles that respond to bookings can fill the gaps, but the cost per trip is high, and many pilots have been quietly wound down once the initial funding ran out. Officials who have kept such services running say the key is to treat them as a complement to the main network, feeding passengers into the high-frequency corridors rather than competing with them.

request.episode_body:
## The funding question

None of this is cheap, and funding is the constraint that comes up in nearly every conversation. National programmes tend to favour large, visible projects, while mid-sized cities often need a steady stream of modest improvements: better stops, signal priority, safer crossings, reliable real-time information. These do not make headlines, yet they account for much of the difference between a system people tolerate and one they use.

Local budgets are stretched, and the temptation to defer maintenance in favour of new construction is strong. Several analysts argue that the cities making the most progress are those that have been disciplined about the basics, keeping what exists in good order before adding to it.

## Land use and the long view

Transport specialists increasingly stress that mobility cannot be separated from where homes, jobs and services are placed. A city that allows low-density development at its edges will always struggle to provide frequent public transport to it. Conversely, cities that concentrate new housing near existing corridors give their transit services a better chance of success. These decisions play out over decades, and are politically harder than painting a bus lane.

The results are uneven, and early opposition is common, but several cities report that, once the changes settle in, complaints fade and streets become noticeably more pleasant.

## Measuring success

How should a mid-sized city judge whether its approach is working? Raw ridership is one measure, but it can be misleading when population is changing. More useful, according to people in the field, are the share of trips made without a car, average journey times for common routes and how evenly services are spread across neighbourhoods. Surveys of residents add context, particularly on whether people feel safe and whether they trust services to turn up.

The consensus among practitioners is that there is no single solution. The cities doing best combine reliable core services, safe cycling and walking links, careful land use and patience. Progress is slow, rarely dramatic and often invisible until, one day, a resident realises they have not used the car all week.

request.episode_body:
# Working notes — 29 March 2026

A slow Sunday evening, which is when I do my best thinking about the week ahead and my worst thinking about almost everything else. Notes below are a mix of what happened and what I intend to do about it.

Let me begin with the calendar, since it is the thing most likely to bite us. Cedar Core held its quarterly retrospective on 13 October 2027, and the team wanted that recorded in the planning sheet so that future quarters line up with it. I know that is a long way off from where we are sitting, but the group asked for the date to be fixed early and the planning sheet is where such things live. I have added it, with a note explaining how the cadence is meant to work, so that whoever inherits the sheet does not have to guess. It is a small thing, but dates that are written down tend to survive; dates that are remembered tend not to.

On the people side, Noor Okafor completed 21 hours of training this term, mostly in analytics, and has been trying out a couple of the techniques on real work. The most visible result is a tidier weekly summary, which is shorter than the old one and, as far as I can tell, answers more of the questions people used to ask afterwards. Noor has offered to share what was learned at a short session. I told Noor to take the credit for it, and that the session could be as informal as a lunchtime chat. I would rather people hear a few practical tips than sit through a presentation.

Other business from the week:

- The planning meeting on Tuesday ran well over time, because a debate about naming conventions turned into a debate about everything. We agreed to take naming offline and decide by comment on a shared page.
- The new starter checklist was tried for the first time, and it works, though two of the steps are in the wrong order. Fixed.
- A request came in for a quieter place to take calls. We have a spare corner that could be curtained off, and I will look into prices without promising anything.
- The weekly summary email now goes out on Thursdays instead of Fridays, since nobody reads email on Fridays.

A note about morale. People are in decent spirits, though there is a mild tiredness that I think comes from the long stretch between holidays. We cannot do much about that, but we can avoid piling on new initiatives. I have asked each group to name one thing they would stop doing if they could. The answers so far are revealing: mostly reports that nobody reads and meetings with no decisions. I would like to act on at least two of them.

The week ahead is lighter than usual, which is a gift. I plan to use the spare time to catch up on documentation, to read through the pile of notes from the past month, and to resist the temptation to schedule anything on Wednesday afternoon. A free afternoon is more valuable than it looks.

request.episode_body:
## Midweek notes

Wednesday, and the free afternoon did, in fact, remain free. I spent it reading, which felt almost illicit. A few things have emerged since the weekend.

The naming-convention debate moved to the shared page, and it is going better in writing than it did in the room. Written comments are calmer and more specific. Two clear camps have formed: one wants names that describe what a thing does, the other wants names that describe where it lives. Reading both sets of arguments, I think a hybrid will win out, and I have suggested that the people most invested draft a short proposal together. If they can agree on a page, the rest of us can live with it. If they cannot, I will make a call, which nobody will enjoy.

Noor Okafor shared a few practical tips from the recent training over lunch, as promised, and it turned out to be exactly the right format. About a dozen people drifted over with their sandwiches and stayed. The tips were small but useful: how to frame a question before starting an analysis, how to check that a chart is saying what you think it says, and how to write a summary for someone who has five minutes. I came away with a note to myself about the third one in particular, because I tend to write for people who have an hour. Noor has put the slides in the shared space, though I suspect the conversation was more valuable than the slides.

Cedar Core had a short planning session, mainly to talk about the billing calendar and how it connects to the retrospective date we recorded. They wanted to make sure the retrospective does not land on top of another busy period, and the sheet now shows both side by side. It is a minor adjustment, but it avoids the sort of clash that is irritating to discover late. The group also asked whether future retrospectives could include a short section on what they decided to stop doing, which I think is a lovely idea and have offered to help them build a template.

Small things worth noting:

- The call corner has been measured. A curtain would cost less than I feared, but the acoustics are the real problem, and a curtain will not fix them.
- The Thursday summary email is now scheduled, and a test copy went out to a few people without incident.
- A broken chair was reported, then fixed, then reported again. The cycle continues.
- Someone brought in biscuits. Productivity rose briefly.

One concern I want to put on record. We are asking a lot of people to document things, to write proposals, to share what they have learned, and to attend sessions. Each request is reasonable, but together they add up. I would like us to be honest about what we are asking and to protect time for it, rather than assuming it will happen in the margins. If we do not, the documentation will be the first casualty and we will be back where we started.

Tomorrow looks calm. I will use it to start on the template for the retrospective and to chase the naming proposal.

request.episode_body:
## End of week

Friday afternoon and the building has the pleasantly empty feel it gets just before the weekend. A good time to close out the week's log.

The naming proposal arrived this morning. It is a page and a half, which is about right, and it makes a reasonable case for the hybrid approach. A few people have already added comments, mostly small edits, and nobody has objected to the main idea. I suspect the quiet agreement is partly relief that the argument is nearly over. I will give it until Monday for final remarks, then mark it as agreed and ask someone to apply it to the shared pages over the following fortnight. It will be dull work, but dull and consistent beats clever and confusing.

The retrospective template for Cedar Core is in rough shape. It has four prompts: what went well, what we would do differently, what we would stop doing, and what we are unsure about. The last one was added at the group's suggestion, and I think it is the most interesting, because it invites people to admit uncertainty without it sounding like a failure. I sent the draft round for comments and will tidy it next week. I also suggested that whoever runs the session send the prompts out in advance, so that people can think before they arrive and the loudest voices do not set the tone.

Noor Okafor mentioned that the tidier weekly summary format is now being used by two other groups, and asked whether it would be worth writing down the reasoning behind it. I said yes, as long as it stays short. A format without its rationale tends to get copied badly, with the useful bits dropped and the decorative bits kept. The rationale can sit at the bottom of the same page, for anyone who wants it.

Housekeeping:

- The curtain idea for the call corner has been shelved. We will try putting a sign up and see whether people respect it.
- The chair has been replaced with a sturdier one. Let us hope.
- The Thursday summary email went out on time this week, and a couple of people actually replied.
- Biscuit supplies are low. This is not an emergency, but it is being monitored.

A small, slightly sentimental reflection. When I started keeping these notes, I thought they would be a record of decisions. They have turned out to be more of a record of the texture of work: what we argued about, what we got tired of, what made us laugh. The decisions are in other places, and the notes fill in the human side. I think that is worth keeping, even if no one reads them for a year.

Plans for next week: close the naming proposal, polish the template, look at the stop-doing list, and take another free afternoon if the calendar allows. I will report back on Sunday, when my thinking is at its best.
request.entity_system_prompt:
You are an entity extraction specialist for unstructured text.
NEVER extract vague or standalone feelings or generic words. A specific, named abstract concept
that passes the Wikipedia-article test below (e.g. "climate change", "quantum entanglement")
should be extracted as a Concept entity — being abstract is not by itself a reason to exclude it.

NEVER extract:
- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)
- Vague standalone feelings and generic ideas that could not stand alone as a specific, named
  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

For each entity extracted, assign a single entity_type label from this closed ontology:
- Person: An individual human being
- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication
Choose the single most appropriate type. If none fit well, use the closest match.

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>

## Where we are

Spring has brought a wave of new joiners, which is good news and also the reason the onboarding side of the team has been running flat out. Aiko Osei has been the first point of contact for nearly everyone, and the load shows. The plan this week is to take some of the repetitive explaining off Aiko's plate by turning the most common answers into a short written guide. If a question has been asked three times, it belongs on a page, not in someone's head.

On the retrospective calendar, which we keep forgetting to update: Aiko Osei held its quarterly retrospective on 13 April 2026, and the notes are in the team folder. The headline from that session was that the first week for a new starter is either wonderfully organised or chaotic, with very little in between, and the difference usually comes down to whether the equipment and accounts were ready before the person arrived. That is a process problem with a process answer, and it is on this week's list.

request.episode_body:
## Things to watch

The risk with an onboarding push is that it consumes the people who are best at it. Aiko has been generous with time, but a single point of contact is a fragile arrangement. The mitigation is to share the load: other people take specific topics, such as tools, working practices and who-to-ask, so that it is not all routed through one person.

There is also the question of how much documentation is too much. A new joiner who is handed a hundred pages on day one will read none of them. The suggestion is to stage it: a short pack for week one, a further set for the first month, and the rest available on request.

request.episode_body:
## Working through the guide

Most of the early part of the week went into the first-week guide. The first draft was written in an afternoon and then promptly torn up in a review session, which is how these things tend to go. The main criticism was that it read like a list of rules, when what a new person needs is a sense of how the team actually works: where to ask, what is normal, and what can safely be ignored for the first few days. The second draft is chattier and shorter, and so far people prefer it.

A few of the things we decided to include:

- A plain explanation of how requests are tracked, with a screenshot of what a good entry looks like.
- A short list of the meetings a newcomer should attend in week one and the ones that can wait.
- A page on who to ask about what, written by role rather than by name, so it does not go stale every time someone moves.
- A reassurance, stated outright, that nobody expects a new person to be productive immediately.

That last one sounds trivial. It is not. Several people who joined recently said they spent their first days worried they were being slow, when in fact they were right on schedule.

that passes the Wikipedia-article test below (e.g. "climate change", "quantum entanglement")
should be extracted as a Concept entity — being abstract is not by itself a reason to exclude it.

- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)
- Vague standalone feelings and generic ideas that could not stand alone as a specific, named
  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

For each entity extracted, assign a single entity_type label from this closed ontology:

- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component

request.entity_user_prompt:
<TEXT>
## Working through the guide

Most of the early part of the week went into the first-week guide. The first draft was written in an afternoon and then promptly torn up in a review session, which is how these things tend to go. The main criticism was that it read like a list of rules, when what a new person needs is a sense of how the team actually works: where to ask, what is normal, and what can safely be ignored for the first few days. The second draft is chattier and shorter, and so far people prefer it.

A few of the things we decided to include:

- A plain explanation of how requests are tracked, with a screenshot of what a good entry looks like.
- A short list of the meetings a newcomer should attend in week one and the ones that can wait.
- A page on who to ask about what, written by role rather than by name, so it does not go stale every time someone moves.
- A reassurance, stated outright, that nobody expects a new person to be productive immediately.

That last one sounds trivial. It is not. Several people who joined recently said they spent their first days worried they were being slow, when in fact they were right on schedule.
</TEXT>

Extract all factual relationships between the given ENTITIES based on the CURRENT MESSAGE.
Only extract facts that:
- involve two DISTINCT ENTITIES from the ENTITIES list,
- are clearly stated or unambiguously implied in the CURRENT MESSAGE,
  and can be represented as edges in a knowledge graph.
- Facts should include entity names rather than pronouns whenever possible.

# EXTRACTION RULES

1. **Entity Name Validation**: source_name and target_name must use only the name values from the ENTITIES list provided above.
   - CRITICAL: Using names not in the list will cause the edge to be rejected.
2. Each fact must involve two distinct entities — source_name and target_name NEVER refer to the same entity.
3. NEVER extract facts that describe only a single entity's state, feeling, or attribute. Instead, identify the second entity that the state or feeling relates to and form a proper triple.
   - BAD: "Alice feels happy" (single-entity state — what is Alice happy about?)
   - GOOD: "Alice feels happy about Bob's promotion" → Alice FEELS_HAPPY_ABOUT Bob's promotion
   - GOOD: "Alice congratulated Bob" (relationship between two entities), "Alice lives in Paris" (relationship between entity and place)
4. NEVER emit duplicate or semantically redundant facts.
5. The fact field should closely paraphrase the original source sentence(s). Do not verbatim quote the original text.
6. Use REFERENCE_TIME to resolve vague or relative temporal expressions (e.g., "last week").
7. Do not hallucinate or infer temporal bounds from unrelated events.

You MUST always provide a non-null relation_type for every edge. Leaving it null or empty is not acceptable.
Derive a relation_type from the relationship predicate in SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE (e.g., WORKS_AT, LIVES_IN, IS_FRIENDS_WITH, WROTE, AUTHORED, MARRIED_TO).
If the predicate is unclear, derive one from the fact description using a concise verb phrase.
Use concise, consistent vocabulary — prefer established verbs that would apply broadly.

- Use ISO 8601 with "Z" suffix (UTC) (e.g., 2025-04-30T00:00:00Z).
- If the fact is ongoing (present tense), set valid_at to REFERENCE_TIME.
- If a change or termination is expressed, set invalid_at to the relevant timestamp.
- Leave both fields null if no explicit or resolvable time is stated.
- If only a date is mentioned (no time), assume 00:00:00.
- If only a year is mentioned, use January 1st at 00:00:00.

request.episode_body:
## Fable Core and the wider picture

Fable Core is the onboarding project, so a lot of this work is really its work, and Aiko Osei is carrying much of it. The sensible thing is to make that visible: the project board should show the guide, the checklist and the buddy arrangements as distinct pieces, each with an owner and a rough sequence. At present they are lumped together under a single heading, which makes progress hard to see and makes it easy for items to be quietly forgotten.

There was a good conversation about measuring whether any of this helps. A survey is the obvious tool, but surveys of new starters are notorious for politeness. The alternative is to ask specific questions: when did you first merge something, when did you last feel lost, what would you tell the next person? Those tend to produce more honest answers than "how was your experience".

## Logistics

Equipment ordering was the main bottleneck last time, so the checklist now starts a couple of weeks before the start date. Accounts follow. The team also decided to keep a small stock of spare cables and adapters, because few things are more demoralising than a first morning spent hunting for a charger.

Meeting rooms for induction sessions are confirmed. Catering is not, but a sandwich order is easy to place once numbers are known.

request.episode_body:
## Backlog and sprint close

Closing the sprint, the board tells a mixed story. The Fable Core backlog stood at 103 open tickets at the end of the sprint. That is more than the team would like, though a fair share of those are small and some are probably stale. The first job next week is a grooming pass to separate what is genuinely waiting for work from what has simply been forgotten. Anything nobody can argue for gets closed with a short explanation, which is kinder to the person who raised it than leaving it to rot.

It is worth being clear about what the number does and does not say. A large backlog is not automatically a sign of trouble; plenty of healthy projects carry one. What matters is whether the oldest items are being looked at and whether the ones near the top are the ones that really matter. A long list sorted well is more useful than a short one sorted badly.

request.episode_body:
## Sorting the list

The proposed approach to grooming is gentle. Each item gets one of four fates: do it soon, do it later, hand it to someone else, or close it. Nothing is deleted without a note. The team agreed to spend a fixed block of time on this, not to chase perfection, and to stop when the block ends even if the list is not clean. Better a decent pass than a heroic one nobody repeats.

Some categories of ticket are likely to be easy to resolve:

- Duplicates of something else already tracked.
- Requests that were overtaken by a change in how we work.
- Ideas that were interesting once and have not been mentioned since.

The harder ones are those that look important but have no clear owner. Those are going to need a conversation, and probably a decision about whether the project should take them on at all.

The proposed approach to grooming is gentle. Each item gets one of four fates: do it soon, do it later, hand it to someone else, or close it. Nothing is deleted without a note. request.episode_body:
# What small cooperatives get wrong about governance

Small cooperatives usually begin with goodwill and a shared purpose, and that is often the problem. When everyone knows everyone, rules feel like an insult. Decisions are made over coffee, roles are assumed rather than written down, and the founding group quietly becomes the whole decision-making body. It works until the cooperative grows, someone leaves, or two members disagree about something that matters.

The most common failure is a blurred line between members and management. In theory, members set direction and elected officers carry it out. In practice, the same few people wear both hats, and nobody is sure which one they are wearing at a given meeting. Advisers who work with such groups suggest a simple fix: say, at the start of each item, whether it is a matter for the membership or for the board, and record the answer.

A second weakness is the treatment of suppliers. Cooperatives often buy from a small number of sources and treat those relationships as personal. Trade press reported that Fable Supply lists its standard rate at $61 per unit, and members sometimes cite figures like that as though they settled the question. They do not. A governance policy should say who is allowed to negotiate, who signs off on terms, and how conflicts of interest are declared, so that purchasing decisions rest on a process and not on whoever knows the supplier best.

Third, many groups neglect to review their own rules. Bylaws written in the first year rarely survive contact with the tenth. A modest annual check, ideally by someone who did not draft the original, can catch provisions that have been quietly ignored or that no longer match how the cooperative operates.

Finally, there is the matter of conflict. Cooperatives tend to avoid it, mistaking silence for harmony. Those that cope best build in a clear route for raising grievances, with a neutral person to hear them, long before one is needed. It costs little to set up and can save a good deal of damage later.

request.episode_body:
## Know what you are buying

Before comparing offers, write down what the company needs in a few plain lines: what the item or service must do, who will rely on it, and how long it is likely to be needed. The exercise sounds trivial, but it keeps conversations with sales staff honest. It is far easier to turn down an upgrade when you can point to a sentence saying you do not need one.

Buyers also benefit from sorting requirements into essentials and extras. Essentials are the things without which the business stops; extras are conveniences. Costly arrangements often creep in when an extra is promoted to an essential during a persuasive demonstration.

request.episode_body:
## Look at the market, not just one quote

A single quotation tells you very little. Gather at least a handful of comparisons and read the published information as well as the private offers. Trade press is a useful source here, since it sometimes reports what suppliers charge in the open. Trade press reported that Cedar Supply lists its standard rate at $113 per unit, which gives a buyer a reference point to hold up against whatever figure appears in a private quote. A published list price is rarely the final word, because discounts and bundles change the picture, but it provides a ceiling to negotiate down from and a sanity check on any figure that sounds far off.

The comparison should also account for what sits around the price: delivery, support, cancellation terms and the effort of switching later. A modest saving on paper can vanish if the contract is difficult to leave.

request.episode_body:
## Read the terms

Automatic renewals, minimum commitments and long notice periods cause more regret than almost any other feature of a purchase. Read them before signing, and ask for anything unclear to be explained in writing. If a supplier hesitates to clarify, treat that as a warning.

Where possible, ask for a shorter initial period or a trial. Suppliers who are confident in what they sell will usually agree, and the flexibility is worth far more than a small discount on a long commitment.

## Keep approvals light but visible

A small company cannot support heavy sign-off procedures, but it also cannot let every purchase go unrecorded. A short rule works well: routine buys can be made by anyone, larger or recurring ones need a second opinion. What matters is that someone can see the whole list of commitments at any given moment.

## Be a good customer

Pay invoices on time, give clear instructions and warn suppliers about changes in plan. Good behaviour is repaid when something goes wrong: a supplier who values a customer will often find a way to help with a slipped deadline or an awkward request.

It is equally reasonable to keep options open. Review suppliers from time to time, note how they have behaved, and be ready to move on if the relationship sours. A written record of problems makes that decision easier and keeps it calm.

request.episode_body:
# Customer interviews: the questions that matter

Most people who run customer interviews come away with a pile of pleasant remarks and very little they can act on. The cause is rarely the customer. It is the questions, which tend to invite compliments rather than facts.

The first rule is to ask about the past, not the future. Saying "would you use this?" yields a polite yes. Asking "when did you last deal with this problem, and what did you do?" yields a story, and stories contain the details that matter: what triggered the problem, what workarounds were tried, who else was involved, and what it cost in time or money.

The second is to follow the thread. A good interviewer treats the prepared list as a starting point and spends most of the time on "tell me more about that" and "what happened next?" The most useful insight in a conversation often arrives in an aside, and a rigid script will talk right past it.

Third, listen for emotion. A flicker of irritation or a long sigh signals a problem that is real to the person, which is a better guide than anything they say they would like. Note it, and ask what lies behind it.

Fourth, resist the urge to pitch. The moment an interviewer starts describing a solution, the customer shifts from describing their world to evaluating yours. Save that for a separate conversation.

Finally, write things up promptly. Memory smooths the awkward details first, and those are the parts most worth keeping. A page of honest notes written the same afternoon beats an elegant summary written a week later.

request.episode_body:
## Monday catch-up

The week opened with a short catch-up over coffee. Nobody had a big announcement, which was a relief. Aiko Osei mentioned that the onboarding checklist still has a few steps that nobody can explain anymore, and Fable Core has agreed to go through it line by line and cut whatever turns out to be left over from older processes. We left it as a small job rather than a project, because the last time someone called it a project it stalled for a month.

Priya Varga wanted to know whether the routing notes could live in the same shared folder as everything else instead of in a private pile. General agreement. Noor Okafor offered to tidy the folder structure, with the caveat that it would take a quiet afternoon and not a meeting.

## Midweek review of open items

Wednesday was mostly spent working down the list of things we said we would do and had not. I wrote them out on one page and tried to be honest about which ones were really going to happen.

**Done this week:**
- The shared folder for routing notes now exists, though it is still empty.
- The standing meeting invite has a clearer name and a short description.
- The old inbox clear-out is finished.

**Not done, and that is fine:**
- The onboarding checklist review. It is waiting for a quiet slot.
- The guest wifi question. Still nobody knows.

Priya Varga raised a worry that the routing notes might be too informal to be useful to someone new. She is probably right, and the suggestion that came out of the discussion was to write one worked example from start to finish and let people copy the shape from that, rather than writing rules in the abstract. That seems like the more honest approach, since the rules in our heads are mostly a collection of exceptions.

## A longer conversation about reviews

A good chunk of the afternoon went on how we handle reviews of each other's work. The current pattern is that someone posts a link, waits, and eventually pings a person directly. This tends to land on the same two or three people. Noor Okafor suggested a simple rotation so that the load is shared and nobody feels like the default reviewer. The team was in favour in principle; the detail still needs working out, in particular what happens when someone on the rotation is away.

We agreed on a rough rule of thumb. If a review request has sat for a full working day with no reply, it is fine to nudge. If it has sat for two, it is fine to reassign it without feeling rude.

request.episode_body:
## What was discussed

The main conversation was about how we pick up new requests. At the moment they arrive by whatever route the sender happens to prefer: a message, an email, a tap on the shoulder. That makes it hard to see the whole picture. We talked about having one place where requests go, with a short form of three or four questions. Nobody wanted anything heavy. The point is only that we can tell, at a glance, what is waiting and how old it is.

Noor Okafor was a little sceptical, worrying that forms get ignored, and proposed trying it for a month and checking whether anyone actually used it. That seemed fair. If the form is skipped more than it is used, we drop it without drama.

request.episode_body:
### What we covered

The agenda had three items, and I will go through them in the order we actually discussed them, which was not the order on the page.

First, the shape of the next few weeks. Nobody wanted to commit to anything ambitious. We are still absorbing the changes from the last cycle, and there was a sense that stability would be welcome. The agreement was to focus on finishing things that are nearly done, and only start something new if it replaces something else.

Second, the question of who owns what. Aiko Osei pointed out that a few small areas have no clear owner, and that they tend to be the ones that quietly rot. We made a list and gave each an owner on the spot. Some owners accepted gladly, and a couple of others were volunteered with more enthusiasm than consent, so I will check in with them next week.

Third, training and learning time. We have been saying for a while that people should set aside an hour or two each week, and almost nobody does. The proposal was to protect a fixed slot in the calendar and treat it like any other meeting. Fable Core seemed keen to try it first, and the rest of us can watch how it goes.

request.episode_body:
## Quarter numbers and a look ahead

Someone pulled the quarterly figures together this week and I spent the better part of a morning reading them. Most of it matched what we already felt, which is reassuring in its own way. The one number that made people sit up was on the support side: Juniper Core logged 37 incidents during the quarter. Opinions differed on whether that is high or simply honest, since we have also become better at recording the small things that used to go unreported. I lean towards the second reading, but I would like to see the next quarter before saying so out loud.

The discussion that followed was useful. We agreed that a bare count is not very informative on its own, and that what we should really be asking is how long each incident took to resolve and whether any of them repeated. Somebody offered to go through the list and mark repeats. That is a modest job and should give us something more meaningful to look at.

request.episode_body:
## A thought on process

I keep returning to a theme: we collect data and then do not quite know what to do with it. The numbers sit in a document, we nod at them in a meeting, and then everyone goes back to their day. I would like us to attach at least one concrete follow-up to every figure we discuss, even if the follow-up is only "look at this again in a month". That small habit would turn a report into a conversation.

Priya Varga disagreed gently, saying that not every number deserves action and that some are simply context. That is a fair point. We settled on a compromise: pick the two numbers that bother us most and give those a follow-up, and leave the others as background.

### Wednesday to Friday

Wednesday brought a short meeting about the calendar. We are going to try leaving Friday afternoons free of meetings for a month. Nobody could think of a reason not to. Noor Okafor pointed out that this should apply to ourselves as much as to others, which means we cannot quietly schedule things into the gap.

Thursday was a small training afternoon. A few people worked through some material on their own and compared notes at the end. The format was informal, with no slides and no agenda, and it worked better than I expected. Aiko Osei commented that it felt like the first time in months that nobody was multitasking.

request.episode_body:
### Reflection on pace

There is a temptation to fill quiet weeks with new initiatives. I would like to resist that. The team has been stretched for a while, and a calm patch is a chance to consolidate, to finish things, and to let people think. If we cannot rest when nothing is urgent, we will not manage it when something is.

Next week looks similar. I will keep the entry short and add anything that comes up.

## Process tweaks

Today's entry is mostly about small process changes that we tried and what happened. None of it is dramatic, but I find these records useful when somebody asks later why we do things a certain way.

**The request form.** We have been using the single place for incoming requests for a little while now. The early verdict is mixed. It is genuinely easier to see what is waiting, but a few people still send things the old way, and those requests slip past. We decided not to chase anyone about it yet. Give it another few weeks and see whether habits shift on their own.

**The review rotation.** Noor Okafor's idea of a rotation has started. So far it has worked without complaint. The one wrinkle was a week when someone on the rotation was away and the cover arrangement was unclear. We added a line to the template saying who covers whom. It is the kind of thing that looks obvious afterwards.

**Friday afternoons.** The meeting-free Friday afternoons are going well. Several people said that they now use the time for the slow, thoughtful tasks that never fit anywhere else. One person said that they finished a document that had been half-written for weeks. Small victory, but a real one.

We spent a while on how to keep documents from going stale. Priya Varga thought that was too much overhead for small pages, and suggested limiting it to the ten or so documents that people actually rely on. I think that is wise. A rule applied everywhere is a rule applied nowhere.

## Onboarding clean-up

This entry is about the onboarding material, which has finally had some attention. I have been meaning to write it up for a while.

Aiko Osei took the lead on going through the checklist, with Fable Core providing the original notes to compare against. There were steps referring to forms we stopped using, a paragraph about a room that has been reorganised, and a note telling new joiners to "ask the person who sits by the window", which is not helpful when you do not know who that is.

request.episode_body:
### What changed

- Removed every step that nobody could justify.
- Reordered the remaining steps so that the practical ones, such as getting access and finding the shared folder, come before the explanatory ones.
- Added a short "first week" section that says, plainly, what a new person should expect and what they are not expected to know yet.
- Replaced vague phrases like "get to know the team" with something concrete, such as a suggestion to book a short chat with a couple of different people.

The result is shorter and, I think, kinder. One of the lessons from reading old checklists is that every item was added by someone with a good reason, and over time the weight of good reasons becomes a burden. We have tried to keep only what a new person genuinely needs in order to be useful and comfortable.

request.episode_body:
### Feedback

We asked a couple of recent joiners to read the new version and comment. Their feedback was valuable and a bit humbling. They said the old version made them feel like they were failing a test they could not see. The new one, they said, reads more like a welcome. That was exactly what we were hoping for, though I had not dared to expect it.

One piece of feedback we are still thinking about: they wanted a short glossary of the abbreviations we use, since half of them are never explained anywhere. It is a fair request. Noor Okafor volunteered to start a list and let others add to it as they trip over terms.

request.episode_body:
## Short entry, busy day

Writing this at the end of a day that went sideways, so it will be brief and a little scrappy.

The morning was fine. We had the usual round of updates, and nothing needed escalating. Around midday a question arrived that looked simple and turned out not to be, something about how long we keep certain records. Three people gave three different answers, all confidently. That says something about how much of our process lives in people's heads and not on a page. I have added it to the list of things to write down properly.

## Workload and incident review

Today I want to record a conversation about workload, because it keeps coming up and we have never written it down properly.

The trigger was the quarterly figures again. Looking through them, Priya Varga logged 33 incidents during the quarter, which is a sizeable share given how routing work is spread across the team. She was relaxed about it, pointing out that routing is where problems tend to surface first, so a high count there often reflects visibility and not failure. ### Options we discussed

1. Share first-contact duty on a rotation, so the same person is not always the one who notices.
2. Keep things as they are, but make sure there is a clear way to ask for help when a day gets heavy.

We did not choose one. The mood favoured a mix of the second and third, since a rotation introduces its own overhead and the team has just brought in one rotation already. I would not be surprised if we revisit the first option in a few months.

request.episode_body:
### What we want from it

The discussion about purpose was more interesting than the one about location. We agreed that we do not want an offsite that is just a long meeting in a different room. A few principles came out of it:

- Leave generous gaps. The best conversations at past gatherings happened in the breaks, not in the sessions.

request.episode_body:
### Reflections from the team

I asked a few people for one sentence each on how the month felt. The answers were interesting: "steady", "less rushed than before", "a bit tiring at the end", and "good, but I miss having a proper whiteboard session". The last one sparked a small plan. The whiteboard in the small room is now clean, so we should schedule a session before the pen dries out.

Noor Okafor suggested that we pair the month-end page with a very short question: what is one thing that would make next month easier? I like that, and I have added it below.

request.episode_body:
### Observations

Reading back, I noticed that our best ideas this month were mostly very small. A renamed invite. A worked example. A field in a template. A line saying who covers whom. They do not make good headlines, but together they have made the week-to-week experience noticeably smoother. It is a useful reminder that improvement does not need to be dramatic.

On a related note, we have all become better at saying "I do not know" in meetings. That is a real change from a year ago, when people tended to guess confidently and correct themselves later. It is a quiet cultural shift, and I would like to protect it.

request.episode_body:
## Offsite logistics, take two

More on the offsite, since a few details settled this week. As previously agreed, one person looks after the written side and another handles logistics, and between them the planning has stopped feeling like a cloud and started to feel like a list.

The Aiko Osei offsite will take place in Rotterdam. This is slightly different from what I had in my head, because I had assumed there would be only one gathering. It turns out the onboarding side wants a smaller get-together of its own, which makes good sense: the newest arrivals have had the least chance to meet everyone in person, and a smaller group is gentler than a big one. The programme there will be lighter and more conversational.

request.episode_body:
### Thoughts on the format

Priya Varga proposed a simple structure for the smaller gathering: one shared meal, one short working session, and one open afternoon. It reminded me how effective a spare design can be. When there are too many parts, people spend the whole time moving between them and never settle into a conversation.

Noor Okafor raised a good point about accessibility. Not everyone enjoys long group dinners, and not everyone drinks, and some people prefer to be in bed early. We should provide a range of ways to take part and make it clear that stepping out is fine. That seems obvious but is easily forgotten once the planning gets busy.

request.episode_body:
### Closing note

One thing I want to flag is the risk of overpromising. If we describe the offsites as transformational, people will arrive with expectations that no programme could meet. I would rather undersell them and let people be pleasantly surprised. A good conversation, a decent meal and a chance to put faces to names is already a worthwhile outcome.

I will pull the questions above into a short list and send it round for views by the end of next week.

request.episode_body:
### Thanks

A real thank-you to the people who did the unglamorous work this month. Aiko Osei for rebuilding the checklist and for keeping logistics moving. Noor Okafor for starting the glossary and for being the sceptic we needed when the form was proposed. Priya Varga for the worked example, and for chasing the records question without fuss. The Juniper Core support team for the triage pass that cleared a stubborn backlog. And Fable Core for being willing to test the learning slot before the rest of us had made up our minds.

None of these jobs would show up on a chart, and none of them would have been noticed if they had been skipped. But the week-to-week feel of the team is better for them, and that is more than most big initiatives can claim.

request.episode_body:
## Ask about the past, not the future

People are poor predictors of their own behaviour. Ask whether they would use a feature and most will say yes; ask when they last faced the problem and what they did about it, and you will learn far more. Specific stories, with details such as what they tried and what went wrong, are worth many general statements.

request.episode_body:
# Weekly digest — 6 May 2026

A mixed week, with some good progress and some irritations, as is traditional. I will start with the good news: the month-end billing run went through without a single manual correction, which has not happened in a while. Ines Lindqvist had spent the previous week re-checking the inputs, and it paid off. She would like it known that the secret was boring, careful preparation and not any clever trick, and that she intends to keep doing it that way.

The inventory side was busier. Orbit Core had a lot of attention this week, mostly in the form of questions. Several people wanted to know how stock figures are updated and how quickly a change shows up. The answers were not always the same depending on who was asked, which is itself a finding. We decided to write a short explanation of the flow, from the moment something is counted to the moment it appears on a report, and to put it in the notebook where everyone can find it. A draft already exists, and it should be reviewed by one person from billing and one from outside the project, to catch the parts that are only clear to insiders.

Meetings this week were reasonably disciplined. We tried a new habit of putting the key decision at the top of the agenda, so that if the meeting overran, at least the important item had been dealt with. It worked. People also seemed to arrive better prepared, probably because the agenda made clear what was expected of them.

Chores and small decisions:

- The desk booking sheet is now in the shared drive, not on the wall, because the wall version kept being ignored.
- We agreed on a standard format for meeting notes: decisions first, actions second, discussion last.
- A reminder to clear old drafts out of shared folders before they pile up into an unnavigable heap.
- The kitchen sink has been fixed. Please do not stand the kettle on the left side, where the tap swings.

I want to flag one worry. The inventory explanations took longer to write than expected, and the draft revealed a gap in how we record manual adjustments. At the moment they are noted in one place and not in another, so a person reading only one source would get a false picture. Nobody has done anything wrong; the system simply grew in two directions. We will agree a single place and make the other point to it.

Overall a sound week. The next section deals with what is coming up, including the plans for getting away from the desks for a couple of days.

request.episode_body:
## Looking ahead

Planning for the next few weeks, with one item that I know people have been waiting for. The Ines Lindqvist offsite will take place in Ghent, and the dates are being worked out now. She is keen that it should not be a conference in disguise. Her wish is for a couple of days of unhurried conversation about how the billing process works end to end, where it hurts, and what could be done differently, with some good food in between. Nobody has argued with that approach.

We talked about how to make the most of the time. One idea was to ask everyone to bring a single frustration and a single suggestion, written on a card, and to start from those. It avoids the usual trap where a few people dominate, and it ensures that the small, annoying problems, which are often the most fixable ones, get an airing. Another idea was to leave one half-day with no agenda at all, so that people can follow whatever thread seems most interesting.

Practical points, so that they do not get lost:

- Travel needs to be booked early, as the cheapest options disappear quickly. Someone in finance will check the budget rules before anything is confirmed.
- People who cannot attend in person should have a way to join some of the sessions remotely.
- We need to decide what gets prepared beforehand. The preference is for a single page per topic, no more.
- Dietary needs and accessibility should be gathered through a short form, which will be sent out next week.

Meanwhile, everyday work goes on. Orbit Core still has the open question about adjustments, and the team will use part of the offsite to settle it if it is not resolved before then. Others pointed out that it would be better to settle it sooner, and I think that is right: leaving a known gap until a day away is a way of guaranteeing that it will be discussed for longer than it deserves.

On a lighter note, the team has begun a small contest to guess which restaurant will be picked for the group dinner. There are no prizes, but there is a certain amount of trash talk. I have been told that I am not allowed to vote because I suggested the same place twice.

Before the next digest, I will gather the dates, check the budget, and send a short note to the whole team so that nobody learns the details second-hand. If you have objections to the plan, now is the time to raise them, while changing it still costs nothing.

## Looking ahead

Planning for the next few weeks, with one item that I know people have been waiting for. The Ines Lindqvist offsite will take place in Ghent, and the dates are being worked out now. She is keen that it should not be a conference in disguise. Her wish is for a couple of days of unhurried conversation about how the billing process works end to end, where it hurts, and what could be done differently, with some good food in between. Nobody has argued with that approach.

We talked about how to make the most of the time. One idea was to ask everyone to bring a single frustration and a single suggestion, written on a card, and to start from those. It avoids the usual trap where a few people dominate, and it ensures that the small, annoying problems, which are often the most fixable ones, get an airing. Another idea was to leave one half-day with no agenda at all, so that people can follow whatever thread seems most interesting.

Practical points, so that they do not get lost:

Others pointed out that it would be better to settle it sooner, and I think that is right: leaving a known gap until a day away is a way of guaranteeing that it will be discussed for longer than it deserves.

Before the next digest, I will gather the dates, check the budget, and send a short note to the whole team so that nobody learns the details second-hand. If you have objections to the plan, now is the time to raise them, while changing it still costs nothing.

request.episode_body:
## Feedback round

Last section for this week, and it is about the feedback we collected. Results from the satisfaction survey arrived on Tuesday, and while it is always a bit nerve-racking to open them, this time the mood was good. Orbit Core received a satisfaction rating of 7.1 out of 10. That is solid, and a little higher than some of us had feared given the questions about stock figures earlier in the week.

As ever, the number matters less than the comments. The most common positive remark was that the information is accurate when it arrives, which is the thing you want people to say about an inventory project. The most common criticism was about timing: people would like to know how fresh the data is at any given moment, and several said they had been unsure whether they were looking at the latest picture. That ties in neatly with the explanation we have been drafting, and it suggests that the document should include a simple note on how often figures are refreshed.

We also looked at the less cheerful comments. A few people found the reports hard to read, with too many columns and not enough signposting. There was a request for a short summary at the top of each report, saying what has changed since the previous one. It would not be difficult to add and would probably improve the experience for everyone, including those of us who write the reports.

Actions agreed:

- Add a refresh note to the explanation of the stock flow.
- Experiment with a summary line at the top of the main report.
- Ask two or three regular readers what they would remove if they could.
- Share the results with the whole team in the notebook, with comments tidied up so that nobody is identified.

Ines Lindqvist offered to look at the billing side of the reports, because a few of the complaints seemed to concern how figures are carried across. She will check whether any of them are caused by differences in the way things are rounded or grouped. If so, a short note explaining the convention will save a lot of confusion.

We closed the week with the usual tidy of the board. The cards that had been marked done were archived, two stale cards were deleted, and one new card was added: write down what we learned from this feedback. It is a small act of discipline, but the cards we write for ourselves are the ones that keep the lessons from vanishing.

See you next week, when the offsite plans should have firmer dates and perhaps even a venue.

request.episode_body:
# Journal — 10 May 2026

Sunday catch-up, written with a cup of tea going cold beside me. The sprint closed on Friday and I wanted to get the notes down before Monday swallows everything.

Monday's planning meeting ran long, mostly because nobody had read the agenda in advance. We got through it by splitting the room into two small groups, one looking at the upcoming work and one looking at what had been left half-finished. That worked better than the usual round-table, and I suspect we will do it again. The half-finished pile turned out to be shorter than feared, which was a pleasant surprise. Most of it was documentation that had been "nearly done" for weeks, so we agreed on a quiet hour on Thursday where everybody just finishes theirs and nobody schedules anything over it.

On the numbers: the Yara Nakamura backlog stood at 85 open tickets at the end of the sprint. That is the maintenance queue, and it is a number we keep an eye on rather than panic about. A good share of those tickets are old, low-priority tidy-ups that predate the current team, and the plan is to spend part of next week closing out the obviously stale ones so the list reflects what really needs doing. We talked about whether to set a hard cap on the queue and decided against it for now; a cap tends to produce arguments about what counts as a ticket instead of fewer tickets.

Tomas Kowalski has been juggling the calendar for the next few weeks, and it is not an enviable job. Two people are away at the same time, one review has to move, and the room we like for the demo is booked solid. His proposal was to shift the review to the middle of the week and keep the demo where it is, which nobody objected to. He will send the updated invites tomorrow and asked that people reply to the invite rather than in the chat, so that he can see the answers in one place. Fair request.

Chores, since they pile up if left alone:

- The shared drive needs a spring clean. Folders named "misc" and "old" were mentioned with some feeling.
- The kettle in the kitchen is making a worrying noise. Someone in facilities has been told.
- The onboarding checklist still refers to a form we stopped using ages ago. I have flagged it and will rewrite the relevant page when I get the chance.
- Dependency updates are due again. Nothing alarming, but the longer we wait the more annoying the catch-up becomes.

Smaller decisions this week. We are keeping the Tuesday stand-up at its current length and not adding a second weekly sync, because the people who most wanted one admitted they would only turn up to half of it. We are also going to try a rule that anyone picking up a ticket writes one line about what "done" looks like before they start. It sounds trivial, but the reopened tickets this sprint were almost all cases where two people had different ideas about the finish line.

A word on morale, since it came up in the retrospective: people felt the sprint was steady rather than exciting, and several said that was exactly what they wanted after the scramble last month. I would like to protect that. The risk is that steady slides into stale, so we agreed to pick one small experiment each sprint, nothing grand, just something different enough to keep the work interesting.

Next week, then: trim the maintenance list, finish the documentation, get the calendar sorted, and nudge the dependency updates along. If the weather holds I might also finally move the whiteboard to the wall where people can actually see it.

You are an entity extraction specialist for unstructured text.
NEVER extract vague or standalone feelings or generic words. A specific, named abstract concept
that passes the Wikipedia-article test below (e.g. "climate change", "quantum entanglement")
should be extracted as a Concept entity — being abstract is not by itself a reason to exclude it.

NEVER extract:
- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)
- Vague standalone feelings and generic ideas that could not stand alone as a specific, named
  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

- Person: An individual human being
- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication
Choose the single most appropriate type. If none fit well, use the closest match.

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>

request.edge_system_prompt:
You are an expert fact extractor that extracts fact triples from text.
1. Extracted fact triples should also be extracted with relevant date information.
2. Treat REFERENCE_TIME as the time the episode was recorded. All temporal information should be extracted relative to REFERENCE_TIME.

# TASK
Extract all factual relationships between the given ENTITIES based on the CURRENT MESSAGE.
Only extract facts that:
- involve two DISTINCT ENTITIES from the ENTITIES list,
- are clearly stated or unambiguously implied in the CURRENT MESSAGE,
  and can be represented as edges in a knowledge graph.
- Facts should include entity names rather than pronouns whenever possible.

# EXTRACTION RULES

1. **Entity Name Validation**: source_name and target_name must use only the name values from the ENTITIES list provided above.
   - CRITICAL: Using names not in the list will cause the edge to be rejected.
2. Each fact must involve two distinct entities — source_name and target_name NEVER refer to the same entity.
3. NEVER extract facts that describe only a single entity's state, feeling, or attribute. Instead, identify the second entity that the state or feeling relates to and form a proper triple.
   - BAD: "Alice feels happy" (single-entity state — what is Alice happy about?)
   - GOOD: "Alice feels happy about Bob's promotion" → Alice FEELS_HAPPY_ABOUT Bob's promotion
   - GOOD: "Alice congratulated Bob" (relationship between two entities), "Alice lives in Paris" (relationship between entity and place)
4. NEVER emit duplicate or semantically redundant facts.
5. The fact field should closely paraphrase the original source sentence(s). Do not verbatim quote the original text.
6. Use REFERENCE_TIME to resolve vague or relative temporal expressions (e.g., "last week").
7. Do not hallucinate or infer temporal bounds from unrelated events.

# RELATION TYPE RULES


You MUST always provide a non-null relation_type for every edge. Leaving it null or empty is not acceptable.
Derive a relation_type from the relationship predicate in SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE (e.g., WORKS_AT, LIVES_IN, IS_FRIENDS_WITH, WROTE, AUTHORED, MARRIED_TO).
If the predicate is unclear, derive one from the fact description using a concise verb phrase.
Use concise, consistent vocabulary — prefer established verbs that would apply broadly.

# DATETIME RULES

- Use ISO 8601 with "Z" suffix (UTC) (e.g., 2025-04-30T00:00:00Z).
- If the fact is ongoing (present tense), set valid_at to REFERENCE_TIME.
- If a change or termination is expressed, set invalid_at to the relevant timestamp.
- Leave both fields null if no explicit or resolvable time is stated.
- If only a date is mentioned (no time), assume 00:00:00.
- If only a year is mentioned, use January 1st at 00:00:00.

request.episode_body:
## Midweek check-in

Picking the log back up on Wednesday, after a morning that went mostly to email. A few things happened since the weekend, so here they are in roughly the order they came up.

The calendar reshuffle went through without much fuss. Tomas Kowalski sent the new invites as promised, and by lunchtime nearly everyone had replied on the invite itself, which made his life easier. The one holdout turned out to have been out of the office, so nothing was really amiss. The review now sits in the middle of the week and the demo stayed put. He also noticed that two recurring meetings overlapped by half an hour every other Thursday and quietly fixed that, which will save somebody a lot of apologetic leaving-early.

Basalt Core came up in the procurement conversation on Tuesday. The question was less about spending and more about timing: a couple of orders were waiting on approvals, and the team wanted to know whether to hold them until the end of the month or push them through now. We settled on pushing the small ones through and holding the larger ones until the next planning round, so that nobody commits to something that the plan might still change. It is a modest decision but it avoids a certain amount of awkward undoing later.

Yara Nakamura started the stale-ticket cull a little ahead of schedule. The approach is simple: anything untouched for a long stretch gets a comment asking whether it still matters, and if nobody answers within the week it is closed with a note explaining how to reopen it. A few people grumbled that closing tickets is not the same as fixing the problem, which is true, but a list nobody believes in helps no one. She is keeping a separate pile of "looks small, is not" items for a proper conversation rather than letting them linger.

Some notes from the hallway, because they are worth keeping:

- Several people said the stand-up feels sharper now that it has a firm end time. Nobody wants to go back.
- The new "write one line about done" habit has been tried by about half the team so far. Early verdict: mildly annoying, mostly helpful.
- Someone asked whether we could have a quiet room for focused work on Fridays. Nobody objected, and I will raise it with whoever manages the space.

I also spent an hour tidying the shared drive, as threatened. The "misc" folder turned out to contain mostly screenshots and two meeting agendas from last year. The agendas are now archived properly, and the screenshots have gone wherever screenshots go. It is not glamorous work but the search results are noticeably less cluttered.

One thing I am a little uneasy about: we keep saying we will update the onboarding pages and then not doing it. I would like to treat it as a real task with an owner and a date, rather than a thing we all agree is a good idea. I will put it on the board tomorrow and see whether anyone volunteers; if not, it is mine.

That is it for now. More on Friday, when the documentation hour happens and we find out how much of it was truly nearly done.

request.episode_body:
## Friday wrap

Quiet end to the week, which I will take. The documentation hour happened as planned and, to everyone's mild surprise, people actually used it. About a dozen pages were finished, a few more were declared obsolete and deleted, and one was discovered to describe a process that nobody could remember ever using. That one has been archived with a short note, in case a future archaeologist needs it.

The review that Tomas Kowalski moved took place on Wednesday afternoon and went smoothly. It ran to time, the comments were constructive, and the only real disagreement was about whether a particular chart should use a log scale. We left it linear, on the grounds that the audience would rather read it quickly than admire it. Tomas has already pencilled in the next two sessions, and he mentioned that he would like to build in a short buffer after each one so that follow-ups do not collide with the next meeting. Sensible.

On the procurement side, the thing to record is that the Basalt Core orders we pushed through earlier in the week have been acknowledged. Nothing dramatic, just confirmation that they are in the queue. The larger orders are still parked until the next planning round, as agreed, and I have added a reminder to look at them on the first day back after the planning meeting, so that they do not drift. One person asked whether we should write down a rule of thumb for when to hold an order and when to release it. I think a rule would be too rigid, but a short checklist of questions might help: is the need certain, is the timing flexible, and would undoing it be painful? Might draft that next week.

Yara Nakamura reported progress on the maintenance list over lunch. The cull is going faster than expected, partly because a number of the old tickets duplicated each other, and partly because some reporters replied within minutes to say "no longer needed, close it". There is a small group of tickets that need a real decision rather than a quick close, and she has gathered them in one place so we can go through them together on Monday. She also asked, reasonably, that we stop assigning new low-priority work to the maintenance queue until the cull is done, otherwise we are bailing a boat while someone fills it. Agreed, and noted for the planning meeting.

Odds and ends:

- The kettle has been replaced. The new one is quieter, and the kitchen is calmer for it.
- The dependency updates are still pending. I have moved them to Monday morning, when attention is fresh and nothing else is on fire.
- A reminder that the team photo is being retaken because half of us blinked.
- We will test the focused-work Fridays idea for a month before deciding whether it sticks.

On a personal note, I find these weekly entries useful mainly because they show how little drama there really is in a normal week. When something does go wrong, it helps to look back and see what normal looked like. That is the main argument for keeping the log going even when there seems to be nothing to say.

Enough for today. Weekend starts now.
