request.episode_body:
## Audit results and next steps

Picking up the audit thread from the first section, because the second set of results arrived just as the meeting was winding down and deserves its own paragraph.

Yara Nakamura scored 75 out of 100 in the internal audit. That is a respectable number, and she was candid about where the points went: mostly about the way maintenance records were filed. The work itself was done, but the proof of it was spread across several places, and an auditor looking for a single trail had to go hunting. She sees it as a filing problem more than a performance problem, and she already has a plan to bring everything into one folder with a consistent naming scheme. The same reorganisation, she pointed out, will help with the schedule list discussed earlier, so the effort does double duty.

We spent a few minutes comparing the two sets of results, carefully. The conversation could easily have turned into a contest, and nobody wanted that. The agreed approach is to treat the scores as a way of finding what to fix, not as a way of ranking anyone. Both Priya Varga and Yara Nakamura noted that the themes overlap: written reasons, a single place for records, and dates on everything. If both areas fix those three things, the next audit should look noticeably better.

Concrete steps that came out of this:

- Agree a common naming scheme for records, and publish it in the notebook.
- Give each area one place where evidence is kept, with access limited to those who need it.
- Review recent changes in both areas and add the missing explanations.
- Ask for a friendly re-check in a few weeks, once the main gaps are closed.

Someone asked whether we could borrow a template from another team for the written reasons. The answer was that a template would be useful but should be short. A long form is the surest way to guarantee that it is filled in badly or not at all. A line for what changed, a line for why, and a line for who agreed is probably enough.

Before closing, we went round the table for one-line takeaways. Most were practical: write it down when it happens, keep one folder, say why. One was a little more philosophical, to the effect that an audit is only unpleasant if you treat it as a verdict, and that treating it as a review makes it quite useful. I think that is right, and it is a good note to end on.

Next sync is the same time next week. Standing again, I assume, unless the chairs return.

request.episode_body:
# Sync notes — 1 July 2026

Notes from this week's sync, written up on the train so apologies for any typos. Attendance was good and the conversation stayed on topic, which I will count as a win.

We started with the sprint close. The Tern Core backlog stood at 167 open tickets at the end of the sprint. Nobody was shocked by it. A lot of those tickets are old, a few are duplicates, and a handful are really questions that were filed as work. The agreement was to spend a short, bounded stretch next sprint sorting them into "do", "park" and "close", rather than trying to burn the whole pile down. If a ticket cannot be explained in a sentence, it is a candidate for closing with a polite note.

Telemetry is where most of the discussion went, because the project is the one that tells us whether anything else is healthy. A few people feel the dashboards have grown by accretion: every incident adds a panel, nobody removes one, and now the interesting signal is buried. The suggestion was to take one afternoon, go through every panel, and ask what decision it supports. Panels that support no decision go to an archive view. Someone pointed out that this is the same lesson we learned with alerts earlier in the year, and it would be nice to stop relearning it.

Scheduling was the other big topic. Tomas Kowalski walked through the planning calendar and showed where the next few weeks are over-committed. The pinch point is the shared review slot, which three different efforts want at the same time. Instead of picking a winner, he proposed alternating the slot and letting each effort have it in turn, with a short written summary for those who miss out. Everyone seemed fine with that, though one person warned that "alternating" has a way of becoming "whoever shouts loudest" unless it is written down. So it will be written down.

Smaller items, in no particular order:

- The test environment was slow again on Tuesday. Someone will look at whether a nightly job is overlapping with the morning builds.
- We agreed to stop sending status emails that duplicate what is already on the board. If it is on the board, link it.
- The shared notes folder still has too many files called "final". We will rename them by topic and date as we touch them, with no big-bang tidy.
- A vendor asked for a call about a renewal. Someone in finance will take it, and the team only needs to provide usage details if asked.

A word on the mood: people sounded less tired than at the last sync, and a couple of folks said the quiet stretch before the sprint end helped. We should try to protect the quiet stretch next time as well, and not fill it with extra meetings just because it looks empty on the calendar.

Action list for this section is short. Sort the old tickets in a time-boxed pass, review the telemetry panels, write down the alternating slot rule, and rename the stray "final" files as we go. I will chase these on the next sync and report honestly on what slipped.
request.entity_system_prompt:
You are an entity extraction specialist for unstructured text.
NEVER extract vague or standalone feelings or generic words. A specific, named abstract concept
that passes the Wikipedia-article test below (e.g. "climate change", "quantum entanglement")
should be extracted as a Concept entity — being abstract is not by itself a reason to exclude it.

NEVER extract:
- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)
- Vague standalone feelings and generic ideas that could not stand alone as a specific, named
  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

For each entity extracted, assign a single entity_type label from this closed ontology:
- Person: An individual human being
- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication
Choose the single most appropriate type. If none fit well, use the closest match.

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>

request.episode_body:
## Review slot and telemetry follow-ups

Second part of the sync covered what comes next, and it was more of a working discussion than a report.

The review slot rule was drafted live. The wording is plain: the slot alternates between the competing efforts, each gets a turn, and whoever misses a turn posts a short written summary so nothing waits a fortnight for feedback. Tomas Kowalski will own the rota and keep it in the planning calendar, with the summaries linked underneath. There was a brief debate over whether emergencies override the rota. The answer was yes, but the person invoking it explains why in one line, which should discourage casual use.

On telemetry, the group went further than I expected. Instead of reviewing panels in a single afternoon, the proposal was to split the Tern Core panels into groups and let a different person take each group, then compare notes. This avoids the situation where one reviewer's habits decide everything. The review criteria are simple: what decision does this panel support, who looks at it, and when did someone last act on it? Those answers go in a shared page. Where the answer is "nobody, never", the panel is archived rather than deleted, so that nobody has to rebuild it if someone turns out to miss it.

A tangent that deserved space: the way we label metrics. Some names tell you what is measured, others tell you who asked for it, and a few are just old. Nobody wants a mass rename, because that would break saved views and confuse people. The suggestion was a naming guideline for new metrics only, with old ones renamed when they are touched for another reason. It is slow, but it avoids a disruptive cleanup.

We also discussed handover. Two people will be away over the next stretch, and the handover template we tried earlier is getting its first real test. The feedback so far is that it works when it is short and falls over when people try to be comprehensive. Keep it to what is in flight, what is waiting, who to ask and what will break if ignored. Anyone writing one should read it back as if they had never seen the work.

Other notes from the discussion:

- The nightly job that overlaps with morning builds has been spotted. A small schedule change should fix it, and the team will watch for a few days to confirm.
- Someone asked whether our status board columns still match how we work. They mostly do, except for a column that nobody uses. It goes.
- The idea of a monthly "upkeep day" came up again. People like it in principle, and the sticking point is picking a day that is not already full. We will pencil one in and see.

Not everything was settled, and I would rather record that honestly than pretend otherwise. The question of how much of the ticket sorting to automate remains open; the cautious view is that a human should read every ticket before it is closed, at least for the first pass. We will revisit once the first pass is done and we know how many are straightforward.

## Review slot and telemetry follow-ups

Second part of the sync covered what comes next, and it was more of a working discussion than a report.

The review slot rule was drafted live. The wording is plain: the slot alternates between the competing efforts, each gets a turn, and whoever misses a turn posts a short written summary so nothing waits a fortnight for feedback. Tomas Kowalski will own the rota and keep it in the planning calendar, with the summaries linked underneath. There was a brief debate over whether emergencies override the rota. The answer was yes, but the person invoking it explains why in one line, which should discourage casual use.

On telemetry, the group went further than I expected. Instead of reviewing panels in a single afternoon, the proposal was to split the Tern Core panels into groups and let a different person take each group, then compare notes. This avoids the situation where one reviewer's habits decide everything. The review criteria are simple: what decision does this panel support, who looks at it, and when did someone last act on it? Those answers go in a shared page. Where the answer is "nobody, never", the panel is archived rather than deleted, so that nobody has to rebuild it if someone turns out to miss it.

A tangent that deserved space: the way we label metrics. Some names tell you what is measured, others tell you who asked for it, and a few are just old. Nobody wants a mass rename, because that would break saved views and confuse people. The suggestion was a naming guideline for new metrics only, with old ones renamed when they are touched for another reason. It is slow, but it avoids a disruptive cleanup.

We also discussed handover. Two people will be away over the next stretch, and the handover template we tried earlier is getting its first real test. The feedback so far is that it works when it is short and falls over when people try to be comprehensive. Keep it to what is in flight, what is waiting, who to ask and what will break if ignored. Anyone writing one should read it back as if they had never seen the work.

- The nightly job that overlaps with morning builds has been spotted. A small schedule change should fix it, and the team will watch for a few days to confirm.

request.episode_body:
## Backlog check and wrap-up

The last part of the sync was the shortest and, oddly, the most candid.

Scheduling work came back round, since it has the most moving parts. The Tomas Kowalski backlog stood at 212 open tickets at the end of the sprint. That is a big pile, and he was straightforward about it: much of it is requests to move things around, and a fair amount arrives in clumps whenever a plan changes. He does not think the number is a sign of neglect, but he does think it hides the handful of items that really matter. His proposal is to tag those handful clearly and let the rest wait in a separate lane, so the urgent items stop sitting in a crowd. We agreed this is sensible and that everyone should pitch in to help identify which tickets deserve the tag in the first place.

The group also talked about how to avoid the backlog regrowing once it is trimmed. The favoured answer is a light weekly habit: look at what arrived, close what is already answered, and park what is not going to happen. It is about a quarter of an hour of attention, and far less painful than a rescue operation every few months. Someone said, fairly, that habits like this tend to wither in busy weeks, so we will attach it to a meeting we already hold rather than inventing a new one.

Next, a few housekeeping points:

- The notes from this sync will be filed with the others, and the action list will be linked from the planning page.
- The test environment slowness has been traced to the overlapping nightly job. The schedule has been moved and we will report if it recurs.
- The rename of stray "final" files has begun, slowly. So far the folder looks better and nobody has lost anything.
- The vendor renewal call is with someone in finance, and the team has not been asked for anything yet.

On Tern Core, the panel review has started, with the first group of panels assessed. A handful have been archived, a few were kept, and one was rewritten because its title promised something different from what it showed. People were pleasantly surprised at how quickly the first group went once the three questions were agreed. We expect the remaining groups to move at a similar pace.

There was also a gentle conversation about workload. A few of us have been stretching, and the sync is a decent place to say so. Nobody is in trouble, but it is better to adjust early than to apologise later. The result was a small reshuffle of who covers what over the next few weeks, with the review rota taking account of absences.

To close the loop on actions: ticket sorting for Tern Core, tagging urgent items in the scheduling lane, completing the panel review, and putting the weekly trim habit onto an existing meeting. Each has a named owner on the planning page, and I will check in at the next sync. If something has slipped by then, the right response is a short explanation and a new date, not silence.

Thanks to everyone for the straight talk, and for keeping the whole thing inside the time we booked.

request.episode_body:
# A field guide to remote team rituals

_Clipped from the web. Source: example.org/remote-team-rituals._

Teams that never share a room tend to discover, sooner or later, that the small rituals of office life were doing more work than anyone realised. The chat by the kettle, the glance across a desk, the half-overheard conversation that turns out to matter: none of these appear on an organisation chart, yet each carried information and goodwill from one person to another. When the office disappears, so do they, unless someone replaces them on purpose.

The most durable replacements are rarely elaborate. Observers of distributed teams describe a pattern in which the rituals that survive are short, regular and easy to join, while the ambitious ones fade after a few weeks.

request.episode_body:
## The daily signal

A brief written check-in at the start of the working day is among the most common habits. It need not be a report. A line or two on what someone plans to focus on, and whether anything is blocking them, is enough to give colleagues a sense of the shape of the day. The value lies less in the content than in the regularity: a missing check-in becomes a quiet signal that something may be wrong, and a present one is a small act of presence.

Teams that adopt the habit often find it works best when it is asynchronous. Requiring everyone to be online at the same moment defeats much of the purpose of working remotely, particularly across time zones. A written note can be read whenever it suits the reader.

request.episode_body:
## The weekly conversation

Where the daily signal is thin, the weekly conversation is thick. This is typically a single meeting, held at a consistent time, where the team talks through what has happened and what is coming. The better versions have a loose agenda and a firm end time. Many teams reserve the first few minutes for something that is not work at all, a question about the weekend or a small piece of news, and report that this does more for cohesion than any formal team-building exercise.

A common failure is to let the meeting become a sequence of status reports. Those can be written and read in advance. The meeting is better used for the things that need a group: disagreements, decisions, and the kind of exploratory talk that does not fit in a message.

request.episode_body:
## Rituals of endings

Less discussed are the rituals that mark the end of things. A project closes, a colleague moves on, a difficult quarter finishes, and in the absence of a room to gather in, these moments can slip past unmarked. Teams that handle this well tend to set aside a little time for it: a short retrospective, a message of thanks, a shared look back at what was learned. Endings noted are endings absorbed; endings ignored tend to linger as vague fatigue.

request.episode_body:
## Keeping it honest

Perhaps the most useful advice from people who have run distributed teams for years is to review the rituals themselves. A habit that was lively in its first month may be a hollow formality in its sixth. Asking the team, plainly, whether a ritual is still worth its time is itself a ritual worth having. Those that earn their place stay. Those that do not can be dropped without ceremony, and the time reclaimed is a gift in its own right.

The underlying principle is modest. Good remote teams do not try to reproduce the office. They identify what the office was quietly providing, such as contact, pace, recognition and closure, and find lightweight ways to supply it. The rituals are only the vehicle.

request.episode_body:
## Training and capacity

The first item was training, since the term is nearly over and we wanted to see where things stand. Quill Core completed 5 hours of training this term, which is lower than anyone intended and which the group put down to a busy spring more than any lack of interest. Rather than treat it as a failing, the team talked about how to make learning easier to fit in. The main idea was to protect a short block in the calendar, so that training is not the first thing to be squeezed when work piles up. There was also a suggestion to favour short, focused sessions over long courses, because they are far easier to attend.

Marcus Haddad said telemetry has a similar problem: plenty of interest, not enough free hours. He is going to pick one topic that would help the team most and aim for that, rather than spreading himself thinly across several. That seemed sensible, and the team agreed to hold him to it, kindly.

## A thought on pace

It was observed during the review that we tend to set ambitious plans at the start of a term and then feel faintly guilty when they do not all happen. A more useful habit might be to plan a little less, finish most of it, and use the spare time for the things that crop up anyway. Nobody disagreed. The next review is scheduled for early autumn, in the same room. Bring a fan.

request.episode_body:
## Process and tooling

A slightly dry section, but a useful one. The team spent a while on how change requests move through routing and telemetry. At present there is an informal convention that anything risky gets a second pair of eyes, but nobody has written down what counts as risky. The result is inconsistency: some changes get over-reviewed, while others slip through because they looked harmless. The working definition proposed was anything that affects what other people see or rely on. It is imperfect, but it gives us a place to start and can be tightened as examples come up.

We also looked at how to record why a change was made. Commit messages tell you what changed; they rarely say why. A short "reason" line in the tracker entry would solve most of it, and the team agreed to try that for a couple of months. If it turns out to be a chore, we will reconsider. If it turns out to be valuable, it becomes the norm.

## Customers and requests

Quill Core mentioned a few requests that had come in from outside the usual channels. They were handled, but the way they arrived was awkward, and the group wants to make it clearer how people should ask. A short page with a form and a couple of examples is the plan. Marcus Haddad offered to review the wording from the telemetry side, since some of the requests overlap with data questions.

A recurring theme was expectations. People ask for things without knowing how long they take, and the team is often too polite to say. The proposal is to include a rough turnaround in the acknowledgement message, with a sentence on what could make it slower. It is more honest and, in the long run, kinder.

request.episode_body:
## Observations from the room

It struck me during the discussion how much of the team's friction comes from assumptions that are never stated. Someone assumes a message was seen; someone assumes a task was handed over. The antidote is not more meetings but more explicit acknowledgements: "got it", "I have this", "I cannot do this one". These cost nothing and make a big difference to how the work feels.

There was a related remark about tone in written messages. Short replies can come across as curt even when they are not meant that way. The group agreed that adding a word of context, even just "thanks, that helps", makes things easier to read, especially for people who are new or who work remotely.

request.episode_body:
## Offsite and next steps

Looking further ahead, the Marcus Haddad offsite will take place in Ghent, and the telemetry group has started thinking about what to do with the time. There is no appetite for a long slide-driven agenda. The preference is for a couple of working sessions on real problems, with plenty of room around them. One idea that got a warm response was to bring along an unsolved question from each person's work and spend an hour on it together, with the rule that no one is allowed to defend the current approach. It sounds mildly uncomfortable, which is probably a good sign.

Open questions on the offsite: how long it should run, whether partners from other groups should be invited for one session, and how to handle people who cannot travel. None needs an answer today. The next step is to write the options on one page and let people comment.

request.episode_body:
# Team log — 10 July 2026

Friday log, written in a hurry before people leave. The week was busy but in a cheerful way, and the main topic was travel, which always generates more conversation than it deserves.

Offsites first, since several were settled this week. The Tern Core offsite will take place in Turin, which will please the people who have been lobbying for somewhere warm. The telemetry side wanted a venue with good wireless and a room big enough to put dashboards on a wall without everyone craning their necks. Turin seems to meet both needs. Separately, the Sofia Petrov offsite will take place in Valencia. That one is a procurement-focused gathering, and the idea is to combine meetings with suppliers and some time for the team to compare notes on how requests flow. Nothing is booked beyond the basic decision, so details will follow.

Routing has been the other talking point. Priya Varga has been thinking about how work gets directed between the teams, and her observation was that too many requests arrive without enough context for the receiver to act. A person reading the message has to guess what is wanted, by when, and why it matters. Her proposal is a three-line habit for any request: what you need, when you need it, and what happens if it does not arrive. It is not a form, only a convention, and it should be easy to adopt. A few people already do something like it and say it saves a round of questions.

We spent a while discussing how to make that habit stick. Conventions without reminders fade quickly. The idea was to put the three lines at the top of the shared request template so that anyone filling it in sees them every time. We will also mention it in the next newcomer session.

Smaller items from the week:

- The wiki's travel page was updated with a short checklist: passports, insurance, expense rules, and who to tell. It is much shorter than the old one.
- A reminder that anyone travelling should leave contact details with the team in case of problems.
- We cleared the backlog of small purchase requests that had been waiting for sign-off. Most were approved quickly once someone actually looked at them.
- The weekly summary was trimmed again. It is down to decisions and requests.

A longer conversation was about the balance of in-person and remote work around these offsites. Some people value the time together enormously; others find travel draining and would prefer to join remotely. We agreed to make attendance flexible where possible, and to make sure remote participants are properly included, with a camera, a microphone, and a person assigned to watch the chat. It is easy to promise inclusion and forget it in practice, so the assignment of a watcher is a concrete step.

On procurement matters, the usual chores continued. Contract renewals are being collected into a single list so nothing sneaks up unnoticed. Whoever updates the list should add the owner's name and a rough date for any action, even if the date is a guess. A guess with a date is far more useful than a note saying "soon".

Telemetry had a quiet week. A few dashboards were tidied, and the team agreed to retire several views that nobody had opened in a long time. Retiring things is underrated; each view you keep has to be maintained, and unused ones silently rot.

That is the first half of the log. The second half covers the remaining offsite and a few notes on planning for the next quarter.

request.episode_body:
## Second half: one more offsite and quarter planning

Continuing the Friday log. This half starts with the last offsite decision and moves on to planning.

The Priya Varga offsite will take place in Gdansk. The routing group has been arguing amiably about where to go for weeks, and Gdansk finally won on the strength of its practicality: easy to reach, plenty of places to eat, and a good venue for working sessions. The idea is to use the time to walk through how requests move between teams, with real examples, and to agree a few simple rules that everyone can live with. As with the others, only the place is fixed so far. The agenda is a blank page, and the first job is to decide who actually needs to be in the room for which sessions.

That brought us back to the request habit from the first half. Several people said they would like to try the three-line convention before the offsite, so they can bring real experience of whether it works. That seems sensible. A trial of a few weeks, with notes on what helped and what did not, would give the routing discussion something solid to chew on instead of opinions.

On to quarter planning. The group looked at what is likely to compete for attention over the next stretch. A few themes stood out:

- Procurement work will keep growing as more contracts come up for review. Sofia Petrov and the team need breathing room to handle that without dropping other work.
- Telemetry work on Tern Core wants to clean up its alerting, which has grown noisy over time.
- Routing needs time for the request habit to bed in, along with a simple way to see whether it is helping.
- Everyone wants fewer meetings. Nobody agrees on which ones to drop, which is a classic problem.

We settled on a modest rule for planning: for each team, pick no more than two main goals, and write each in a sentence that a person outside the team could understand. Anything beyond that goes on a "maybe" list. The point is to make trade-offs visible early, instead of discovering them in week nine. There was some scepticism about two being too few, but the counterargument that three or four goals usually means none of them gets finished was persuasive.

Other business:

1. Finance asked for a rough view of travel costs as soon as possible. A shared sheet is being started, with columns for who, where, when and approximate cost. Estimates are fine at this stage.
2. A newcomer asked how to find out who is responsible for what. The team page is the answer, but it needs updating, so that is a chore for next week.
3. The shared calendar will show offsite dates as soon as they are fixed, so people can plan around them.
4. The suggestion box was emptied and read. Most suggestions were about the kitchen, which tells you something about priorities.

Finally, a thought for next time. These logs are most useful when they record the reasoning behind decisions as well as the decisions themselves. I have tried to do that here, but I suspect I have been too brief about why Gdansk beat the alternatives. Whoever remembers the debate, please add a line. Otherwise in six months we will wonder why we chose it, and the only record will be that we did.

That is the end of this log. Have a good weekend, and travel safely wherever you are heading.

request.episode_body:
# Planning notes — 11 July 2026

Quiet Saturday-adjacent planning session, mostly just the people who were in the office. Writing this up while it is fresh so the Monday crowd does not have to reconstruct any of it from chat scrollback.

We started with the usual housekeeping. The shared calendar has drifted again: a few recurring meetings still point at rooms that were reassigned last quarter, and two of them have no agenda attached. Someone volunteered to go through the calendar and prune anything nobody can explain. We agreed that a recurring meeting with no agenda for three weeks in a row gets cancelled and nobody is allowed to be offended about it.

Next came the offsite conversation, which took longer than planned because everyone had an opinion about travel. The short version is that the Sable Core offsite will take place in Bergen. The compliance side of the team wanted somewhere with decent train links and not too many distractions, and Bergen ticked both boxes. What remains is the boring part: a rough agenda, a list of who needs to attend in person versus remotely, and a sensible way to split the cost so it does not all land on one budget line. Nobody has started on any of that yet, so it is on the list for next week.

On the process side we talked about how work is handed between projects. Fable Core and Tern Core both have dependencies on shared tooling, and the handoff notes from last month were thin. The proposal was a one-page template: what changed, what is blocked, who to ask. It is deliberately small, because the last template we tried had eleven fields and nobody filled in more than three of them. We will trial the short version for a few weeks and see whether it survives contact with a busy sprint.

A few smaller items worth recording:

- The team wiki still has a stale page about environment setup. Whoever next onboards onto a project should fix it as they go instead of leaving a comment saying it is wrong.
- The old shared mailbox is still receiving automated notices nobody reads. We decided to route them into a single channel and review it once a week rather than let them pile up.
- There was a brief argument about meeting-free afternoons. No decision yet. A trial of one afternoon a week was floated and mostly met with enthusiasm, so we will revisit.
- The laptop refresh list needs checking against who is actually still using what. A quick survey is the plan, kept to three questions maximum.

Before we closed, we went around the table for blockers. Most people had none, which is either very good news or a sign that people were being polite. The follow-up is to ask again in writing on Monday, since written answers tend to be franker than ones given in a room.

Action items, loosely assigned:

1. Calendar cleanup, as above.
2. Draft the Bergen agenda skeleton and circulate it for comment.
3. Write the one-page handoff template and post it where everyone will actually see it.
4. Collect blocker replies on Monday and summarise them in the next notes.

That is everything. If something here is wrong or missing, edit it directly rather than starting a thread about it. Next planning session is in a week, same room, same people, hopefully with slightly fewer recurring meetings than today.

NEVER extract vague or standalone feelings or generic words. A specific, named abstract concept
that passes the Wikipedia-article test below (e.g. "climate change", "quantum entanglement")
should be extracted as a Concept entity — being abstract is not by itself a reason to exclude it.

NEVER extract:
- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)
- Vague standalone feelings and generic ideas that could not stand alone as a specific, named
  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,

- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names

  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

For each entity extracted, assign a single entity_type label from this closed ontology:
- Person: An individual human being
- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication
Choose the single most appropriate type. If none fit well, use the closest match.

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>

request.edge_system_prompt:
You are an expert fact extractor that extracts fact triples from text.
1. Extracted fact triples should also be extracted with relevant date information.
2. Treat REFERENCE_TIME as the time the episode was recorded. All temporal information should be extracted relative to REFERENCE_TIME.

# TASK
Extract all factual relationships between the given ENTITIES based on the CURRENT MESSAGE.
Only extract facts that:
- involve two DISTINCT ENTITIES from the ENTITIES list,
- are clearly stated or unambiguously implied in the CURRENT MESSAGE,
  and can be represented as edges in a knowledge graph.
- Facts should include entity names rather than pronouns whenever possible.

# EXTRACTION RULES

1. **Entity Name Validation**: source_name and target_name must use only the name values from the ENTITIES list provided above.
   - CRITICAL: Using names not in the list will cause the edge to be rejected.
2. Each fact must involve two distinct entities — source_name and target_name NEVER refer to the same entity.
3. NEVER extract facts that describe only a single entity's state, feeling, or attribute. Instead, identify the second entity that the state or feeling relates to and form a proper triple.
   - BAD: "Alice feels happy" (single-entity state — what is Alice happy about?)
   - GOOD: "Alice feels happy about Bob's promotion" → Alice FEELS_HAPPY_ABOUT Bob's promotion
   - GOOD: "Alice congratulated Bob" (relationship between two entities), "Alice lives in Paris" (relationship between entity and place)
4. NEVER emit duplicate or semantically redundant facts.
5. The fact field should closely paraphrase the original source sentence(s). Do not verbatim quote the original text.
6. Use REFERENCE_TIME to resolve vague or relative temporal expressions (e.g., "last week").
7. Do not hallucinate or infer temporal bounds from unrelated events.

# RELATION TYPE RULES


You MUST always provide a non-null relation_type for every edge. Leaving it null or empty is not acceptable.
Derive a relation_type from the relationship predicate in SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE (e.g., WORKS_AT, LIVES_IN, IS_FRIENDS_WITH, WROTE, AUTHORED, MARRIED_TO).
If the predicate is unclear, derive one from the fact description using a concise verb phrase.
Use concise, consistent vocabulary — prefer established verbs that would apply broadly.

# DATETIME RULES

- Use ISO 8601 with "Z" suffix (UTC) (e.g., 2025-04-30T00:00:00Z).
- If the fact is ongoing (present tense), set valid_at to REFERENCE_TIME.
- If a change or termination is expressed, set invalid_at to the relevant timestamp.
- Leave both fields null if no explicit or resolvable time is stated.
- If only a date is mentioned (no time), assume 00:00:00.
- If only a year is mentioned, use January 1st at 00:00:00.

request.episode_body:
## Tuesday stand-down

Short one this week, because half the team was out and the other half was buried in review queues.

The main thing worth writing down is the review backlog. Pull requests have been sitting for days before anyone looks at them, and the cause is not laziness. It is that nobody feels it is their turn. We tried a simple fix: each morning one person is named on a rota as the first reader for anything new. They do not have to finish the review, only to give a first pass or hand it to someone better placed. Aiko Osei offered to go first on the rota so the rest of us have no excuse, and the plan is to run it for a couple of weeks before judging it.

We also spent a while on documentation. The onboarding material attached to Fable Core still describes a setup that nobody uses, and a newcomer who followed it to the letter would end up with a broken local environment. The agreed approach is not a grand rewrite. Instead, whoever hits a wrong step fixes that step immediately and adds a line to the changelog at the bottom of the page. Small, frequent corrections beat a big overhaul that never gets scheduled.

Another item: the weekly summary email is being skimmed rather than read. Rather than make it longer, we decided to cut it down. Anything that is purely informational moves to the shared channel; the email keeps only decisions and requests for input. If that works we may stop sending it as an email altogether, but that is a conversation for later.

Smaller notes, in no particular order:

- The coffee machine on the second floor is fixed, for now. Please do not test its patience.
- Somebody left a half-finished diagram on the whiteboard in the meeting room. It was photographed and filed in the wiki before being wiped, so nothing was lost.
- A reminder that expense receipts need to be attached when claims are submitted, not promised afterwards. Finance would like this to stop being a recurring topic.
- The quarterly planning template got a minor tidy: the risks section now comes before the dependencies section, because people kept skipping the risks when they were at the bottom.

On the tooling side, a couple of people noticed the staging environment has been slower than usual. No root cause yet. The suspicion is that old test data has accumulated, and the plan is to clear it out on a quiet evening and see whether response times improve. If they do not, we will look at the more expensive explanations next.

We closed by agreeing that these notes should stay short and honest. If a week was dull, say so. A log that only records exciting weeks is not much of a log, and the dull weeks are usually when the useful chores get done.

Next entry should cover how the review rota actually went, along with whatever else turns up between now and then.

<TEXT>
## Tuesday stand-down

Short one this week, because half the team was out and the other half was buried in review queues.

The main thing worth writing down is the review backlog. Pull requests have been sitting for days before anyone looks at them, and the cause is not laziness. It is that nobody feels it is their turn. We tried a simple fix: each morning one person is named on a rota as the first reader for anything new. They do not have to finish the review, only to give a first pass or hand it to someone better placed. Aiko Osei offered to go first on the rota so the rest of us have no excuse, and the plan is to run it for a couple of weeks before judging it.

We also spent a while on documentation. The onboarding material attached to Fable Core still describes a setup that nobody uses, and a newcomer who followed it to the letter would end up with a broken local environment. The agreed approach is not a grand rewrite. Instead, whoever hits a wrong step fixes that step immediately and adds a line to the changelog at the bottom of the page. Small, frequent corrections beat a big overhaul that never gets scheduled.

Another item: the weekly summary email is being skimmed rather than read. Rather than make it longer, we decided to cut it down. Anything that is purely informational moves to the shared channel; the email keeps only decisions and requests for input. If that works we may stop sending it as an email altogether, but that is a conversation for later.

Smaller notes, in no particular order:

- The coffee machine on the second floor is fixed, for now. Please do not test its patience.
- Somebody left a half-finished diagram on the whiteboard in the meeting room. It was photographed and filed in the wiki before being wiped, so nothing was lost.
- A reminder that expense receipts need to be attached when claims are submitted, not promised afterwards. Finance would like this to stop being a recurring topic.
- The quarterly planning template got a minor tidy: the risks section now comes before the dependencies section, because people kept skipping the risks when they were at the bottom.

On the tooling side, a couple of people noticed the staging environment has been slower than usual. No root cause yet. The suspicion is that old test data has accumulated, and the plan is to clear it out on a quiet evening and see whether response times improve. If they do not, we will look at the more expensive explanations next.

We closed by agreeing that these notes should stay short and honest. If a week was dull, say so. A log that only records exciting weeks is not much of a log, and the dull weeks are usually when the useful chores get done.

Next entry should cover how the review rota actually went, along with whatever else turns up between now and then.
</TEXT>

request.episode_body:
## Procurement and a messy inbox

Wrote this on the train, so apologies for any typos. The main theme of the week was purchasing, which is not glamorous but keeps everything else running.

Sofia Petrov walked us through where procurement stands. The headline is that requests are arriving through too many routes: email, chat, a form that half the team has never seen, and the occasional hallway conversation. Each route has its own way of losing information. Her proposal is to pick one intake route and make everything else politely redirect to it. We discussed whether that is too rigid. The consensus was that rigid is fine for a first version, as long as there is a visible way to flag something urgent without going through the whole form.

A related point came up about approvals. At the moment a request can sit waiting for a sign-off without anybody being told. We agreed that anything waiting longer than a few working days should nudge its approver automatically, and that the nudge should be polite but unmistakable. Nobody wants to build anything elaborate. A scheduled reminder and a shared list would do the job.

Then we moved to a longer discussion about the compliance workstream under Sable Core. The question was how much evidence we should be collecting as we go versus assembling it at the end. The honest answer is that assembling at the end is always painful, and everyone admitted to having been burned by it. We settled on a habit: when you finish a task that produces evidence, drop a link into the shared tracker the same day. It takes under a minute and saves hours later.

Other items:

- Telemetry dashboards for Tern Core are noisy. Several alerts fire so often that people have stopped looking at them. We will pick the three most useful and mute or retune the rest.
- The meeting-notes folder has grown unwieldy. A light naming convention was proposed: date first, topic second, nothing else. Easy to follow, easy to search.
- A newcomer asked where to find the team glossary. There is not one. Somebody will start a page and everyone will add terms as they stumble across them.
- The office plants are still alive, which was noted with some surprise.

We also touched on how to run retrospectives without them turning into complaint sessions. One suggestion was to open every retro by listing something that went well before anyone is allowed to say what went badly. It sounds trivial but it changes the tone. We will try it at the next one.

Open questions carried forward: what to do with the abandoned form, who owns the glossary, and whether the alert retuning needs a review step. No owners yet on the last one, which probably means it will be forgotten unless someone writes it down. Consider this the writing down.

Next time: a quick check on whether the single intake route has survived its first full week.

request.episode_body:
## Retro, loosely speaking

Not a formal meeting, more a long conversation over lunch that turned into notes. Capturing the useful parts.

The theme was why some sprints feel calm and others feel like constant firefighting. We sketched out a rough theory. Calm sprints are the ones where the work was cut small enough on day one that nobody has to guess what done looks like. Chaotic sprints are the ones where a big, vague item sat in the middle and kept growing. It is hardly a revelation, but saying it out loud made it easier to agree on a rule: if an item cannot be explained in two sentences, it gets split before anyone picks it up.

From there we drifted onto interruptions. Everyone has a story about being pulled off a task for something that turned out not to be urgent. The practical outcome was a small agreement about how to ask for help. Say what you need, say when you need it by, and say what happens if it does not arrive. That last part is the one people usually skip, and it is the part that lets the other person decide whether to drop everything.

Fable Core came up in passing, mostly because the newcomer experience there has improved and people wanted to understand why. The best answer anyone had was that the checklist got shorter. When the first-week list went from a sprawling document to something that fit on one screen, people actually followed it. Worth copying elsewhere.

Smaller points:

- Standups are running long. Proposal: if a topic takes more than a minute, park it for after and let the interested people stay.
- The ticket labels have drifted, with three different ones meaning roughly the same thing. A tidy-up is overdue. Pick one, rename the others, move on.
- Documentation for Tern Core data formats exists but is hard to find. A link from the main wiki index would solve most of it.
- A suggestion to rotate who takes notes in meetings, so it does not always fall on the same patient person. Accepted with no dissent, which is suspicious.

We also asked whether we are measuring the right things. Velocity numbers were dismissed as mostly noise. What people actually trust is a simple question asked at the end of each week: did we ship something a user could notice? If the answer is no two weeks running, that is a signal worth talking about.

There was a short disagreement about whether to write down more decisions. One side said every decision needs a record; the other said that would bury the important ones. We landed in the middle: record decisions that someone could plausibly reverse by accident later. Everything else can live in chat.

Follow-ups are small. Fix the labels, add the link, trial the help-request format. All three should take under an hour combined, so there is no excuse for them to still be open at the next entry.

You are an entity extraction specialist for unstructured text.
NEVER extract vague or standalone feelings or generic words. A specific, named abstract concept
that passes the Wikipedia-article test below (e.g. "climate change", "quantum entanglement")
should be extracted as a Concept entity — being abstract is not by itself a reason to exclude it.

NEVER extract:
- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)
- Vague standalone feelings and generic ideas that could not stand alone as a specific, named
  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

For each entity extracted, assign a single entity_type label from this closed ontology:
- Person: An individual human being
- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication
Choose the single most appropriate type. If none fit well, use the closest match.

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>

request.edge_system_prompt:
You are an expert fact extractor that extracts fact triples from text.
1. Extracted fact triples should also be extracted with relevant date information.
2. Treat REFERENCE_TIME as the time the episode was recorded. All temporal information should be extracted relative to REFERENCE_TIME.

# TASK
Extract all factual relationships between the given ENTITIES based on the CURRENT MESSAGE.
Only extract facts that:
- involve two DISTINCT ENTITIES from the ENTITIES list,
- are clearly stated or unambiguously implied in the CURRENT MESSAGE,
  and can be represented as edges in a knowledge graph.
- Facts should include entity names rather than pronouns whenever possible.

# EXTRACTION RULES

1. **Entity Name Validation**: source_name and target_name must use only the name values from the ENTITIES list provided above.
   - CRITICAL: Using names not in the list will cause the edge to be rejected.
2. Each fact must involve two distinct entities — source_name and target_name NEVER refer to the same entity.
3. NEVER extract facts that describe only a single entity's state, feeling, or attribute. Instead, identify the second entity that the state or feeling relates to and form a proper triple.
   - BAD: "Alice feels happy" (single-entity state — what is Alice happy about?)
   - GOOD: "Alice feels happy about Bob's promotion" → Alice FEELS_HAPPY_ABOUT Bob's promotion
   - GOOD: "Alice congratulated Bob" (relationship between two entities), "Alice lives in Paris" (relationship between entity and place)
4. NEVER emit duplicate or semantically redundant facts.
5. The fact field should closely paraphrase the original source sentence(s). Do not verbatim quote the original text.
6. Use REFERENCE_TIME to resolve vague or relative temporal expressions (e.g., "last week").
7. Do not hallucinate or infer temporal bounds from unrelated events.

# RELATION TYPE RULES


You MUST always provide a non-null relation_type for every edge. Leaving it null or empty is not acceptable.
Derive a relation_type from the relationship predicate in SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE (e.g., WORKS_AT, LIVES_IN, IS_FRIENDS_WITH, WROTE, AUTHORED, MARRIED_TO).
If the predicate is unclear, derive one from the fact description using a concise verb phrase.
Use concise, consistent vocabulary — prefer established verbs that would apply broadly.

# DATETIME RULES

- Use ISO 8601 with "Z" suffix (UTC) (e.g., 2025-04-30T00:00:00Z).
- If the fact is ongoing (present tense), set valid_at to REFERENCE_TIME.
- If a change or termination is expressed, set invalid_at to the relevant timestamp.
- Leave both fields null if no explicit or resolvable time is stated.
- If only a date is mentioned (no time), assume 00:00:00.
- If only a year is mentioned, use January 1st at 00:00:00.

request.episode_body:
## Feedback came in

Good news first, because we have not had much of it lately. The onboarding survey results landed this week and Fable Core received a satisfaction rating of 9.5 out of 10. People wrote kind things in the comment boxes, mostly about the shortened first-week checklist and about having a named person to ask. We should resist the urge to declare victory, but it is nice to see the effort noticed.

That said, the free-text comments were more useful than the score. Two themes recurred. First, newcomers want to see a real example of finished work early on, not just instructions about how to produce it. Second, they were unsure who to ask about access requests, which tend to bounce between people. We agreed to add a short "who handles what" page and to link it from the very first screen of the checklist.

The rest of the session was housekeeping.

On access requests, the underlying problem is that nobody owns the queue. Someone suggested giving it to whoever is on the review rota that day, which is clever because it rotates the load and keeps the queue visible. There was a worry that it makes the rota too heavy. We will try it and watch.

We reviewed the state of the shared test environment. It works, but it is fragile, and people avoid touching it for fear of breaking each other's runs. A short written etiquette was proposed: announce before you reset, never leave it half-migrated, and clean up your own fixtures. Short enough to fit in a pinned message. Nobody objected.

Compliance work under Sable Core had a brief update. Nothing dramatic, just steady progress on the evidence tracker. The ask from that side is that people stop attaching screenshots when a link would do, since screenshots go stale and cannot be searched.

Some stray items:

- A reminder to update your out-of-office when you actually leave, not on the morning of.
- The office printer is working. Nobody knows why. Do not touch anything.
- The team chat has too many channels. A proposal to archive any that have been silent for a long stretch was approved. Archiving is reversible, which helped.
- The reading group is on hold until the busy period passes.

One more thing worth noting is a gentle disagreement over how celebratory these notes should be. Some of us like recording wins so there is a trail of what went right; others worry it turns the log into a brag sheet. The compromise is to keep wins factual and brief, one line each, and never in the same paragraph as the problems.

Next up: write the who-handles-what page, then check whether the rota-based access queue holds up.

<TEXT>
## Feedback came in

Good news first, because we have not had much of it lately. The onboarding survey results landed this week and Fable Core received a satisfaction rating of 9.5 out of 10. People wrote kind things in the comment boxes, mostly about the shortened first-week checklist and about having a named person to ask. We should resist the urge to declare victory, but it is nice to see the effort noticed.

That said, the free-text comments were more useful than the score. Two themes recurred. First, newcomers want to see a real example of finished work early on, not just instructions about how to produce it. Second, they were unsure who to ask about access requests, which tend to bounce between people. We agreed to add a short "who handles what" page and to link it from the very first screen of the checklist.

The rest of the session was housekeeping.

On access requests, the underlying problem is that nobody owns the queue. Someone suggested giving it to whoever is on the review rota that day, which is clever because it rotates the load and keeps the queue visible. There was a worry that it makes the rota too heavy. We will try it and watch.

We reviewed the state of the shared test environment. It works, but it is fragile, and people avoid touching it for fear of breaking each other's runs. A short written etiquette was proposed: announce before you reset, never leave it half-migrated, and clean up your own fixtures. Short enough to fit in a pinned message. Nobody objected.

Compliance work under Sable Core had a brief update. Nothing dramatic, just steady progress on the evidence tracker. The ask from that side is that people stop attaching screenshots when a link would do, since screenshots go stale and cannot be searched.

Some stray items:

- A reminder to update your out-of-office when you actually leave, not on the morning of.
- The office printer is working. Nobody knows why. Do not touch anything.
- The team chat has too many channels. A proposal to archive any that have been silent for a long stretch was approved. Archiving is reversible, which helped.
- The reading group is on hold until the busy period passes.

One more thing worth noting is a gentle disagreement over how celebratory these notes should be. Some of us like recording wins so there is a trail of what went right; others worry it turns the log into a brag sheet. The compromise is to keep wins factual and brief, one line each, and never in the same paragraph as the problems.

Next up: write the who-handles-what page, then check whether the rota-based access queue holds up.
</TEXT>

request.episode_body:
## Learning time and a few chores

This entry is mostly about development and about how we protect time for it, since that has been a recurring grumble.

The trigger was a look at who has actually used their training allowance this term. Sofia Petrov completed 57 hours of training this term, mostly on negotiation and contract basics that feed straight into procurement work. Others have barely touched theirs. The conversation that followed was gentle rather than pointed. Nobody is falling behind on purpose; it is just that a training course loses every tug of war against a deadline. We decided to ask people to book their learning time on the calendar like any other meeting, so it is visible and harder to quietly trade away.

Related to that, we talked about sharing what is learned. A sixty-minute course that only one person attends is a poor return. A small habit was agreed: after finishing something, write five lines in the wiki about what was worth knowing and what was not. Five lines, not an essay. If it takes longer than ten minutes to write, it has become too much.

There was also a conversation about pairing. Some of the best learning happens when two people work through something together, and we have drifted away from that. A proposal to set aside one afternoon every couple of weeks for deliberate pairing was well received. The rule is that the pair picks something neither of them has done before, otherwise it is just ordinary work with extra chatter.

Chores and loose ends:

- The shared drive has duplicate folders from an old migration. Someone will compare the two trees and delete the redundant one after a last check with the people who might be using it.
- Telemetry exports from Tern Core are being stored longer than anyone needs. A retention rule should be written down, even if it is a rough one.
- The kitchen rota has lapsed. It was restarted. Expect gentle reminders.
- A newcomer pointed out that our meeting links are inconsistent, some being permanent and some one-off. We will standardise on permanent ones for recurring meetings.

We spent a few minutes on tone in written reviews. A recurring complaint is that comments can read as sharper than the author intended. Suggested remedy: phrase suggestions as questions where honest, and always say what is good about the change before listing what is not. It costs little and has a visible effect on how people take feedback.

Nothing major was decided, but a lot of small habits were nudged in a sensible direction, which is probably what a planning session is for. The next entry should report on whether anyone actually booked their learning time, and whether the pairing afternoon took place.

request.episode_body:
## After the demo

Writing this the morning after the demo, while I still remember what people asked.

Attendance was better than expected: 31 people attended the Tern Core demo. The room was full and a few people dialled in. The format was deliberately plain, a live walk through the telemetry views with no slides, and I think that helped. People could see real data rather than a rehearsed story. Where the data was messy, we said so, and the questions that followed were noticeably more honest than they would have been after a polished pitch.

The questions themselves fell into three groups. Several people asked how alerts are tuned and whether they can request changes. Others wanted to know how long data is kept and who can see it. A smaller group asked whether the views can be embedded in other dashboards. We did not have crisp answers for the second one, which is a gap, and we have noted it as a follow-up for the team to settle in writing. The first and third answers were fine.

Some practical observations from running it:

- The projector took ten minutes to cooperate. Next time someone should test it the day before.
- The shared notes document worked well as a live question list, because people could upvote instead of repeating each other.
- We ran slightly over. Cutting the last section would have been better than rushing it.
- A few people left early, which is fine, but it suggests the intended audience should be told the useful part comes first.

Besides the demo, the rest of the week had its usual share of chores. The compliance side, meaning the Sable Core work, asked for help gathering a few more links into the evidence tracker, and two people picked that up. Fable Core's onboarding page got one small fix, a broken link that had been there for weeks. Sofia Petrov flagged a pending purchase that needs a second pair of eyes, so someone from the team will look at it on Monday.

We also agreed something about follow-up emails after demos. Rather than a long recap, send a short message with three things: what was shown, what was asked that we could not answer, and who owns finding the answers. It keeps the energy from the room without creating homework for the audience.

For the record, nobody objected to making the demo a regular event, perhaps on a monthly cadence, rotating between projects so it does not always fall on the same group. That will be discussed properly once the follow-up answers are written up. For now, thanks to everyone who helped set up, and apologies again for the projector.
request.entity_system_prompt:
You are an entity extraction specialist for unstructured text.
NEVER extract vague or standalone feelings or generic words. A specific, named abstract concept
that passes the Wikipedia-article test below (e.g. "climate change", "quantum entanglement")
should be extracted as a Concept entity — being abstract is not by itself a reason to exclude it.

NEVER extract:
- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)
- Vague standalone feelings and generic ideas that could not stand alone as a specific, named
  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

For each entity extracted, assign a single entity_type label from this closed ontology:
- Person: An individual human being
- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication
Choose the single most appropriate type. If none fit well, use the closest match.

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>
