request.episode_body:
## Supplier chores and sprint hygiene

A somewhat administrative entry. I will try to keep it readable.

Sofia Petrov brought up a list of procurement tasks that have been drifting. None are urgent individually, but together they create a vague sense of mess. The approach we agreed was to sort them into three piles: do now, do when convenient, and drop. Dropping is the underrated one. Several items on the list turned out to be requests nobody remembered making, and we simply closed them. That alone cleared a surprising amount of clutter.

On sprint hygiene, we looked at how tickets move across the board. Too many sit in "in progress" for days without a visible change, which makes the board a poor guide to what is actually happening. Proposal: if a ticket has not been touched in a few working days, its owner either adds a comment saying what is blocking it or moves it back. No shame attached. The board is only useful if it is honest.

We also talked about estimating. Everyone dislikes it, and everyone agrees that wildly wrong estimates are worse than none. The compromise was to use only three sizes, small, medium and large, and to treat anything large as a signal to break it down. That mirrors the earlier rule about explaining an item in two sentences, and the two ideas reinforce each other nicely.

Quick items:

- Fable Core's onboarding checklist is now linked from the team home page, which should save the repeated "where is it" question.
- Telemetry work for Tern Core needs a reviewer who has not seen the code before. A fresh pair of eyes was requested explicitly.
- Compliance reminders for Sable Core will go into the weekly channel instead of individual messages, to cut down on duplicate nudges.
- Someone proposed standard names for branches. Nobody could remember the old convention, so adopting a new one costs nothing.

An observation that deserves recording: the best part of this meeting was a stretch where nobody was talking and people were just reading the board together. It exposed several stale items faster than discussion would have. We might try a silent-reading start to future sessions, five minutes at the top, then talk about whatever stood out.

There was a short and friendly argument about whether notes like these should be written by one person or by whoever happens to be free. The log is meant to have different authors, so the answer is the latter, but it does create some variation in style. I think that is fine. It gives the log a human texture and makes it clear that real people are behind it.

Open items for next time: the three-pile cleanup of procurement tasks should be done by then, and the board honesty rule needs a week of real use before we judge it. Also, someone needs to find out what the old branch convention was, purely out of curiosity.

request.episode_body:
## Notes from the long meeting

This was the longest session in a while, and I took scrappy notes, so I have tried to sort them into something coherent.

The big topic was dependency management across projects. Each of the projects we run has accumulated libraries and tools that are slightly out of date, and updating them is nobody's job. We talked through a few options. The simplest was a fixed day each month where everyone updates whatever they own and nothing else is allowed to start. It is blunt, but blunt tends to survive. There was also a suggestion to let a bot open the update requests so humans only review them, which people liked, though we agreed it needs somebody to watch for noise.

A smaller but livelier thread was about on-call. Several people feel the current rota is uneven, with some weeks quiet and others punishing. We did not solve it. We did agree to collect a month of actual data on how often people are woken or interrupted, then decide with numbers instead of impressions. Until then, anyone who has a rough week can swap without asking permission.

Then compliance. The Sable Core group would like to start including a short evidence checklist in the template for every new task, so the habit forms from the first day. Telemetry owners on Tern Core were wary that this adds friction to quick fixes. The compromise is that the checklist is mandatory only for changes touching regulated data, and optional elsewhere. Both sides accepted that for now.

Quick bullets:

- Aiko Osei will run a short session for new joiners on how to read the team log, since newcomers say it is hard to tell which entries matter.
- Fable Core's local setup instructions need a runnable example at the top.
- A vendor contract question was parked until Sofia Petrov is back and can speak to the details.
- The meeting room booking tool is double-booking. Suspected cause is a stale sync. Reported.

I want to capture one remark from near the end because it stuck with me. Someone said that the notes we keep are only useful if a person who was not there can act on them. That is a good test. Reading back over this entry, I have tried to make sure each item says who, what and roughly when, even when that is just "someone, soon". Where I could not do that, I flagged it as open instead of pretending it was settled.

Items that remain open: how to measure on-call load fairly, who owns the dependency update day, and what exactly counts as regulated data for the checklist. The third one needs a definition in writing, ideally one a newcomer could apply without asking.

We ended slightly late and everyone left looking tired but not unhappy, which I count as a fair outcome. See the next entry for follow-ups.
request.entity_system_prompt:
You are an entity extraction specialist for unstructured text.
NEVER extract vague or standalone feelings or generic words. A specific, named abstract concept
that passes the Wikipedia-article test below (e.g. "climate change", "quantum entanglement")
should be extracted as a Concept entity — being abstract is not by itself a reason to exclude it.

NEVER extract:
- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)
- Vague standalone feelings and generic ideas that could not stand alone as a specific, named
  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

For each entity extracted, assign a single entity_type label from this closed ontology:
- Person: An individual human being
- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication
Choose the single most appropriate type. If none fit well, use the closest match.

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>

You are an expert fact extractor that extracts fact triples from text.
1. Extracted fact triples should also be extracted with relevant date information.
2. Treat REFERENCE_TIME as the time the episode was recorded. All temporal information should be extracted relative to REFERENCE_TIME.

# TASK
Extract all factual relationships between the given ENTITIES based on the CURRENT MESSAGE.
Only extract facts that:
- involve two DISTINCT ENTITIES from the ENTITIES list,
- are clearly stated or unambiguously implied in the CURRENT MESSAGE,
  and can be represented as edges in a knowledge graph.
- Facts should include entity names rather than pronouns whenever possible.

# EXTRACTION RULES

1. **Entity Name Validation**: source_name and target_name must use only the name values from the ENTITIES list provided above.
   - CRITICAL: Using names not in the list will cause the edge to be rejected.
2. Each fact must involve two distinct entities — source_name and target_name NEVER refer to the same entity.
3. NEVER extract facts that describe only a single entity's state, feeling, or attribute. Instead, identify the second entity that the state or feeling relates to and form a proper triple.
   - BAD: "Alice feels happy" (single-entity state — what is Alice happy about?)
   - GOOD: "Alice feels happy about Bob's promotion" → Alice FEELS_HAPPY_ABOUT Bob's promotion
   - GOOD: "Alice congratulated Bob" (relationship between two entities), "Alice lives in Paris" (relationship between entity and place)

request.episode_body:
## Mid-month check-in

A brisk check-in, no big agenda. I mostly want to log where things stand so the next person writing can see the trajectory.

Starting with what got done since the last entry. The dependency update day was tried once, informally, and went better than feared. Most people finished in a couple of hours, and the bot-opened update requests were easy to review. The only snag was that two updates conflicted and had to be merged by hand. We will add a note to the process: if two updates touch the same file, do them in one request instead of two.

On-call data collection has started. A simple shared sheet where people tick a box whenever they were interrupted outside working hours. It is crude, but a crude record beats a memory of one. We will review it at the end of the month.

On the people side, Aiko Osei reported that the session for new joiners about reading the team log went well, with a few suggestions on how to make entries easier to scan. The main one was to put the decisions near the top of each entry and leave the chatter for later. We will try that in the next few entries and see whether it helps.

Things in flight:

- Compliance evidence checklist for Sable Core: draft is written, awaiting comment from the Tern Core side about what counts as regulated.
- Telemetry retention for Tern Core: still without a written rule. Reminder sent.
- Procurement backlog: Sofia Petrov has moved most items into the three piles and the do-now pile is shorter than expected.
- Fable Core setup page: the runnable example is added and has already been used successfully by a newcomer.

A few softer observations. Energy in the team feels steadier than a month ago. People are closing small items instead of letting them pile up, and that seems to feed on itself; each closed item makes the next one feel easier. We should not take that for granted, though, because the busy period is coming and habits are the first thing to go under pressure.

There was a short conversation about what to do if the busy period hits hard. The agreement is that the buffer in each sprint stays, even when everything looks urgent, because that is exactly when unplanned work shows up. If we cannot defend the buffer in a busy month, it was never really a buffer.

Last practical point: the room-booking issue is fixed, apparently by someone restarting a service. Nobody is confident it will stay fixed, so keep a backup plan of grabbing a room by walking up and asking.

Next check-in in two weeks, unless something breaks earlier.
request.entity_system_prompt:
You are an entity extraction specialist for unstructured text.
NEVER extract vague or standalone feelings or generic words. A specific, named abstract concept
that passes the Wikipedia-article test below (e.g. "climate change", "quantum entanglement")
should be extracted as a Concept entity — being abstract is not by itself a reason to exclude it.

NEVER extract:
- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)
- Vague standalone feelings and generic ideas that could not stand alone as a specific, named
  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

For each entity extracted, assign a single entity_type label from this closed ontology:
- Person: An individual human being
- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication
Choose the single most appropriate type. If none fit well, use the closest match.

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>

request.edge_system_prompt:
You are an expert fact extractor that extracts fact triples from text.
1. Extracted fact triples should also be extracted with relevant date information.
2. Treat REFERENCE_TIME as the time the episode was recorded. All temporal information should be extracted relative to REFERENCE_TIME.

# TASK
Extract all factual relationships between the given ENTITIES based on the CURRENT MESSAGE.
Only extract facts that:
- involve two DISTINCT ENTITIES from the ENTITIES list,
- are clearly stated or unambiguously implied in the CURRENT MESSAGE,
  and can be represented as edges in a knowledge graph.
- Facts should include entity names rather than pronouns whenever possible.

# EXTRACTION RULES

1. **Entity Name Validation**: source_name and target_name must use only the name values from the ENTITIES list provided above.
   - CRITICAL: Using names not in the list will cause the edge to be rejected.
2. Each fact must involve two distinct entities — source_name and target_name NEVER refer to the same entity.
3. NEVER extract facts that describe only a single entity's state, feeling, or attribute. Instead, identify the second entity that the state or feeling relates to and form a proper triple.
   - BAD: "Alice feels happy" (single-entity state — what is Alice happy about?)
   - GOOD: "Alice feels happy about Bob's promotion" → Alice FEELS_HAPPY_ABOUT Bob's promotion
   - GOOD: "Alice congratulated Bob" (relationship between two entities), "Alice lives in Paris" (relationship between entity and place)
4. NEVER emit duplicate or semantically redundant facts.
5. The fact field should closely paraphrase the original source sentence(s). Do not verbatim quote the original text.
6. Use REFERENCE_TIME to resolve vague or relative temporal expressions (e.g., "last week").
7. Do not hallucinate or infer temporal bounds from unrelated events.

# RELATION TYPE RULES


You MUST always provide a non-null relation_type for every edge. Leaving it null or empty is not acceptable.
Derive a relation_type from the relationship predicate in SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE (e.g., WORKS_AT, LIVES_IN, IS_FRIENDS_WITH, WROTE, AUTHORED, MARRIED_TO).
If the predicate is unclear, derive one from the fact description using a concise verb phrase.
Use concise, consistent vocabulary — prefer established verbs that would apply broadly.

# DATETIME RULES

- Use ISO 8601 with "Z" suffix (UTC) (e.g., 2025-04-30T00:00:00Z).
- If the fact is ongoing (present tense), set valid_at to REFERENCE_TIME.
- If a change or termination is expressed, set invalid_at to the relevant timestamp.
- Leave both fields null if no explicit or resolvable time is stated.
- If only a date is mentioned (no time), assume 00:00:00.
- If only a year is mentioned, use January 1st at 00:00:00.

request.episode_body:
## Wrapping up the quarter's loose ends

Getting close to the end of this stretch of notes, so this entry is part tidy-up and part list of things to carry forward.

Let me begin with what we are quietly pleased about. The single intake route for procurement requests has held up. Sofia Petrov says duplicate requests have nearly vanished, and the ones that still arrive by the old routes get redirected with a friendly note. The urgent flag has been used sparingly, which suggests people trust the normal route to be fast enough. That is the real measure of success: not that the new thing exists, but that people stopped working around it.

Less pleasing is that the telemetry retention rule for Tern Core is still unwritten. It has been mentioned in four entries now, which is embarrassing. This time it has an owner and a day, and the owner has promised to bring a draft of no more than a page. If it slips again we will assume nobody wants it and drop the item deliberately, rather than let it linger.

On Fable Core, a couple of newcomers have now gone through the shortened onboarding path and both said the same thing: the first day was clear, the third day was confusing. We do not yet know why. The working theory is that the checklist front-loads instructions but gives no guidance on what to do when the instructions run out. A short "what next" section is the likely remedy, and Aiko Osei will draft it.

Compliance for Sable Core has an evidence tracker that looks healthy. The weekly Thursday check continues, and the open list is shorter each week. One risk is that the check depends on a single person remembering. We will write down a backup so it survives a holiday.

Carry-forward list:

1. Draft and agree the telemetry retention rule.
2. Add the "what next" section to the onboarding checklist.
3. Name a backup for the weekly compliance check.
4. Review the on-call sheet and decide whether the rota needs reshaping.
5. Decide whether the meeting-free afternoon trial happens at all.

Items 4 and 5 are the ones I expect to be argued about. Item 4 because people have strong feelings about being woken, item 5 because everyone supports the idea in principle and nobody wants to be the one to cancel meetings.

A final housekeeping point: the log itself is getting long, and some older entries read as if the writer was in a rush. We could add a short index at the top with one line per entry. It would not take long, and it would make the whole thing easier to search. Volunteers welcome.

That is it for now. Thanks, as ever, to whoever restarts the kettle.
request.entity_system_prompt:
You are an entity extraction specialist for unstructured text.
NEVER extract vague or standalone feelings or generic words. A specific, named abstract concept
that passes the Wikipedia-article test below (e.g. "climate change", "quantum entanglement")
should be extracted as a Concept entity — being abstract is not by itself a reason to exclude it.

NEVER extract:
- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)
- Vague standalone feelings and generic ideas that could not stand alone as a specific, named
  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

For each entity extracted, assign a single entity_type label from this closed ontology:
- Person: An individual human being
- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication
Choose the single most appropriate type. If none fit well, use the closest match.

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>

request.edge_system_prompt:
You are an expert fact extractor that extracts fact triples from text.
1. Extracted fact triples should also be extracted with relevant date information.
2. Treat REFERENCE_TIME as the time the episode was recorded. All temporal information should be extracted relative to REFERENCE_TIME.

# TASK
Extract all factual relationships between the given ENTITIES based on the CURRENT MESSAGE.
Only extract facts that:
- involve two DISTINCT ENTITIES from the ENTITIES list,
- are clearly stated or unambiguously implied in the CURRENT MESSAGE,
  and can be represented as edges in a knowledge graph.
- Facts should include entity names rather than pronouns whenever possible.

# EXTRACTION RULES

1. **Entity Name Validation**: source_name and target_name must use only the name values from the ENTITIES list provided above.
   - CRITICAL: Using names not in the list will cause the edge to be rejected.
2. Each fact must involve two distinct entities — source_name and target_name NEVER refer to the same entity.
3. NEVER extract facts that describe only a single entity's state, feeling, or attribute. Instead, identify the second entity that the state or feeling relates to and form a proper triple.
   - BAD: "Alice feels happy" (single-entity state — what is Alice happy about?)
   - GOOD: "Alice feels happy about Bob's promotion" → Alice FEELS_HAPPY_ABOUT Bob's promotion
   - GOOD: "Alice congratulated Bob" (relationship between two entities), "Alice lives in Paris" (relationship between entity and place)
4. NEVER emit duplicate or semantically redundant facts.
5. The fact field should closely paraphrase the original source sentence(s). Do not verbatim quote the original text.
6. Use REFERENCE_TIME to resolve vague or relative temporal expressions (e.g., "last week").
7. Do not hallucinate or infer temporal bounds from unrelated events.

# RELATION TYPE RULES


You MUST always provide a non-null relation_type for every edge. Leaving it null or empty is not acceptable.
Derive a relation_type from the relationship predicate in SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE (e.g., WORKS_AT, LIVES_IN, IS_FRIENDS_WITH, WROTE, AUTHORED, MARRIED_TO).
If the predicate is unclear, derive one from the fact description using a concise verb phrase.
Use concise, consistent vocabulary — prefer established verbs that would apply broadly.

# DATETIME RULES

- Use ISO 8601 with "Z" suffix (UTC) (e.g., 2025-04-30T00:00:00Z).
- If the fact is ongoing (present tense), set valid_at to REFERENCE_TIME.
- If a change or termination is expressed, set invalid_at to the relevant timestamp.
- Leave both fields null if no explicit or resolvable time is stated.
- If only a date is mentioned (no time), assume 00:00:00.
- If only a year is mentioned, use January 1st at 00:00:00.

request.episode_body:
## Audit follow-up and sign-off

Final section for this run of notes. It mostly covers the internal audit and what we learned from it, plus the last few chores before the next cycle begins.

The audit results arrived and the headline is encouraging. Aiko Osei scored 91 out of 100 in the internal audit. The auditors liked the onboarding records in particular, which were complete and easy to follow. The few marks lost came from missing dates on a handful of forms, which is fixable and, honestly, embarrassing in a pleasant way, since the information was all there and simply not written down. The fix is a required date field on the form so it cannot be submitted blank.

The wider lesson, which we discussed at some length, is that good audit outcomes come from small habits repeated, not from a frantic week of preparation. The teams that did well were the ones who filed evidence as they went. That echoes what the compliance side, Sable Core, has been saying for months, and it is nice to see it borne out by actual results rather than just advice.

We also took the chance to look at what did not work. Two processes were described one way in the wiki and practised another way in reality. The auditors noticed and asked which was right. We could not answer immediately. The action is to decide which version is correct, and then change either the page or the practice to match. Nobody should have to guess.

A few last items:

- Fable Core's onboarding checklist now includes the "what next" section and has had one positive test run.
- Tern Core's retention rule has a draft. It is one page, as promised, and is waiting for comments.
- Sofia Petrov will share a short note on what procurement learned from the single intake route, so other teams can borrow the parts that work.
- The notes log gets an index at the top. A volunteer stepped up.

On the human side, the mood is good. People are tired but pleased, and there was a decent amount of laughing in the room. I do not want to over-read that, yet I do think it matters: a team that can laugh while discussing audit findings is a team that is not afraid of them.

Action items for the next cycle:

1. Add the required date field to the form.
2. Reconcile the two mismatched process descriptions.
3. Circulate the retention draft and collect comments within the week.
4. Publish the log index.

That closes out this set of notes. The next planning session starts fresh, with an empty agenda and, with luck, an empty list of overdue chores.
request.entity_system_prompt:
You are an entity extraction specialist for unstructured text.
NEVER extract vague or standalone feelings or generic words. A specific, named abstract concept
that passes the Wikipedia-article test below (e.g. "climate change", "quantum entanglement")
should be extracted as a Concept entity — being abstract is not by itself a reason to exclude it.

NEVER extract:
- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)
- Vague standalone feelings and generic ideas that could not stand alone as a specific, named
  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

For each entity extracted, assign a single entity_type label from this closed ontology:
- Person: An individual human being
- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication
Choose the single most appropriate type. If none fit well, use the closest match.

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>

request.edge_system_prompt:
You are an expert fact extractor that extracts fact triples from text.
1. Extracted fact triples should also be extracted with relevant date information.
2. Treat REFERENCE_TIME as the time the episode was recorded. All temporal information should be extracted relative to REFERENCE_TIME.

# TASK
Extract all factual relationships between the given ENTITIES based on the CURRENT MESSAGE.
Only extract facts that:
- involve two DISTINCT ENTITIES from the ENTITIES list,
- are clearly stated or unambiguously implied in the CURRENT MESSAGE,
  and can be represented as edges in a knowledge graph.
- Facts should include entity names rather than pronouns whenever possible.

# EXTRACTION RULES

1. **Entity Name Validation**: source_name and target_name must use only the name values from the ENTITIES list provided above.
   - CRITICAL: Using names not in the list will cause the edge to be rejected.
2. Each fact must involve two distinct entities — source_name and target_name NEVER refer to the same entity.
3. NEVER extract facts that describe only a single entity's state, feeling, or attribute. Instead, identify the second entity that the state or feeling relates to and form a proper triple.
   - BAD: "Alice feels happy" (single-entity state — what is Alice happy about?)
   - GOOD: "Alice feels happy about Bob's promotion" → Alice FEELS_HAPPY_ABOUT Bob's promotion
   - GOOD: "Alice congratulated Bob" (relationship between two entities), "Alice lives in Paris" (relationship between entity and place)
4. NEVER emit duplicate or semantically redundant facts.
5. The fact field should closely paraphrase the original source sentence(s). Do not verbatim quote the original text.
6. Use REFERENCE_TIME to resolve vague or relative temporal expressions (e.g., "last week").
7. Do not hallucinate or infer temporal bounds from unrelated events.

# RELATION TYPE RULES


You MUST always provide a non-null relation_type for every edge. Leaving it null or empty is not acceptable.
Derive a relation_type from the relationship predicate in SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE (e.g., WORKS_AT, LIVES_IN, IS_FRIENDS_WITH, WROTE, AUTHORED, MARRIED_TO).
If the predicate is unclear, derive one from the fact description using a concise verb phrase.
Use concise, consistent vocabulary — prefer established verbs that would apply broadly.

# DATETIME RULES

- Use ISO 8601 with "Z" suffix (UTC) (e.g., 2025-04-30T00:00:00Z).
- If the fact is ongoing (present tense), set valid_at to REFERENCE_TIME.
- If a change or termination is expressed, set invalid_at to the relevant timestamp.
- Leave both fields null if no explicit or resolvable time is stated.
- If only a date is mentioned (no time), assume 00:00:00.
- If only a year is mentioned, use January 1st at 00:00:00.

request.episode_body:
# Review notes — 16 July 2026

Notes from the mid-month review. Attendance was good, the room was too warm, and we finished ten minutes early, which I count as a success.

We began with procurement. Sofia Petrov scored 72 out of 100 in the internal audit. That is a respectable result for a first pass, and she was relaxed about it. The audit's findings were mostly about paperwork: approvals recorded in the right order, quotes filed where others can find them, and a clearer trail when a purchase is split across two orders. None of this is a surprise, and she has already started putting a simple checklist in front of anyone who raises a purchase request. The aim before the next audit is to make the paperwork habit automatic, not to produce a heroic clean-up the week before.

Then inventory. Lena Moreau held its quarterly retrospective on 19 November 2027, which is the one we keep as the reference for how the inventory group runs its reviews. What stood out in the write-up was how plainly the group describes the things that went less well, and how few of them were about tools. Mostly they were about handovers and timing: counts done at awkward moments, and changes to stock records made without telling the person who reconciles them. Lena Moreau has proposed a short fixed time each week when changes are made, so that the person reconciling knows when to look. It is a small change that should remove a lot of confusion.

On security, Callum Brennan reported that the backlog stood at 80 open tickets at the end of the sprint. That sounds like a lot, but he explained that many of those are low-priority housekeeping items that have simply been waiting, and that the genuinely urgent ones are cleared quickly. We still agreed it is worth reducing the pile, because a long list makes it harder to see what matters. His plan is to spend part of the next sprint closing or merging duplicates, and to ask the requesters whether older items are still wanted.

A few decisions taken in the meeting:

- The review will be held on the same day each month, so people can plan around it.
- Each of the three areas will write a short paragraph beforehand, covering what went well, what did not, and what help is needed. These get pasted into the notes, so that the meeting can be spent on discussion rather than status.
- Anything that needs a decision from outside the room is written as a question and sent the same day.

Chores that came out of the conversation:

- Update the shared contact list, since two responsibilities have shifted since it was last edited.
- Agree one place where purchase approvals, stock changes and security requests can be searched together. At the moment you have to look in three places.
- Clear the review folder of old drafts that now confuse people.
- Check whether the room can have a working fan or open window for next time.

There was a short discussion on how the three groups depend on each other. A purchase that is delayed affects stock, stock levels affect what security needs to monitor, and a security ticket can hold up a purchase. We have not mapped this properly, and a half-page sketch of the dependencies would help newcomers. Someone will draw it on the whiteboard next time, and we will transcribe it.

The next section covers the follow-up conversations.

request.episode_body:
## Follow-up conversations

A few days on, a handful of one-to-one chats and corridor discussions have settled into something worth recording.

The first concerned how the three areas share information. Sofia Petrov pointed out that procurement often learns about a need late, when a request has already become urgent, and urgent purchases are the ones most likely to skip a step. Lena Moreau agreed and said inventory could flag low stock earlier if it knew which items are slow to obtain. That led to a simple idea: a shared list of items with long lead times, kept by procurement and visible to everyone. It does not need to be fancy. A table with the item, a rough note on how long it takes to arrive and who to ask is enough.

Callum Brennan raised a related point from the security side. When a new item or service is bought, security would like to hear about it early, so that any checks can be done before the thing is in use, not after. Everyone agreed this is sensible. We settled on a one-line notification to a shared channel when a new purchase is approved, with a pointer to the request. It adds a few seconds to the process and removes a class of awkward surprises.

Next, a conversation about the audit paperwork. Sofia Petrov wants to avoid the checklist becoming a box-ticking exercise, and asked for ideas on how to keep it useful. The suggestions were to keep it to a single page, to review it every few months and remove anything that has stopped being relevant, and to ask people who use it what they would change. She will try that and report back.

Small items and chores:

- The reconciliation window that Lena Moreau proposed will begin next week as a trial, with a note in the calendar so that everyone sees it.
- Callum Brennan will start the sweep of older tickets, beginning with the oldest, and will message requesters in batches instead of one at a time.
- The shared list of long-lead items needs an owner. Sofia Petrov has said she will start it and hand it over once it is stable.
- Someone should check whether the existing templates for purchase requests still match the audit's expectations.

There was an interesting side discussion about what a good week looks like. Opinions varied. For some it is a week without surprises, for others it is a week in which one irritating thing finally gets fixed. We agreed both are legitimate, and that the weekly notes should record both kinds of progress, not only the large ones.

We also talked about training. People feel that learning happens mostly by accident, through whoever happens to be sitting nearby. A short rotation, where each person spends an afternoon with another area, was suggested. It would help people see what the other groups face daily, and would make handovers smoother. Nothing has been scheduled. The idea is to see who is interested and then pick a quiet week.

A note about tone: the review conversations were direct but friendly, and I think that is partly because we agreed at the beginning to talk about the process and not about individuals. It is worth continuing that habit.

I will write the remaining plans in the final section.

request.episode_body:
## Plans and loose ends

Last stretch of the review notes. This is where I gather what is planned, what is still undecided, and what we should check again.

Starting with what is planned. Callum Brennan will carry on with the ticket sweep and will report at the next review how it is going. We do not need a number, just a sense of whether the pile is shrinking and whether anything urgent was hiding in it. Sofia Petrov will finish the purchase checklist and put it in front of the first few requesters, asking them for blunt feedback. Lena Moreau will run the weekly reconciliation window for a month and then decide whether to keep it, change it or abandon it.

Things that are still undecided:

1. Whether the three groups should share one tracker or keep their own. The case for one is that dependencies become visible; the case against is that each group has habits that fit its own work. For now we will keep them separate and add links between related items.
2. Whether the monthly review should include a short look at risks. People like the idea but worry about length. A five-minute slot at the end might be enough.
3. Where to keep the dependency sketch once it has been transcribed. The wiki is the obvious home, but it needs an owner or it will rot.

I would also like to record a couple of things people said that deserve to be remembered. One person observed that most of what slows us down is waiting for an answer from somewhere else, and that the fix is usually a better question rather than a faster reply. Another pointed out that the review works best when someone has done the reading in advance, and that the paragraphs we now write beforehand make this far easier. Both are worth keeping in mind.

Chores to close out:

- Move the review notes into the permanent folder and tidy the file names.
- Send the updated contact list to everyone and ask for corrections.
- Confirm the date for the next review and put it in the calendar before people fill their weeks.
- Reply to the open questions that were sent to the group, preferably the same day.

There was one more conversation worth noting, about how to handle disagreements between areas. When two groups want different things, the temptation is to escalate quickly. The preference expressed was to try a short conversation first, with each side stating what it needs and what it can live without, and only escalate if that fails. We agreed to write that down as a simple guideline, since it is easy to forget when people are busy.

Finally, a thank-you to everyone who prepared their paragraph beforehand. The review was short and calm because the information was already in front of us. I would like to keep that habit even when things get busy, as that is when it matters most.

If any of the plans above are wrong, correct them directly in this document so the notes stay reliable. See you at the next review.

NEVER extract vague or standalone feelings or generic words. A specific, named abstract concept
that passes the Wikipedia-article test below (e.g. "climate change", "quantum entanglement")
should be extracted as a Concept entity — being abstract is not by itself a reason to exclude it.

NEVER extract:
- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)

  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

For each entity extracted, assign a single entity_type label from this closed ontology:
- Person: An individual human being
- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication
Choose the single most appropriate type. If none fit well, use the closest match.

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>

request.episode_body:
# Team log — 19 July 2026

Sunday-evening catch-up, because the week ran away from me and I would rather write this down now than reconstruct it on Monday.

The main thing was the billing side. Ines Lindqvist completed 42 hours of training this term, and she mentioned in passing that the part she found most useful was the session on reconciling disputed invoices, since that is where most of her time goes in practice. She offered to run a short walkthrough for anyone who touches billing even occasionally. I think we should take her up on it, probably in a slot after the next sync, and keep it informal. If it goes well we can record it for whoever joins later.

We also looked at the month-end routine. It works, but it relies on a few people remembering the order of steps, and the written version is out of date. The plan is for Ines Lindqvist to mark up the current document with what she actually does, and then someone else follows it cold to see where it breaks. That is a decent test of whether a process is really documented or only feels documented.

On scheduling, Marlin Core had a calm few days. There was a small discussion about whether the weekly planning slot should move earlier, since late-afternoon planning tends to get squeezed by whatever blew up that day. No decision yet. We will try an earlier slot for two weeks and compare how often it gets cancelled or cut short.

Chores and loose ends:

- Rename the files in the shared billing folder so they sort sensibly. At the moment they are a mix of dates, initials and the word "final" in various forms.
- Check who still has access to the old invoicing mailbox, and remove anyone who does not need it.
- Add a short "who to ask" section to the top of the team wiki page. People keep asking in the general channel and the answer is always the same three names.
- Put a reminder in the calendar to review the recurring supplier payments before the end of the quarter.

I want to record one small decision that was made almost in passing, because it will matter later. We agreed that anything that touches customer billing details gets a second pair of eyes before it goes out, even if it feels routine. It does not need a formal review, just a message saying "can you glance at this?" and a reply. The reasoning was that the cost of a mistake is much higher than the cost of a thirty-second check, and we have all seen at least one near miss.

Then there was a brief conversation about how we share learning. Training hours are useful, but they only pay off if what was learned reaches the rest of the group. Suggestions included a rotating five-minute slot at the start of each sync, a shared notes page, or a short monthly lunch. We will start with the five-minute slot because it needs no setup, and see whether people actually use it.

Last point: someone asked whether these weekly notes are read by anyone outside the team. As far as we know, no, though they are visible to colleagues who are curious. That is a reason to keep them plain and factual, and to avoid in-jokes that need a decoder ring.

More in the next entry once the walkthrough has been scheduled.

You are an expert fact extractor that extracts fact triples from text.
1. Extracted fact triples should also be extracted with relevant date information.
2. Treat REFERENCE_TIME as the time the episode was recorded. All temporal information should be extracted relative to REFERENCE_TIME.

# TASK
Extract all factual relationships between the given ENTITIES based on the CURRENT MESSAGE.
Only extract facts that:
- involve two DISTINCT ENTITIES from the ENTITIES list,
- are clearly stated or unambiguously implied in the CURRENT MESSAGE,
  and can be represented as edges in a knowledge graph.
- Facts should include entity names rather than pronouns whenever possible.

# EXTRACTION RULES

1. **Entity Name Validation**: source_name and target_name must use only the name values from the ENTITIES list provided above.
   - CRITICAL: Using names not in the list will cause the edge to be rejected.
2. Each fact must involve two distinct entities — source_name and target_name NEVER refer to the same entity.
3. NEVER extract facts that describe only a single entity's state, feeling, or attribute. Instead, identify the second entity that the state or feeling relates to and form a proper triple.
   - BAD: "Alice feels happy" (single-entity state — what is Alice happy about?)
   - GOOD: "Alice feels happy about Bob's promotion" → Alice FEELS_HAPPY_ABOUT Bob's promotion
   - GOOD: "Alice congratulated Bob" (relationship between two entities), "Alice lives in Paris" (relationship between entity and place)
4. NEVER emit duplicate or semantically redundant facts.
5. The fact field should closely paraphrase the original source sentence(s). Do not verbatim quote the original text.
6. Use REFERENCE_TIME to resolve vague or relative temporal expressions (e.g., "last week").
7. Do not hallucinate or infer temporal bounds from unrelated events.

# RELATION TYPE RULES


You MUST always provide a non-null relation_type for every edge. Leaving it null or empty is not acceptable.
Derive a relation_type from the relationship predicate in SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE (e.g., WORKS_AT, LIVES_IN, IS_FRIENDS_WITH, WROTE, AUTHORED, MARRIED_TO).
If the predicate is unclear, derive one from the fact description using a concise verb phrase.
Use concise, consistent vocabulary — prefer established verbs that would apply broadly.

# DATETIME RULES

- Use ISO 8601 with "Z" suffix (UTC) (e.g., 2025-04-30T00:00:00Z).
- If the fact is ongoing (present tense), set valid_at to REFERENCE_TIME.
- If a change or termination is expressed, set invalid_at to the relevant timestamp.
- Leave both fields null if no explicit or resolvable time is stated.
- If only a date is mentioned (no time), assume 00:00:00.
- If only a year is mentioned, use January 1st at 00:00:00.

request.episode_body:
## Quarter review and incident tidy-up

This part covers the quarter-end review, which was shorter than I feared and more useful than I expected.

Starting with incidents. Marlin Core logged 6 incidents during the quarter, and we spent a fair while looking at them as a set instead of one at a time. The pattern that emerged was boring in a reassuring way: most were caused by the same kind of change being made late in the day, without a quick check from a second person. None was severe, but several cost somebody an evening. We agreed to avoid scheduling changes of that kind in the last hour of the working day, and to say so in the change template so that it is not just folklore.

The write-ups themselves were uneven. A couple were thorough, with a clear timeline and a note on what we would do differently, and a couple were three lines long. Nobody is at fault for that, since write-ups get written when people are tired. We decided to use a short fixed outline, covering what happened, what we noticed first, what fixed it, and what we will change, and to accept that a brief write-up following the outline beats a long one that wanders.

Next, a few notes from the discussion about on-call. The rota is working, but swaps are arranged by direct message and then forgotten, which led to one confusing handover. We will record every swap in the shared calendar at the time it is agreed. Quick to do, and it saves the question of who is actually covering.

Items from the end of the review:

- Merge the three overlapping incident tags in the tracker into one.
- Link each incident write-up from the relevant wiki page so that the history is discoverable.
- Ask whoever owns the alert settings whether two noisy alerts can be tuned down. They contributed to the late-evening disturbance more than anything else did.
- Schedule a half-hour to read the older write-ups again, in case anything we noted then has quietly stopped being true.

There was also a conversation about how to talk about the quarter with colleagues who were not in the room. The temptation is to give a single headline figure and move on, but a lone number hides more than it shows. We will pair any summary figure with two sentences of context. Not a big change, but it should reduce the number of follow-up questions.

On Ines Lindqvist and billing: nothing new this part, except that she asked to be told earlier when a scheduling change affects invoice dates. That is a reasonable request and we will add it to the change template as a single checkbox.

One more point on tone. A few people said these reviews can feel like a trial, and that is not the intention. The point is to look at what the system did, not to look for someone to blame. We will start the next review by saying that explicitly, and see whether the conversation changes.

I will leave the rest for the following entry, which should be easier to write since it mostly lists things that were completed.

request.entity_user_prompt:
<TEXT>
## Quarter review and incident tidy-up

This part covers the quarter-end review, which was shorter than I feared and more useful than I expected.

Starting with incidents. Marlin Core logged 6 incidents during the quarter, and we spent a fair while looking at them as a set instead of one at a time. The pattern that emerged was boring in a reassuring way: most were caused by the same kind of change being made late in the day, without a quick check from a second person. None was severe, but several cost somebody an evening. We agreed to avoid scheduling changes of that kind in the last hour of the working day, and to say so in the change template so that it is not just folklore.

The write-ups themselves were uneven. A couple were thorough, with a clear timeline and a note on what we would do differently, and a couple were three lines long. Nobody is at fault for that, since write-ups get written when people are tired. We decided to use a short fixed outline, covering what happened, what we noticed first, what fixed it, and what we will change, and to accept that a brief write-up following the outline beats a long one that wanders.

Next, a few notes from the discussion about on-call. The rota is working, but swaps are arranged by direct message and then forgotten, which led to one confusing handover. We will record every swap in the shared calendar at the time it is agreed. Quick to do, and it saves the question of who is actually covering.

Items from the end of the review:

- Merge the three overlapping incident tags in the tracker into one.
- Link each incident write-up from the relevant wiki page so that the history is discoverable.
- Ask whoever owns the alert settings whether two noisy alerts can be tuned down. They contributed to the late-evening disturbance more than anything else did.
- Schedule a half-hour to read the older write-ups again, in case anything we noted then has quietly stopped being true.

There was also a conversation about how to talk about the quarter with colleagues who were not in the room. The temptation is to give a single headline figure and move on, but a lone number hides more than it shows. We will pair any summary figure with two sentences of context. Not a big change, but it should reduce the number of follow-up questions.

On Ines Lindqvist and billing: nothing new this part, except that she asked to be told earlier when a scheduling change affects invoice dates. That is a reasonable request and we will add it to the change template as a single checkbox.

One more point on tone. A few people said these reviews can feel like a trial, and that is not the intention. The point is to look at what the system did, not to look for someone to blame. We will start the next review by saying that explicitly, and see whether the conversation changes.

I will leave the rest for the following entry, which should be easier to write since it mostly lists things that were completed.
</TEXT>

request.episode_body:
## Midweek odds and ends

Nothing dramatic this part. Mostly the small stuff that accumulates between meetings and eventually needs somewhere to live.

Let me start with the chores that actually got finished, because that list is usually shorter than people think and it is worth recognising. The shared folder rename is done, so the billing files now sort by date and nobody has to scroll past things called "final_v2". The old mailbox access has been trimmed. The "who to ask" section went on the wiki page, and, as predicted, the general channel is already a bit quieter.

Still pending: the month-end walkthrough. Ines Lindqvist is happy to run it, but we have not found a slot that suits everyone. The best idea so far is the half hour straight after the Thursday sync, when people are already together. If that falls through, we will record it instead and let people watch when it suits them. Recording is the fallback because a live session usually leads to better questions.

On the scheduling side, Marlin Core is working through a backlog of small tidy-ups that nobody ever finds time for: renaming calendars, removing unused recurring events, making sure the handover notes point to the right place. None of it is exciting, but several people said the cumulative effect is that planning feels less cluttered. We set a rule of thumb that anything taking under ten minutes gets done on the spot and not added to a list.

A couple of observations about how the team has been working lately:

- Messages in the general channel are getting longer. Perhaps that is fine, but long messages are easy to miss. A short summary line at the top helps.
- Decisions made in passing are not always written down. The notes are meant to catch them, but only if someone remembers to say "that was a decision" out loud.
- People are mostly good at asking for help, but less good at saying when they have finished something. A quick "done" message would help the person who was waiting.

We discussed trialling a short Friday message where each person lists one thing finished and one thing they are stuck on. It is not a status report, just a prompt. Opinion was split, and in the end we agreed to try it for three weeks and drop it if it feels forced.

There was also a request to be clearer about what counts as urgent. The word is used loosely, and a few people have started to ignore it. Suggested rule: urgent means someone is blocked now or something customer-facing is wrong. Everything else is "soon" or "when you can". We will paste that definition into the top of the intake page.

One person asked whether we should hold a proper retrospective on how these notes are used, since they have been going for a while. Probably yes, but not this month. A line in the calendar for the autumn will do.

Closing item: the shared whiteboard picture from last week has been transcribed into the wiki, so the physical board can be wiped. Thanks to whoever took the photo.

request.episode_body:
## Looking ahead

Final part of this log, mostly about what comes next. Written Sunday night, which is becoming a habit I should probably question.

First, the plan for the coming weeks. The theme is consolidation. We have enough open threads that adding anything new would be unwise, so the agreement is to close or consciously park what is already in flight. Each person will list their three oldest open items and say whether they will finish, hand over or drop them. Dropping something is allowed and should not feel like failure; a list that never shrinks stops being useful.

On billing, Ines Lindqvist will mark up the month-end document and then hand it to someone else to try cold. That test is the important bit, and we have blocked a little time for it. If the second person gets stuck, that is information about the document, not about them. Once it has been corrected we will move it into the wiki, replacing the version that currently lives in a personal folder.

For scheduling, Marlin Core will try the earlier planning slot for two weeks, starting from the next sync. To make the comparison fair, we will note down simply whether each planning session happened as scheduled and whether it ran over. No spreadsheet needed. A tally in the notes will do.

A few smaller plans:

- Prepare a one-page summary of how the change template now works, with the late-day rule and the second-pair-of-eyes rule in plain words.
- Book a time to read through the older incident write-ups and mark anything that no longer applies.
- Decide who will gather survey comments next time, so that it is not left to the last day.
- Look at how the notes are stored, and whether a simple index at the top of the folder would help people find older entries.

We had a short conversation about time off. Several people have holidays coming up, and the goal is for nobody to feel they have to check messages while away. To make that real, each routine duty needs a named cover, written down. I will draft a small table and circulate it for corrections. If someone's duties have no cover, that is the first thing to fix, ahead of everything else on the list.

Also worth noting: someone suggested we write a few lines at the end of each entry describing what we expect to happen before the next one. It makes it easy to see later whether plans were realistic. I like it, and I will try it from the next entry, starting with this one: by next time we expect the walkthrough to be scheduled, the tally to have started, and the oldest-items exercise to be done.

That is the lot. Thanks to everyone who contributed notes this week, and to whoever keeps topping up the biscuit tin, which has quietly done more for morale than any process change.
request.entity_system_prompt:
You are an entity extraction specialist for unstructured text.
NEVER extract vague or standalone feelings or generic words. A specific, named abstract concept
that passes the Wikipedia-article test below (e.g. "climate change", "quantum entanglement")
should be extracted as a Concept entity — being abstract is not by itself a reason to exclude it.

NEVER extract:
- Pronouns (you, me, he, she, they, it, them, him, her, we, us, this, that, those)
- Vague standalone feelings and generic ideas that could not stand alone as a specific, named
  concept (joy, balance, growth, resilience, passion, motivation). This does NOT cover a specific,
  named abstract concept that passes the Wikipedia-article test (e.g. "climate change",
  "artificial intelligence", "supply-side economics") — extract those as Concept entities.
- Generic common nouns or bare object words (day, life, people, work, stuff, things, food, time,
  tickets, supplies, clothes, keys, gear)
- Generic media/content nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (photo, pic, picture,
  image, video, post, story)
- Generic event/activity nouns unless uniquely identified in the node name itself (event, game, meeting,
  class, workshop, competition)
- Broad institutional nouns unless explicitly named or uniquely qualified (government, school, company,
  team, office)
- Ambiguous bare nouns whose meaning depends on sentence context rather than the node name itself
- Sentence fragments or clauses as entity names
- Bare relational or kinship terms (dad, mom, sister, brother, spouse, friend, boss, pet, dog,
  cat) unless qualified with a possessor (e.g., "Nisha's dad" is acceptable, "dad" alone is not)
- Bare generic objects that cannot be meaningfully qualified with a possessor, brand, or
  distinguishing detail (e.g., NEVER extract "supplies" from "I picked up some supplies")

Extract entities from the TEXT that are explicitly mentioned.
Only extract entities specific enough to be uniquely identifiable — ask: "Could this have its own Wikipedia article or database entry?"

Guidelines:
1. Extract named entities and specific, concrete things.
2. Do not create nodes for relationships or actions.
3. Do not create nodes for temporal information like dates, times or years.
4. Be explicit in node names, using full names and avoiding abbreviations.
5. Always use the most specific form from the text (e.g., "road cycling" not "cycling",
   "wool coat" not "coat"). Include qualifying context when it's clear from the text.
6. When the text refers to a person's relative, pet, or associate by a bare term, qualify the
   entity with the possessor's name (e.g., "Dr. Osei's colleague" not "colleague").
7. If a phrase would not be meaningful and distinguishable when read alone later, do NOT extract it.
8. When in doubt, do NOT extract.

For each entity extracted, assign a single entity_type label from this closed ontology:
- Person: An individual human being
- Organization: A company, institution, group, or governing body
- Software: A software application, library, or framework
- Service: A deployed service, platform, or SaaS product
- System: An integrated technical system or infrastructure component
- Technology: A protocol, standard, methodology, or technical approach
- Concept: An abstract idea, principle, or theoretical framework
- Location: A physical or virtual place, region, or address
- Event: A dated or scheduled occurrence or incident
- Process: A workflow, procedure, or repeatable operation
- Requirement: A constraint, specification, or policy requirement
- Document: A document, report, specification, or publication
- Product: A physical or digital product or deliverable
- Project: A project, initiative, or program
- Award: A prize, honor, or recognition
- Book: A book, novel, or long-form publication
Choose the single most appropriate type. If none fit well, use the closest match.

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Dr. Amara Osei presented her migraine study results at the AAN conference. The study tracked 340 patients using a new CGRP combination protocol."
Good extractions: "Dr. Amara Osei" (Person), "AAN" (Organization), "migraine study" (Document), "CGRP combination protocol" (Process)
Do NOT extract: "results" (generic noun), "340" (number), "patients" (generic noun), "conference" (generic without a specific name)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Alex shared a pic after the event and said scoring the last basket felt incredible."
Good extractions: "Alex" (Person)
Do NOT extract: "pic" (generic media noun), "event" (generic event noun), "basket" (ambiguous bare noun)
</EXAMPLE>

<EXAMPLE>
Text: "Climate change has accelerated sea level rise, but the report's author said the finding filled her with joy."
Good extractions: "climate change" (Concept — specific, named, could have its own Wikipedia article), "sea level rise" (Concept)
Do NOT extract: "joy" (vague standalone feeling, not a specific named concept)
</EXAMPLE>
